Clang Tracer Guide

Install the tracer, capture a C++ call, and build reusable probes and analysis workflows.

Clang Tracer user guide

Clang Tracer attaches to a running Linux x86-64 C++ process. A session identifies an attachment and a probe runs a C++ observer when a selected function is called. PRE runs before the original call and POST runs after a normal return. The injected agent sends events to the server, where clients can stream, retain, or record them.

Interface Use it for
clang-tracer-repl Explore a local process, prepare and install probes, record and analyze events in C++.
clang-tracer Run one tracing operation at a time in a shell or script.
clang-tracer-module Index and inspect compiled ELF files and their debug information from the shell.

Start with the first probe below, then use the tutorials, advanced guide, command appendix, and C++ API appendix.

Install and check the tools

On the c++17 branch, the native Linux x86-64 backend builds as C++20 and the native REPL builds as C++17. Use matching LLVM/Clang 21 or 22 development libraries, CMake, Protobuf, gRPC and SQLite development packages. The injected agent needs compatible runtime libraries on the target machine. Build the target with debug info, preserve its ELF or separate debug files, and use a compiler and ABI supported by the agent. The tracer must have permission to attach to the target under the host's Linux tracing policy.

From the repository root, configure, build and install into a user-owned prefix. Replace the toolchain path with the matching LLVM/Clang installation.

bash
./build-rhel.sh --toolchain-root /opt/llvm-21 --build-dir build-rhel \
  --prefix "$HOME/.local/clang-tracer" --examples
./deploy-rhel.sh --build-dir build-rhel
export PATH="$HOME/.local/clang-tracer/bin:$PATH"
clang-tracer-server --help
clang-tracer-repl --help
clang-tracer-module --help

For a split LLVM installation, CMake options, staging, tarball and RPM packaging, see Build and deploy on RHEL-compatible Linux. For GCC 8.5 SDK targets, use the SDK compatibility build. If you already have the native package, put its binary directory on PATH and run the help commands. The server finds its matching installed agent automatically. The native REPL starts and owns a private server unless you specify an endpoint.

Open the interactive guide

Open the HTML guide directly in a browser. It includes a collapsible navigation sidebar, section filtering, and copy buttons. For HTTP access, run the launcher with Python 3.8 or newer. It defaults to 127.0.0.1:8000 and accepts any bind address available on the host, including IPv6. It serves the documentation directory only.

bash
# From a source checkout
./docs/guide/serve.sh --bind 127.0.0.1 --port 8000
# From a default runtime installation
/usr/local/share/doc/clang_tracer/docs/guide/serve.sh --bind 0.0.0.0 --port 8080

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000/ for the first command. For a wildcard bind, use the host's actual IP address or hostname in the browser. Ctrl+C stops the guide server.

Create a target and a basic probe

Work in a scratch directory that both terminals can access. Save this as target.cpp. The target prints its PID and waits for Enter so you control when the probe fires. When the SDK headers expose PR_SET_PTRACER, the demo requests permission for a tracer in the second terminal.

cpp
#include <cstdio>
#include <poll.h>
#include <sys/prctl.h>
#include <unistd.h>

__attribute__((noinline)) int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }

int main() {
#ifdef PR_SET_PTRACER
  if (prctl(PR_SET_PTRACER, PR_SET_PTRACER_ANY, 0, 0, 0) == -1) {
    perror("PR_SET_PTRACER");
    return 1;
  }
#endif
  std::printf("PID %ld | press Enter to call add, Ctrl+C to exit\n",
              static_cast<long>(getpid()));
  std::fflush(stdout);

  pollfd input{STDIN_FILENO, POLLIN, 0};
  while (true) {
    // Check stdin without blocking in a read while the tracer attaches.
    if (poll(&input, 1, 0) > 0) {
      char byte;
      if (read(STDIN_FILENO, &byte, 1) != 1) break;
      if (byte == '\n') {
        std::printf("add(20, 22) = %d\n", add(20, 22));
        std::fflush(stdout);
      }
    }
    usleep(20'000);
  }
}

Save the observer as hook.cpp. Specialize Interceptor<int(int, int)> to match the return and parameter types of add. Clang Tracer supplies the primary template and Call, so the callback can read typed arguments and results directly.

cpp
template <>
class Interceptor<int(int, int)> {
public:
  void pre(const Call& call) {
    call.field("left", call.argument<0>());
    call.field("right", call.argument<1>());
  }

  void post(const Call& call) {
    call.field("sum", call.result());
  }
};

Start the target in terminal one with debug information and a predictable function entry. Keep the target running throughout the session.

bash
c++ -g -O0 -fno-omit-frame-pointer -fno-pie -no-pie -Wl,--build-id target.cpp -o target
./target

In terminal two, run clang-tracer-repl from the same directory. Replace 12345 with the printed PID. You can also use %attach without a PID to open the process picker.

bash
%attach 12345
%symbols --filter "add("
%probe resolve "add(int, int)"
%probe validate "add(int, int)" --callback hook.cpp
%probe inject "add(int, int)" --callback hook.cpp --print-arguments --print-result
%collect --name "add(int, int)" --count 2 --timeout 30 --as first

Press Enter once in terminal one while %collect is waiting. The target prints 42; the retained events include the arguments and the sum. You can inspect the pair and read the result as a C++ value.

bash
%events list first
%events show first --index 1
%events calls first
cpp
auto first_call = tracer.batch("first");
first_call.at(1).result_as<int>()
bash
%detach
%quit

Stop the target with Ctrl+C. If discovery is empty, confirm the attached PID, use %modules to confirm the binary, and check that it still has its debug information. If attachment is refused, confirm the target is yours, its tracing policy permits the attachment, and no debugger already owns it.

Index debug information and prepare a probe from a binary

A module index is a SQLite file built from a Linux x86-64 executable or shared library and its matching DWARF debug information. Use it to inspect signatures, ELF symbols, and known type layouts before attaching to a process. You can also prepare a probe from the index with just the matching ELF and your callback.

Build and browse the index

Use target and hook.cpp from the first probe. Start a fresh native REPL in that directory. These commands work without a target attachment.

bash
%module index --file ./target --output target.sqlite
%module types --filter int
%module symbols --filter "add*"
%module show --symbol "add(int, int)"
%module show --type int

The symbol details include the linkage name, ELF address, return type and parameters when available. The type details report size and, for records, known fields and their offsets. Use the full signature or copy an ID from a listing when a name is ambiguous. Use --exported on %module symbols when you want only dynamic exports, such as the exported functions of a shared library. Regular functions in the first-probe executable can be indexed even when they are absent from that export list.

Omit --output to write <ELF>.tracer.sqlite. Choose a new filename when rebuilding an index. The REPL selects the index after creating it. In a new REPL, use %module use target.sqlite to select it again, or pass --index target.sqlite on an individual query.

When DWARF lives in a separate file, let the indexer find a matching debug companion or pass --debug-file FILE. For example, create a separate-debug copy of the lab binary and index that copy.

bash
cp target target-split
objcopy --only-keep-debug target-split target-split.debug
objcopy --strip-debug --add-gnu-debuglink=target-split.debug target-split
clang-tracer-module index --file ./target-split --debug-file ./target-split.debug --output target-split.sqlite
clang-tracer-module info --index target-split.sqlite

If you already have a local target attached to the REPL's own server, you can index a loaded image using %modules --details. Copy the exact path and mapping token from its output. The mapped ELF must have a build ID. If the output says build_id=unavailable, use file indexing instead.

bash
%module index --module /absolute/path/to/target --mapping TOKEN --output live-target.sqlite

An ELF without usable DWARF can still provide symbols, including exports, but preparation needs a supported signature and sufficient type information. Split DWARF units are reported as unresolved. If you see debug_file_mismatch, use the debug file from the same build.

Generate declarations and install the indexed probe

Back in the REPL, select the original index. Emitting headers is optional. It writes declarations.hpp, views.hpp for supported read-only field access, and manifest.json. The final command below prepares a package using the generated files and verifies them against the selected index entry.

bash
%module use target.sqlite
%module emit --symbol "add(int, int)" --output recovered-add
%probe prepare "add(int, int)" --module-index target.sqlite --module ./target --generated recovered-add --output prepared-add

Leave out --generated to let the preparer generate the same declarations internally. The package binds to the indexed ELF build and embeds the declarations it needs. Keep the package with your callback and use the same binary for the live step. If the application is rebuilt, index the new ELF and prepare a new package.

Run ./target in another terminal. Replace 12345 with its printed PID and use the same hook.cpp from the first lab.

bash
%attach 12345
%probe validate "add(int, int)" --callback hook.cpp --prepared prepared-add --prepared-mode require
%probe inject "add(int, int)" --callback hook.cpp --prepared prepared-add --prepared-mode require --print-result
%collect --name "add(int, int)" --count 2 --timeout 30 --as indexed
%events list indexed
%detach

Confirm that validation reports prepared_used: true. Press Enter in the target terminal while the capture waits. The POST event reports sum=42. The index and debug companion are needed to recover metadata. A completed prepared package can be reused for injection without either file.

See module index commands for all options, the native REPL walkthrough for a callback that reads recovered record fields, and the native C++ module API for a programmatic workflow inside the REPL or a C++ application.

Trace changes to C++ objects

Use a native REPL method watch to compare a live receiver before and after a call in a prebuilt executable. Select private members, strings, nested records, or containers with --field. Pair vector elements by a stable ID and map entries by key using --key, then inspect the typed changes from the SQLite recording. Individual write watches identify the actual store instruction for supported typed fields inside a selected vector element, ordered or unordered map entry, or pointee. See the native REPL object watch walkthrough.

Clang Tracer tutorials

Start with the first probe. The labs below use that target and callback unless stated otherwise. Start a fresh REPL for each live lab or remove the previous probe before installing another on the same function. Replace example IDs, addresses, and tokens with the values shown by your session. Create recordings and manifests in a scratch directory.

Inspect a process and a function entry

Attach to the running target, list its threads and modules, and find a verified function address. Paginated symbol listings use the next-page token with the same filter and page size.

bash
%attach 12345
%threads
%modules --details
%symbols --filter "add(" --addresses --limit 20
%memory maps
%probe entry "add(int, int)" --mapping MEMORY_TOKEN
%memory read ENTRY_ADDRESS --mapping MEMORY_TOKEN --count 16

Use the runtime address from the entry preview. Copy the first two bytes from the hex dump into the scan pattern, replacing the second byte with ?? to match any byte.

bash
%memory scan ENTRY_ADDRESS --mapping MEMORY_TOKEN --count 16 --pattern "55 ??" --limit 4

The scan matches 55 ?? only when the first byte is 55. Change it to the first byte you observed. If a token expires after a mapping change, take a new snapshot. Use the module mapping token from %modules --details to reverse-lookup the entry PC with %symbols --address ENTRY_ADDRESS --mapping MODULE_TOKEN.

Edit, validate, reload, and restore

Load the first lab's observer as a draft. Edit it in the REPL if desired, entering a complete replacement and ending with .end. Upload the validated draft.

bash
%interceptor load hook.cpp --as demo
%interceptor show demo
%interceptor validate demo --target "add(int, int)"
%interceptor upload demo --target "add(int, int)" --print-result
%probes

Save a separate updated.cpp with the field name changed from sum to new_sum. Replace PROBE_ID with the ID shown by %probes, then reload it and capture another call.

bash
%probe reload PROBE_ID --callback updated.cpp
%collect --count 2 --timeout 30 --as updated
%events show updated --index 1
%probes

The POST event now includes new_sum; the target still returns 42. Remove the active probe ID shown by %probes and detach.

Trace a function template instantiation

Save this function in echo.hpp and add #include "echo.hpp" to the first lab's target.cpp. Inside the existing newline branch, add std::printf("echo<int>(42) = %d\n", echo<int>(42)); before the flush. Rebuild and restart the target. Use the compilation database setup with the compiler used to build the target.

cpp
template <class T>
__attribute__((noinline)) T echo(T value) {
  volatile T saved = value;
  return saved;
}

Save this observer as echo-hook.cpp. tracer::ResolvedSignature lets the same callback source specialize against the type of the selected instantiation. For echo<int>, writing Interceptor<int(int)> explicitly would select the same signature.

cpp
template <>
class Interceptor<tracer::ResolvedSignature> {
public:
  void pre(const Call& call) {
    call.field("input", call.argument<0>());
  }

  void post(const Call& call) {
    call.field("output", call.result());
  }
};

Start a fresh REPL and attach using the new PID. Quote the complete selector, including the concrete template arguments and function parameters. Build a prepared package from echo.hpp to supply the concrete signature on this branch.

bash
%attach 12345
%symbols --filter "echo<"
%probe prepare "echo<int>(int)" --include echo.hpp --translation-unit target.cpp --module ./target --output prepared-echo
%probe validate "echo<int>(int)" --callback echo-hook.cpp --prepared prepared-echo --prepared-mode require
%probe inject "echo<int>(int)" --callback echo-hook.cpp --prepared prepared-echo --prepared-mode require --print-result
%collect --name "echo<int>(int)" --count 2 --timeout 30 --as echo_call
%events list echo_call

Press Enter in the target terminal while capture waits. The events show input=42 in PRE and output=42 in POST. Detach before exiting. For a member template, use the complete selector for the concrete method, including its class, template arguments, parameter list, and qualifiers.

Preview and apply bulk tracing

Preview an exact selector, save the selection as a reusable manifest, then install it as a batch. Use repeated include or exclude patterns to broaden or narrow the selection on a larger target.

bash
%trace preview --exact "add(int, int)" --save trace.textproto
%trace apply --manifest trace.textproto --callback hook.cpp
%collect --count 2 --timeout 30 --as bulk
%events stats bulk
%trace remove BATCH_ID

Trigger a call during collection. The summary should show one PRE/POST pair. To see a caller edge, have the callback call capture_stack(8, false) in PRE before applying the batch. The manifest can be previewed against another session using %trace preview --manifest trace.textproto.

Capture and inspect complete native stacks

bash
%probe inject "add(int, int)" --callback hook.cpp --stack-depth full --stack-application-only false --print-result
%collect --count 2 --timeout 30 --as fullstack
%events stack fullstack --index 0
%events stats fullstack

Trigger one call. The stack shows the entry and available caller frames, with native PC, function/module, and source location where recovered. Both phases describe the entry stack. full follows the supported unwind chain and can report a partial unwind. If a deep stack exceeds shared transport capacity, raise the managed server's --context-event-bytes and, if needed, --context-transport-memory-bytes before starting a new session. See the stack lab sources for application-only filtering and callback-side symbolization.

Capture in the background and query in C++

Use the probe with --print-result from the stack lab. Start a background range, which returns immediately, then iterate it. Iteration waits for events and yields each one as the agent streams it, so trigger the two target calls while the loop runs. The predicate and transformation run in the REPL.

cpp
using namespace tracer_repl;
auto range = tracer.events_async(session, 4, 60);
cpp
auto sums = range
    | filter([](const Event& event) { return event.phase() == "POST"; })
    | transform([](const Event& event) { return event.result_as<int>(); });
for (auto value : sums) std::cout << value << '\n';
range.stop();

Each 42 prints as its call returns. The loop ends after the four requested events, at the 60-second timeout, on range.stop(), or on Ctrl+C, which leaves the collector running. range.snapshot() returns the events retained so far without waiting. Try first() to get the first optional match, take(1) to limit iteration, or enumerate() to pair each retained event with an index. %cpp load analysis.cpp can run an analysis script and %cpp reset resets only the interpreter and its capture handles. See event ranges and adaptors for further examples.

Record and replay offline

Keep the probe with --print-result active. For each recording command, trigger one new call while it waits, or read available history starting from the requested cursor. Use --after with the previous recording's last sequence to start a fresh window.

bash
%record calls.pb --count 2 --timeout 30
%record calls.db --sqlite --count 2 --timeout 30
%detach
%quit

Start a fresh REPL and load the recordings. Offline startup can still launch a private server, but replay requires no target attachment.

bash
%events open calls.pb --as framed
%events open calls.db --as saved
%events calls saved
%events export saved --format json --output calls.json

Use a typed query for POST events and read the recorded result.

cpp
tracer_repl::EventQuery query;
query.names = {"add(int, int)"};
query.phase = "POST";
auto recorded = tracer.replay("calls.db", query);
recorded.at(0).result_as<int>()

Expect 42. In a live CLI session, use clang-tracer events PID --sqlite copy.db --count 2 to copy events without consuming server history, or clang-tracer drain PID --sqlite consumed.db to persist and acknowledge the retained snapshot. See storage and recovery for loss counters, deduplication and failure behavior.

Prepare a reusable probe

Move the declaration of the first lab's add to add.hpp, include it from target.cpp, and keep the function definition in target.cpp. If your build does not produce a database, create this example compile_commands.json in the scratch directory. Replace the directory and compiler path with those of your target.

json
[
  {
    "directory": "/absolute/path/to/demo",
    "file": "target.cpp",
    "arguments": ["/usr/bin/c++", "-g", "-O0", "-fno-pie", "-c", "target.cpp"]
  }
]

Rebuild and restart the target. Generate a package with a new output directory and explicit source entry.

bash
%probe prepare "add(int, int)" --include add.hpp --translation-unit target.cpp --module ./target --output prepared
%attach 12345
%probe validate "add(int, int)" --callback hook.cpp --prepared prepared --prepared-mode require
%probe inject "add(int, int)" --callback hook.cpp --prepared prepared --prepared-mode require --print-result
%collect --count 2 --timeout 30 --as prepared_call
%events show prepared_call --index 1

Trigger one call and check for 42. require verifies that injection uses the package. Multiple --include options can bring in callback payload declarations. --cwd runs the probe command relative to another project directory, and --extra-arg passes supplemental compiler flags. Use the offline preparer from the command reference for the equivalent shell workflow. Run the prepared method lab to capture a receiver and replay a custom typed event.

Decode objects, containers, and method receivers

Run the installed typed-values example. It starts a debug target and checks record, scalar, string, sequence, and associative-container decoding. The native runtime and Development example sources must be present. Substitute the install prefix and data directory if customized.

bash
cd /usr/local/share/clang-tracer/examples/native-repl-values
./run.sh all

To map your own public record, set the local interpreter's compilation options before its first C++ input. Load the mapping and open the collection with the matching argument snapshot.

bash
%cpp options compdb build/compile_commands.json --file src/target.cpp
%cpp generate model.hpp --type app::Order --output mappings.hpp
%cpp load mappings.hpp
cpp
auto sample = tracer.batch("orders").at(0);
auto order = sample.argument_as<app::Order>(0);

Alternatively %cpp import model.hpp --type app::Order generates, caches, and loads a mapping in one step. Automatic mapping requires supported public members and an accessible default constructor. Use EventCodec<T> for construction through a factory, or argument_snapshot(0).field("id") to inspect fields without a mapping. For a method receiver, inspect receiver_snapshot() in the client and use call.self() in the agent. The typed C++ argument example covers references, pointers, headerless DWARF recovery, and opt-in application headers.

Observe shared context and thread propagation

Run the shared-context example from a configured source checkout with examples enabled. Start the server and target, then install the same observer on the outer and worker functions.

bash
cmake --build build-rhel --target shared-context-target
export CLANG_TRACER_ENDPOINT=127.0.0.1:50051
clang-tracer-server --listen "$CLANG_TRACER_ENDPOINT" > server.log 2>&1 &
server_pid=$!
./build-rhel/shared-context-target > target.log 2>&1 &
target_pid=$!
# Wait for clang-tracer list to succeed before attaching.
clang-tracer attach "$target_pid"
callback="$PWD/examples/shared-context/interceptor.cpp"
clang-tracer trace "$target_pid" 'process_request(int)' --callback "$callback" --callback-print-arguments true
clang-tracer trace "$target_pid" 'calculate_total(int)' --callback "$callback" --callback-print-arguments true
clang-tracer events "$target_pid" --context-field request_id,calls,last_result --count 24 --timeout 20
clang-tracer detach "$target_pid"
kill "$target_pid" "$server_pid"
unset CLANG_TRACER_ENDPOINT

Look for request.step events sharing the same request ID. The worker inherits context through supported pthread_create propagation and reports twice the request ID. The outer call reports the worker result plus one. For an explicit scope or a durable producer/collector journal, follow Shared context.

Collect every call of one request

A service handles a request by calling several functions, and concurrent requests interleave their calls. This lab installs one probe per function, connects the probes through one shared state, and publishes a single event per request that lists every call the request made. The files are in lesson 15.

Save the service as target.cpp. handle_checkout is one request; each Enter serves two requests on two threads at once.

cpp
// A small checkout service: every request runs the same four steps.
// Ordinary application code with no dependency on the tracer.
#include <cstdio>
#include <poll.h>
#include <sys/prctl.h>
#include <thread>
#include <unistd.h>

// The pauses make the two requests of a round overlap.
__attribute__((noinline)) int authenticate(int user) {
  usleep(30'000);
  return user % 2; // 1 = accepted
}

__attribute__((noinline)) int price_item(int sku, int quantity) {
  usleep(30'000);
  return sku / 10 * quantity;
}

__attribute__((noinline)) int charge_card(int user, int amount) {
  usleep(30'000);
  return amount > 0 ? 9000 + user : -1; // receipt number
}

// One request. Everything it calls belongs to this request.
__attribute__((noinline)) int handle_checkout(int request, int user) {
  if (!authenticate(user))
    return -1;
  int total = price_item(120, 2) + price_item(350, 1);
  if (request % 2 == 0)
    total += price_item(990, 3);
  return charge_card(user, total);
}

int main() {
#ifdef PR_SET_PTRACER
  if (prctl(PR_SET_PTRACER, PR_SET_PTRACER_ANY, 0, 0, 0) == -1) {
    perror("PR_SET_PTRACER");
    return 1;
  }
#endif
  std::printf("PID %ld | press Enter to serve two overlapping requests, Ctrl+C to exit\n",
              static_cast<long>(getpid()));
  std::fflush(stdout);

  int request = 0;
  pollfd input{STDIN_FILENO, POLLIN, 0};
  while (true) {
    // Check stdin without blocking in a read while the tracer attaches.
    if (poll(&input, 1, 0) > 0) {
      char byte;
      if (read(STDIN_FILENO, &byte, 1) != 1) break;
      if (byte == '\n') {
        const int first = ++request, second = ++request;
        int receipts[2] = {0, 0};
        // Two clients at once: their calls interleave in time.
        std::thread a([&] { receipts[0] = handle_checkout(first, 41); });
        usleep(15'000);
        std::thread b([&] { receipts[1] = handle_checkout(second, 77); });
        a.join();
        b.join();
        std::printf("request %d -> receipt %d | request %d -> receipt %d\n",
                    first, receipts[0], second, receipts[1]);
        std::fflush(stdout);
      }
    }
    usleep(20'000);
  }
}
bash
c++ -g -O0 -fno-omit-frame-pointer -fno-pie -pthread -no-pie -Wl,--build-id target.cpp -o target
./target

Save the shared state as state.hpp. Every observer includes it, so all of them see the same RequestState type.

cpp
// The state every probe of this lesson shares. Each hook file includes it.
// The callback compiler supplies Call, State and shared_state.
#include <string>
#include <vector>

struct RequestScope {};

// One traced call made while serving a request.
struct Step {
  std::string function;
  int argument = 0; // sku for price_item, otherwise the user
  int result = 0;
};

// One object exists per request. The engine creates it when the outermost
// probed call starts and releases it when that call returns, so overlapping
// requests on different threads never see each other's steps.
struct RequestState : shared_state<RequestScope> {
  int request = 0;
  std::vector<Step> steps;
};

Save the request observer as request.cpp. It records the request number on entry and publishes the state when the request returns.

cpp
// Probe for handle_checkout(int, int): it opens the request and reports it.
#include "state.hpp"

struct Interceptor {
  // Asks the engine to create or reuse RequestState. Declaration only.
  Interceptor(State<RequestState>);

  // The outermost call of the request: the state is fresh here.
  void pre(const Call& call, RequestState& state) {
    state.request = call.arg<int>(0);
  }

  // By now the step probes have appended every call the request made.
  // Publish the whole list as one event.
  void post(const Call& call, RequestState&) {
    call.field("receipt", call.result<int>());
    call.context().event("request.completed");
  }
};

Save one step observer per called function. This is price_item.cpp; create authenticate.cpp and charge_card.cpp the same way, changing only the name in the string.

cpp
// Probe for price_item: appends this call to the request it runs in.
#include "state.hpp"

struct Interceptor {
  Interceptor(State<RequestState>);

  void post(const Call& call, RequestState& state) {
    state.steps.push_back({"price_item", call.arg<int>(0), call.result<int>()});
  }
};

Start the REPL in the same directory and install the four probes. Press Enter once in the target terminal while %collect waits.

bash
%attach 12345
%probe inject "handle_checkout(int, int)" --callback request.cpp --print-arguments --print-result
%probe inject "authenticate(int)" --callback authenticate.cpp
%probe inject "price_item(int, int)" --callback price_item.cpp
%probe inject "charge_card(int, int)" --callback charge_card.cpp
%collect --name request.completed --count 2 --timeout 30 --as requests
%events list requests

The collection holds two POST events of handle_checkout, one per request. Print the steps each one carries. The lesson has this loop as report.cpp for %cpp load report.cpp.

cpp
for (const auto& event : tracer.batch("requests")) {
  auto state = event.state_snapshot();
  std::cout << "request " << state.field("request").as<int>() << ':';
  for (const auto& step : state.field("steps").elements())
    std::cout << ' ' << step.field("function").as<std::string>() << '('
              << step.field("argument").as<int>() << ")="
              << step.field("result").as<int>();
  std::cout << '\n';
}
text
request 1: authenticate(41)=1 price_item(120)=24 price_item(350)=35 charge_card(41)=9041
request 2: authenticate(77)=1 price_item(120)=24 price_item(350)=35 price_item(990)=297 charge_card(77)=9077

All four observers declare Interceptor(State<RequestState>), and RequestState derives from shared_state<RequestScope>, so probes that run inside the same request receive the same object. The state starts with the outermost probed call, here handle_checkout, and ends when that call returns, which keeps the two overlapping requests apart. Only request.cpp publishes an event, and %collect --name selects it, so you receive one event per request instead of one per call. %events show requests --index 0 prints the same state as a decoded state RequestState line without any C++. Finish with %detach. Shared context describes the state API.

Trace from the native CLI

Use the first-probe target. Start a server in a separate terminal.

bash
clang-tracer-server --listen 127.0.0.1:50051

In the client terminal, set PID to the PID printed by the target and use the same loopback endpoint. Save this entry-only observer as legacy.cpp. nm ./target can confirm the linkage name for the example build.

cpp
extern "C" long long trace_callback(const TraceContext& context) {
  context.log("legacy add entry");
  return context.arguments[0].signed_value + context.arguments[1].signed_value;
}
bash
export CLANG_TRACER_ENDPOINT=127.0.0.1:50051
clang-tracer attach "$PID"
clang-tracer trace "$PID" --function _Z3addii --return int32 \
  --arg int32 --arg int32 --callback legacy.cpp
clang-tracer events "$PID" --count 1 --timeout 30
clang-tracer detach "$PID"

Expect one entry event with callback value 42. To see the diagnostic, start the target with CLANG_TRACER_AGENT_LOG="$PWD/agent.log" ./target before attaching. Stop the server and target when finished.

Run the installed end-to-end JIT demo

The runtime ships the JIT example target when the REPL is enabled. Install the Development component for the runner and source files. Run the demo from the installed example directory.

bash
cd /usr/local/share/clang-tracer/examples/native-repl-jit
./run.sh
./run.sh --interactive

The first run performs bulk trace setup, capture, SQLite recording, and offline C++ analysis. It reports JIT_EXAMPLE_PASSED=3. The interactive run lets you explore mapping inspection, function entry previews and observer reload. See the example walkthrough.

Lesson 16: follow polymorphic items through two probes

Build and start the lesson 16 project on Linux. Use the compiler and standard library from the tracer's build profile. For a GCC 8.5 SDK tracer, pass the SDK's clang++ as make CXX=/path/to/sdk/bin/clang++ (and set its runtime search path if required by that SDK). Mixing system and SDK headers can leave only addresses with an unsupported standard-library diagnostic.

bash
cd examples/lessons/16-polymorphic-items
make
./target

Start clang-tracer-repl in a second terminal in the same directory and substitute the PID printed by the target. Prepare and inject the factory first:

bash
%attach PID
%probe prepare "ItemFactory::create(const std::string&) const" --include item_factory.hpp --translation-unit target.cpp --output prepared-create
%probe inject "ItemFactory::create(const std::string&) const" --prepared prepared-create --prepared-mode require --snapshot-return-pointee
%collect --name "ItemFactory::create(const std::string&) const" --phase POST --count 3 --timeout 30 --as items

Press Enter once while collecting. Run %cpp load report.cpp: expect ItemV1, ItemV2, and ItemV3 and their inherited fields and containers. Continue in the same REPL:

bash
%probe prepare "Item::encode(const std::string&) const" --include item_factory.hpp --translation-unit target.cpp --output prepared-encode
%probe inject "Item::encode(const std::string&) const" --prepared prepared-encode --prepared-mode require
%collect --name "Item::encode(const std::string&) const" --phase POST --count 3 --timeout 30 --as encoded

Press Enter once more. Expect the second injection to report reused imported types: rather than redefining the shared classes. Run %cpp load encoded.cpp. The factory result snapshot owns the returned item's fields. For encode, use the receiver snapshot to find impl_snapshot and use result_as<std::string>() for the encoded text. Finish with %detach and %quit. Try the explicit pointer policy next.

Lesson 17: trace writes without rebuilding the target

Use the prebuilt object-watch exercise. Build the fixture once, start it, and leave it running. In the REPL, prepare a plan with --field value --backend code-cache from its existing ELF, attach, and preview. Preview should report binding=same-build and a verified store site. Start the plan and record two object.trace events to SQLite. Enter g in the fixture while recording.

Replay in the REPL after stopping the watch and detaching:

bash
%events open object-writes.db --as saved
%events list saved
%events show saved --index 1
%events stack saved --index 1

Expect one creation and a write from 17 to 23. Check %object status WATCH_ID after stopping: the watch should be inactive with no restoration pending. Restart the fixture, use a fresh recording path, and add --no-values to start. Expect a FIELD_WRITTEN event without before or after samples. This distinction matters when a store writes back the same value. For logical container changes during a method, use the advanced method-watch lesson.

Lesson 18: stream and release a counted range

Use the first-probe target, attached with its add probe installed. In the REPL start a counted background range and iterate:

cpp
auto live = tracer.events_async(session, 4, 30);
for (const auto& e : live) std::cout << e.phase() << ' ' << e.sequence() << '\n';
auto retained = live.snapshot();

Press Enter once in the target while iteration waits. Expect PRE and POST immediately, with the REPL still waiting. Press Enter again to reach four events and return to the prompt. Check retained.complete and retained.size(). You can start another capture while holding live: the completed range only keeps storage for its retained events. Release range copies when done. If iteration ends early, inspect live.error() and the snapshot counters before assuming every call was captured.

Advanced capture and custom adapters

Start with the polymorphic items lesson. It uses automatic capture. Use the following controls when you need to select what is copied, change its shape, or interpret the saved data differently.

Goal Where the code runs Extension point
Select which pointers a prepared probe follows Preparation tool FollowPointers policy
Copy a smaller or redacted record from the target Target agent during the probe Custom snapshot encoder
Construct your own type from an existing event Client REPL, also offline EventCodec decoder
Report logical method changes and register any payloads Object-watch adapter in the target Method snapshots and AnyPayloads

Write a FollowPointers policy

In the lesson 16 project, write item-policy.hpp beside item_factory.hpp:

cpp
#pragma once
#include "item.hpp"

namespace tracer_snapshot {
template<class Record> struct FollowPointers;

template<> struct FollowPointers<Item> {
  static constexpr const char* fields[] = {"impl"};
};
}

Put the callable's declaration header first and repeat --include for the policy and any additional implementation definitions. From the attached lesson REPL, prepare a new package and inject it:

bash
%probe prepare "ItemFactory::create(const std::string&) const" --include item_factory.hpp --include item-policy.hpp --translation-unit target.cpp --output prepared-policy
%probe inject "ItemFactory::create(const std::string&) const" --prepared prepared-policy --prepared-mode require --snapshot-return-pointee
%collect --name "ItemFactory::create(const std::string&) const" --phase POST --count 3 --timeout 30 --as policy_items

Press Enter once in the target while collecting. Inspect the concrete implementation:

cpp
auto root = tracer.batch("policy_items").at(0).result_snapshot();
if (root.fields().count("impl_snapshot")) {
  std::cout << root.field("impl_snapshot").cpp_type() << '\n';
}

Expect ItemV1 for the first item. The record keeps impl as an address and adds impl_snapshot as an owned copy. The policy names direct raw pointer or reference members for that record, in arguments, receivers, and results. It replaces automatic selection for that record. The agent needs a compatible admitted layout and a live, stable pointee at capture time; null or unknown dynamic types can leave only an address. The outer pointer result requires --snapshot-return-pointee; an outer reference result already captures its referent.

For a comparison, prepare a separate package without the policy and with --no-automatic-members. Expect the address and no followed member. Read the followed-member limits before increasing capture depth, breadth, or byte budgets. A runtime limit cannot restore a member left out during preparation.

Write a target-side snapshot encoder

The custom PIMPL example contains the encoder source and REPL script. The prepared adapter declares the implementation type before compiling this callback. Add an overload for the concrete type you want to project:

cpp
namespace tracer_snapshot {
struct V2Projection {
  int summary;
};

V2Projection encode(const HFW::ItemV2& item) noexcept {
  return {static_cast<int>(item.generation) + 1000};
}
}

The encoder runs on the target thread. Return a supported record by value, keep the work bounded, and avoid reading storage whose lifetime or synchronization is uncertain. Pass the encoder as --callback at injection; the file can contain just the encoder. Other implementations keep automatic capture. The payload retains its original C++ type name even though its fields have changed, so do not decode it using an automatic layout that expects the old fields.

From the repository root on Linux, after a full build in build, run:

bash
./examples/prepared-injectors/run-native.sh --pimpl-custom --smoke

Expect NATIVE_PIMPL_CUSTOM=1. The check verifies a one-field projection with summary=1002 for HFW::ItemV2 and unchanged automatic fields for V1 and V3. Omit --smoke to get the commands at an interactive prompt.

Write a client-side decoder

After collecting the custom encoder events as captured (the interactive example does this), define a separate local type. Put this declaration in a C++ file and load it with %cpp load before the first typed conversion:

cpp
struct ItemSummary {
  int summary;
};

template<> struct tracer_repl::EventCodec<ItemSummary> {
  static ItemSummary decode(const tracer_repl::EventValue& root) {
    return {root.field("_imp_snapshot").field("summary").as<int>()};
  }
};

At the REPL, check the payload before using the decoder because the collection also contains other implementations:

cpp
for (const auto& e : tracer.batch("captured")) {
  if (e.result() == "0x0") continue;
  auto item = e.result_snapshot();
  if (item.fields().count("_imp_snapshot") &&
      item.field("_imp_snapshot").fields().count("summary")) {
    std::cout << e.result_as<ItemSummary>().summary << '\n';
  }
}

Expect 1002 for a projected item. The decoder can call a constructor or factory, rename fields, or explicitly handle older schemas. It runs on owned data, so the same decoder works on a compatible recording after the target exits. For a default-constructible record with assignable members, EventRecord is a simpler mapping. If decoding yields a Reconstructed<T>, use it for inspection: application constructors and destructors did not run, virtual dispatch is unavailable, and embedded pointers refer to local copies.

Watch logical state at method boundaries

A method watch compares receiver state at verified entry and return. It shows net changes; use a write watch for individual admitted stores. Work through the Portfolio method-watch commands for compilation database, plan creation, preview, recording, and replay.

For a direct std::any field, register specific types in the policy header given to %object prepare --policy. The snapshot test policy is a full example. For a Portfolio with a field called extension holding a demo::RiskState:

cpp
#include "portfolio.hpp"
#include <tuple>

namespace tracer_snapshot {
template<class Record> struct AnyPayloads;

template<> struct AnyPayloads<demo::Portfolio> {
  using extension = std::tuple<demo::RiskState>;
};
}

Select --field extension_snapshot to report the typed projection. Register only types the original compilation inputs define. An unregistered payload can appear as a coverage gap. For map or vector snapshots, --key PATH=MEMBER specifies a stable logical key so a reorder need not masquerade as a change. Use capture limits for large data and inspect gaps before interpreting absent changes.

Compare two recorded receiver samples

For a prepared method probe, enable independent return sampling and record both phases. This is useful when you already need the PRE and POST call events as well as the delta:

bash
%probe inject "demo::Portfolio::rebalance()" --prepared prepared-rebalance --prepared-mode require --snapshot-receiver-at-return
%record rebalance.db --sqlite --probe PROBE_ID --count 2 --timeout 20
%events open rebalance.db --as rebalance
%events diff rebalance --pre 0 --post 1 --key legs=id --key risk=key

Prepare prepared-rebalance with %probe prepare and the same header, policy as an extra include, translation unit and ELF used for the method watch. Invoke rebalance once during recording. Use the actual PRE and POST indexes if your recording has other events. The diff checks the invocation, receiver, and order before reporting deltas.

Choose the synchronization contract based on the target: thread-confined for a graph accessed by one thread, caller-lock if the caller protects the full graph through both samples, or stable-at-boundaries if the target ensures stable entry and return samples. The flag declares an existing guarantee; it does not lock application memory for you.

Command appendix

Choose a command for its syntax, behavior, and an example. Run percent commands in the native REPL. Replace uppercase placeholders with values from your run. Examples that change the target require a test process you control and the matching setup; follow the linked walkthroughs first. The syntax follows the C++17 REPL help. Use %help "events diff" for a multiword topic in the running REPL.

Command object

Example

Object-watch lesson and method snapshots.

Command object prepare

Save a reusable object definition and verified ELF bindings without attaching. Use --on METHOD, --include HEADER, and --synchronization for a typed method watch.

Usage

%object prepare TYPE --module ELF --field FIELD --code SELECTOR --output DIRECTORY

Example

%object prepare demo::PlanRecord --module ./build/repl-object-plan-target --field value --code "demo::write_value(demo::PlanRecord &)" --backend code-cache --output record-watch

Use a fresh plan directory for prepare. Preview and start accept a saved plan; method plans use --on METHOD --include HEADER --policy HEADER --synchronization MODE at preparation.

Object-watch lesson and method snapshots.

Command object preview

Resolve the plan against the selected process and check live code bytes without installing patches.

Usage

%object preview --plan DIRECTORY

Example

%object preview --plan record-watch

Use a fresh plan directory for prepare. Preview and start accept a saved plan; method plans use --on METHOD --include HEADER --policy HEADER --synchronization MODE at preparation.

Object-watch lesson and method snapshots.

Command object start

Start a native watch with matching DWARF. Ptrace is the diagnostic default. Code cache translates supported writers and lifecycle fragments. Repeat --code to select multiple writers for a standalone main-image field. Use --follow-calls to resolve callees at runtime from the selected scope, with --runtime-limit N to bound translations. Use --shared-file PATH to correlate shared storage across live processes. Use --pointee PATH with a verified --mutation to follow a DWARF-resolved pointer path. On AArch64, --rendezvous selects an existing single-threaded userspace checkpoint. On x86-64, use --module for a shared writer and --caller to verify an Image::get borrow followed by an indirect call. Use --writer-entry for all entries into an admitted standalone leaf. Use --vector with --element-key FIELD=UINT32 or --map with --map-key KEY to track collection storage generations. Select a verified --mutation SYMBOL and declare --synchronization for native collection capture. Use --owner-add, --owner-get, --owner-remove and --owner-snapshot to select ownership boundaries. Use --no-values to record every completed write and omit field samples. Record observations with %record FILE --sqlite --name object.trace.

Usage

%object start --type TYPE --field FIELD --code SELECTOR [--base BASE --owner OWNER --collection FIELD] [--snapshot-field FIELD] [--module MODULE] [--caller SELECTOR] [--rendezvous SYMBOL] [--backend ptrace|code-cache] [--no-values] [--stack-depth N] [--max-elements N] [--max-string-bytes N]

Example

%object start --plan record-watch --stack-depth 4

Use a fresh plan directory for prepare. Preview and start accept a saved plan; method plans use --on METHOD --include HEADER --policy HEADER --synchronization MODE at preparation.

Object-watch lesson and method snapshots.

Command probe entry

Verify and disassemble a function entry and show the copy-only detour window and bounded control flow.

Usage

%probe entry SELECTOR --mapping TOKEN [--module MODULE] [--cwd DIRECTORY]
  or %probe entry --module PATH --elf-address ADDRESS --abi linux-x86-64-sysv --mapping TOKEN [--cwd DIRECTORY]

Example

Probe options and prerequisites and advanced adapters.

Command probe prepare

Build a reusable probe package from source, an explicit signature, or the module index. Without headers or an explicit signature, preparation uses the default index. Repeat --include for extra headers. Preparation uses compile_commands.json in the command's working directory by default. It prefers the first include's recorded compile command and falls back to the first source beside it. Use --module to pin the package to a specific build. Prepared headers can declare tracer_snapshot::FollowPointers<Record> specializations listing direct raw pointer fields to follow; pointee types and polymorphic implementations are discovered from the included source inputs. This policy applies to prepared argument, receiver and result records. Use --snapshot-return-pointee when injecting a raw pointer-return probe. Use --metadata-only to skip the separate C++ adapter files. Pointer and reference members are followed automatically; --no-automatic-members follows none. Capture limits, each visible in the event when it cuts something: --follow-depth N (default 3, 0-40, prepare): levels of pointees followed below a captured record (0 follows none); --follow-members N (default 48, 0-unlimited, prepare): followed members per probe, policy-named ones first (about 160 bytes of wrapper stack each); --record-members N (default 32, 0-unlimited, prepare): automatically discovered pointer members per record; --nested-depth N (default 2, 0-unlimited, prepare): levels of by-value records and smart pointers searched for pointer members; --string-bytes N (default 4000, 0-65536, run time): bytes kept of one string in a followed member; bounded by the slice; --vector-elements N (default 4096, 0-unlimited, run time): elements of a vector in a followed member; a larger vector is not followed; --checked-reads N (default 256, 1-unlimited, run time): checked memory reads one followed member may spend (each is a system call); --snapshot-reserve N (default 8192, 0-unlimited, run time): bytes of the per-thread storage that members captured at entry leave for later roots; --snapshot-arena N (default 16384, 16384-unlimited, run time): per-thread storage for snapshots; only grows, the largest request of any probe wins; --snapshot-slice N (default 4096, 4096-65536, run time): bytes of one snapshot payload; only grows, the largest request of any probe wins; 'unlimited' selects the largest value (for --follow-depth, --string-bytes and --snapshot-slice that is a fixed maximum the tracer imposes), 'off' selects 0 where 0 is allowed. Prepare-time options shape the package; %probe inject accepts all of them and its value wins, but members that were not discovered at prepare time cannot be added. Each option is also read from the environment variable TRACER_PREPARE_<NAME> by the prepare tool; docs/native-repl.md lists them. With --signature, supply the C++ result and explicit parameter types, for example 'const int&()'. Qualified methods receive an opaque receiver. Pass --member for an unqualified instance method.

Usage

%probe prepare SELECTOR --include HEADER --output NEW_DIRECTORY
  [--compdb PATH] [--translation-unit FILE] [--module ELF] [--metadata-only] [--no-automatic-members] [--cwd DIRECTORY] [EXTRA COMPILER ARGUMENTS]
  [--follow-depth N] [--follow-members N] [--record-members N] [--nested-depth N]
  [--string-bytes N] [--vector-elements N] [--checked-reads N] [--snapshot-reserve N] [--snapshot-arena N] [--snapshot-slice N]
  or %probe prepare SELECTOR --signature TYPE --module ELF --output NEW_DIRECTORY [--member] [--metadata-only] [--cwd DIRECTORY]
  or %probe prepare SELECTOR [--module-index INDEX] [--module ELF] [--id ID] [--generated DIR] --output NEW_DIRECTORY

--cwd DIRECTORY sets the base for relative paths and shell expansions for this command. Server-side inputs must be available at the resulting paths on the server host.

Extra compiler arguments

--extra-arg ARG | --extra-args "-I dir -DNAME=1" | --extra-args `my-conf --cxxflags`

Repeat these options to add fallback include paths and new macro definitions. Compilation database settings take priority. Set startup defaults with --extra-arg=ARG or --extra-args "$(my-conf --cxxflags)".

Example

%probe prepare "add(int, int)" --include add.hpp --output prepared

Probe options and prerequisites and advanced adapters.

Command probe resolve

--cwd DIRECTORY sets the base for relative paths and shell expansions for this command. Server-side inputs must be available at the resulting paths on the server host.

Resolution options

--include SERVER_HEADER --compdb SERVER_PATH [--translation-unit SERVER_FILE]
--module TEXT --compile-option FLAG
--prepared DIRECTORY --prepared-mode off|prefer|require
[EXTRA COMPILER ARGUMENTS]

The default mode, prefer, uses an available prepared package and falls back to DWARF. With a typed prepared package, --compdb supplies include paths, forced includes and macros to the callback. Extra headers must coexist with the prepared declarations. Use --translation-unit to override the donor.

Command probe inject

Use --snapshot-receiver-at-return on a supported prepared method to sample the receiver independently at POST for %events diff. Omit --callback to capture events with the built-in observer. For prepared implementation member snapshots, a callback file can define tracer_snapshot::encode(const Implementation&) noexcept to return a custom record by value. Snapshot returned record pointees only when the live layout matches and the pointee remains stable through POST; result() gives its address and result_as<T>() copies the record.

Usage

%probe inject SELECTOR [--callback FILE] [RESOLUTION OPTIONS] [DEPLOYMENT OPTIONS] [--cwd DIRECTORY]
  [--allow-arg-overrides] [--allow-result-override] [--allow-replacement] [--allow-call-original] [--trace-exceptions] [--reclaimable] [--snapshot-return-pointee] [--backend auto|entry] [--caller SELECTOR]
  [--follow-depth N] [--follow-members N] [--record-members N] [--nested-depth N]
  [--string-bytes N] [--vector-elements N] [--checked-reads N] [--snapshot-reserve N] [--snapshot-arena N] [--snapshot-slice N]

--cwd DIRECTORY sets the base for relative paths and shell expansions for this command. Server-side inputs must be available at the resulting paths on the server host.

Resolution options

--include SERVER_HEADER --compdb SERVER_PATH [--translation-unit SERVER_FILE]
--module TEXT --compile-option FLAG
--prepared DIRECTORY --prepared-mode off|prefer|require
[EXTRA COMPILER ARGUMENTS]

The default mode, prefer, uses an available prepared package and falls back to DWARF. With a typed prepared package, --compdb supplies include paths, forced includes and macros to the callback. Extra headers must coexist with the prepared declarations. Use --translation-unit to override the donor.

Extra compiler arguments

--extra-arg ARG | --extra-args "-I dir -DNAME=1" | --extra-args `my-conf --cxxflags`

Repeat these options to add fallback include paths and new macro definitions. Compilation database settings take priority. Set startup defaults with --extra-arg=ARG or --extra-args "$(my-conf --cxxflags)".

Deployment options

--stack-depth N|full --stack-application-only true|false
--print-arguments --print-result --snapshot-return-pointee

Example

%probe inject "add(int, int)" --callback hook.cpp --stack-depth 16
