The original application is linux-dev:/tmp/tracer-gcc85-cxx17.Zsojgj/old-runtime, SHA-256 331d285b8290e3713ba36c9e0b823953d424ae2b9c8e3bc2a2e546d95f35c749. It retains its original GCC 8.5 C++17 binary, loader and runtime selection. add(int, int), Calculator::multiply(int, int) const, and inspect(const Packet&) each produced three correctly paired PRE/POST calls with the expected results, no reported trace drops and restored entry bytes. The application and server stopped cleanly afterward.

by_value(Packet) remains rejected because the target's DWARF lacks the required pass-by-value ABI evidence. This is an explicit existing signature limitation, not a successful compatibility test. Fully stripped busy-main attach on legacy libc also remains rejected when the exact main boundary cannot be proven; the legacy regression verifies that rejection. Idle attach remains available. This work does not add RIP-relative entry instruction relocation or establish support for a Linux 2.6.32 kernel. The validation host runs Linux 5.14.

The implementation and rebuild recipe are in gcc85-compatibility.md. The script captures dependency pins, validates downloaded SQLite content, and rejects unrelated modifications to pinned dependency sources. The dependency builds and final tracer build were performed in the existing scratch layout; the script consolidates that recipe rather than claiming a second clean download/build run.

Benchmark comparison and limits

The benchmark below records the original compatibility build, before the external-machine follow-up described at the end of this report. It has not been rerun for that follow-up.

The baseline is the current installed /usr/local/bin/clang-tracer-server and /usr/local/lib64/libclang_tracer_agent.so; the candidate is the SDK build above. Both trace the same immutable GCC 8.5-built C++17 libcalculator.so and the same workload source. The executable is linked once to the modern host runtime for the baseline and once to the original SDK runtime for the candidate. The installed baseline cannot load into the old-runtime target, so this comparison measures the complete supported profiles, including runtime, compiler/build, LLVM and dependency effects. It does not isolate compatibility-helper cost.

The benchmark runs nine paired rounds, alternates build order, rotates modes, and starts a fresh target/server for each trial. The target and its threads are pinned to CPU 6; the server is pinned to CPU 7. The host is a KVM guest exposing eight Intel i9-7900X CPUs. An existing unrelated performance campaign remained running; its coordinator has affinity 0–7, so shared-host interference remains possible despite pinning these trials. No build or full test suite ran during the measured campaign.

Each trial warms up 100 calls. Untraced batches contain 5,000,000 calls; instrumented batches contain 1,500 calls. Measurement encloses only the target loop; server startup, attach, callback compilation and probe installation are recorded separately. Times are batch means per call summarized across rounds, not individual-call latency percentiles. The tiny untraced function makes application-wide percentage slowdowns unrepresentative: use absolute added time multiplied by the rate of traced calls.

Modes have distinct work:

  • off: no tracer attached.
  • trace: ordinary empty PRE/POST callbacks with two trace records per call.
  • stack: the same trace records with application-only native stacks, depth 24.
  • shared: guarded shared-state increments in PRE/POST, without explicit context snapshots; shared hooks do not emit ordinary native trace records. This measures state access without snapshot serialization or transport.

Every trace/stack trial validates 3,200 warmup-plus-measured records, sequence continuity, call pairing, arguments, results, drops and entry restoration. Stack records must be complete and contain application frames. All instrumented modes check callback errors and restoration; every target checks its workload checksum and exits cleanly. Shared-state semantics are also covered by the SDK integration suite.

Measured overhead

All 72 trials passed. The 36 ordinary trace/stack trials validated 115,200 records, including 57,600 complete stack records. All 54 instrumented trials reported zero callback errors, restored their entry bytes and stopped cleanly. No reported drops or input-binary hash changes occurred.

The table shows median target wall time per call across nine batches. The percentage column compares those two medians. The last column instead takes the median of the nine paired round-by-round percentage changes; these are different statistics, especially for noisy short operations.

Mode Current build, µs/call SDK build, µs/call Ratio of medians Median paired change
Untraced workload 0.0105 0.0121 +14.9% +12.7%
PRE/POST tracing 7.020 7.319 +4.3% +0.25%
Tracing with native stacks 249.258 319.702 +28.3% +28.1%
Shared-state increments, no snapshots 5.603 5.909 +5.5% +2.9%

Stack capture was slower in every pair: +24.1% to +36.2% wall time. Calling thread CPU time confirms the cost: 241.194 versus 309.280 µs/call, with a median paired increase of 28.3%. The SDK profile adds about 70.4 µs per stack-traced call compared with the installed build for this workload.

Ordinary tracing and shared-state results are much noisier. Paired wall-time changes range from −37.8% to +27.4% for tracing and −36.6% to +53.8% for shared state. The measured +4.3% and +5.5% ratios do not establish a reliable small regression under this shared-host run. Calling-thread CPU medians are 4.448 versus 4.963 µs for tracing and 5.526 versus 5.836 µs for shared state; their paired changes also span both signs. The untraced difference occurs without any tracer loaded and must not be attributed to tracing overhead.

Subtracting each profile's untraced median gives approximate SDK costs of 7.306 µs per ordinary traced call, 319.690 µs with stacks, and 5.896 µs for guarded state increments without snapshots. Application impact depends on how often those probes execute. For example, 1,000 stack-traced calls per second would add approximately 0.32 seconds of target elapsed work per second for this fixture; asynchronous drain and other application work can change the result. This is not a whole-application slowdown prediction.

Setup is outside these loop timings. Median attach was about 122–124 ms for both profiles. Ordinary probe installation/compilation was 0.825 s current versus 0.670 s SDK; shared-state installation was 6.442 versus 6.775 s. These are host-dependent setup observations, not per-call costs.

Local raw evidence is retained under /Users/husam/.codex/worktrees/gcc85-runtime/clang-tracer/benchmark-results/gcc85-runtime/; remote evidence is under linux-dev:/tmp/tracer-gcc85-build-20261102/. External-machine failure follow-up

A separate machine reported 6/21 passing, with GCC 11 headers included beside SDK GCC 8 headers and native admission failing before attach. The fixes add:

  • Explicit native C++ header roots with -nostdinc++, rather than automatic host C++ header fallback. A foreign standard-library search-path regression failed before this change. Both production activation and the SDK agent's generated compiler arguments now isolate that profile; test compilation uses the same restriction.
  • Complete interval and file-offset validation of ELF load segments, replacing the assumption that every segment starts a separate mapping. A real merged file mapping reproduces the old rejection and passes with the fix. A same-inode mapping at the wrong offset is still rejected, as are ambiguous complete mappings and changed identities. The fixture also passes with a host GCC 11-built DSO containing four load segments.
  • More specific admission errors, separating missing device/inode identity from incomplete PT_LOAD coverage and naming the file involved.

The missing __udivti3 JIT message in the supplied log belongs to an intentional negative test for compiler-generated helpers; that check completed successfully. It is not the cause of the subsequent owner-activation parse failure.

The mapping message alone does not establish the external host's exact ELF layout. Its updated build still needs to be rerun there. Follow-up source and fresh build are under linux-dev:/tmp/tracer-gcc85-external-fix-20261102/; the application build uses the script's SDK configuration and the previously built pinned dependencies. Failing-before/fixed-after evidence is retained locally under benchmark-results/gcc85-runtime/external-fix/.

The follow-up fresh SDK application build passes all 21 native CTests in 200.82 seconds, including the header-isolation and merged-mapping regressions. The modern macOS portable/analysis suite passes 6/6 in 37.57 seconds. These results validate the retained Linux host and macOS build; they do not claim that the inaccessible external machine has already passed. The follow-up installed runtime also passes the same three supported probes against the unchanged original GCC 8.5 application. Original application and installed-baseline hashes remain unchanged.

The external retest then passed 7/21, including owner activation, but all 14 native cases still rejected executable file identity on device 0:87. A private OverlayFS namespace reproduced this remaining class of failure: stat(/proc/<pid>/exe) reported the overlay device/inode while /proc/<pid>/maps reported the underlying file's device/inode. Copy-up can also change the backing inode while preserving the overlay's visible origin inode. Thus the merged-segment fix alone does not resolve these identity differences.

The same SDK module-identity executable failed when run from the overlay view and passed when run through a private bind mount of its native XFS directory. At that point the identity checks remained intact. The interim workaround used a normal filesystem bind-mounted into the container, with executable/module identities matching their process mappings. That check covered the module-identity test rather than a rerun of all external tests; the session-fixed policy below supersedes this workaround.

Reproduction script and output are retained at linux-dev:/tmp/tracer-overlay-identity-repro.sh and linux-dev:/tmp/tracer-overlay-identity-repro.log.

Session-fixed binary policy

The user confirmed that rebuilding requires a new tracing session. Native admission, symbol relocation, runtime-call translation and stack-image lookup now use canonical mapped paths plus ELF offsets, executable ranges and load bias. Device/inode equality and file timestamp/rebuild polling have been removed from binary validation. File-format, size, CFI, mapping ambiguity, runtime-entry instructions and installed probe-byte checks remain in place.

Native stack metadata is shared by probes in a session and cleared for a new session after all prior-session callbacks and transport have drained. This also handles the agent remaining loaded after detach without reusing old ELF metadata for a later session.

The focused admission/module tests accept metadata-only timestamp changes, still reject unmapped modules and incorrect ELF file offsets, and pass from a private OverlayFS mount. The full-suite overlay runner is retained as tests/overlay_integration.sh; it mounts only inside a private test namespace.

The full SDK suite passes 21/21 inside OverlayFS in 210.17 seconds, including attach, threaded/busy/shared-module tracing, native stack capture and durable collector reconnect. A focused overlay regression also accepts an existing module whose literal filename ends in (deleted) (1/1 passed). The runner preserves the host network namespace for TCP delivery tests and does not modify the host build tree. Threaded fixtures now wait for their own child PID's startup record, avoiding stale log data during overlay copy-up.

Blocked-main attach backport

The blocked-main fixes from main commit ecb3930 were backported to c++17 and tested on linux-dev on 2 November 2026. The fresh tracer build used the supplied SDK's Clang/LLVM 21.1.8, GCC 8.5 headers and libstdc++, glibc 2.23, and SDK loader. It reused the existing pinned SDK-built gRPC, Protobuf and SQLite dependencies; no host runtime dependencies were substituted.

The full SDK suite passed 28/28 in 422.76 seconds. The seven blocked-main regressions also passed from OverlayFS (7/7 in 43.89 seconds), including sleeping and raw pthread workers, all-blocked failures, and preserved external job-control stops. Legacy worker CFI validates exact start_thread in the separate mapped libpthread.so.0, then exact __clone in libc. The existing exact-main startup proof remains available without requiring libpthread.

A separate fixture was compiled with actual GCC 8.5.0 and -std=c++17. The same binary failed with the previous tracer (gRPC 13 and shutdown status 1) and passed with the backport across futex, epoll, poll, pipe read, accept, pause and sigwait. Probe events, removal, detach, thread release, no-host FAILED_PRECONDITION, and clean shutdown were verified. Its SHA-256 remained 8fbd4452d33a62f2c0d6ee1495816ba2b1afd0fc1b2c664aaf66eb731bcbe265.

Old-header test fixtures provide guarded Linux ptracer constants. The SDK's process-vm stubs use the existing direct syscall wrapper, and an explicit NOP test entry keeps the supported patch subset stable with SDK PIE code generation. Production instruction decoding and blocked-syscall eligibility were not widened.

Build logs, test output, compiler/runtime checks and the GCC-built fixture are retained at linux-dev:/tmp/tracer-gcc85-blocked-main-20261102/. Earlier benchmark measurements above remain historical; this backport did not rerun benchmarks.

Native C++17 REPL

For runnable examples of structs/classes, strings, optionals, sequence containers, maps, sets and nested containers, see examples/native-repl-values.

clang-tracer-repl manages a tracing session from one prompt. Commands start an owned local server, attach to a process, upload C++ interceptor source, and collect and inspect events. Ordinary C++ input runs locally through Clang Interpreter. Python is not required to run the console.

Build

The new console, its controller, generated RPC bindings and command parser are compiled as C++17. The c++17 base branch still selects C++20 for the existing backend; the REPL does not inherit that requirement. Build the client alone on Linux or macOS:

sh
cmake -S . -B build-repl -G Ninja -DTRACER_REPL_ONLY=ON \
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DLLVM_DIR=/path/to/llvm/lib/cmake/llvm \
  -DClang_DIR=/path/to/llvm/lib/cmake/clang
cmake --build build-repl -j2
ctest --test-dir build-repl --output-on-failure

Supply a matching LLVM/Clang 21 or 22 development installation, the gRPC and Protobuf development packages and compiler plugin, and the SQLite development package. The implementation has separate embedding paths for LLVM 21.1.8 and 22.1.8. Set CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH for dependencies outside the system search path. The existing full Linux build includes the REPL by default; -DTRACER_BUILD_REPL=OFF keeps the prior backend-only build.

The two new dependency downloads have exact archive checksums:

Package Version SHA256
replxx 0.0.4, tag release-0.0.4 a22988b2184e1d256e2d111b5749e16ffb1accbf757c7b248226d73c426844c4
ANTLR C++ runtime 4.13.2 0ed13668906e86dbc0dcddf30fdee68c10203dea4e83852b4edb810821bee3c4

Use FETCHCONTENT_SOURCE_DIR_TRACER_REPLXX and FETCHCONTENT_SOURCE_DIR_TRACER_ANTLR with pre-extracted versions for offline builds. Their licenses are installed with the console. gRPC and Protobuf use the build's existing package selection; the REPL does not impose new versions.

Stage an installation without changing the live installation:

sh
cmake --install build-repl --prefix "$PWD/build-repl/stage" --component Runtime

The runtime includes the facade header under share/clang-tracer/repl/api.hpp. Clang/LLVM libraries, builtin headers and a compatible C++ SDK must remain available. --cpp-arg ARG adds an interpreter compiler argument; repeat it for include directories or other options. The prelude uses the build compiler's standard-library include roots. Installing the client alone does not install a Linux server or agent.

Prepare a probe from a binary without headers

Build a module index from a Linux x86-64 ELF executable or shared library. Embedded DWARF and matching separate debug files provide type and signature information. ELF exports remain searchable in stripped modules.

bash
%module index --file ./libdemo.so
%module types --filter "demo::*"
%module symbols --exported --filter "demo::*"
%module show --type demo::Packet
%module show --symbol "demo::score(demo::Packet const&)"
%module emit --symbol "demo::score(demo::Packet const&)" --output recovered
%probe prepare "demo::score(demo::Packet const&)" --generated recovered --output prepared-score

The index defaults to libdemo.so.tracer.sqlite. Use --output INDEX to name it or --debug-file FILE to supply a matching companion. To index a live module using the REPL's local server, run %modules --details and pass its exact module path and token to %module index --module PATH --mapping TOKEN.

Indexing selects the new index for the session. In another REPL, %module use INDEX selects a saved index. With no headers or explicit signature, preparation checks the explicit --module-index first, then the <ELF>.tracer.sqlite sidecar when you pass --module ELF, then the selected index, then module-index.sqlite in the command's working directory. When --module is omitted, it uses the ELF path recorded in the index.

List commands accept glob filters, --format json, and optional --limit N and --page TOKEN. Use the full C++ signature to select an overload, or --id ID when a name is ambiguous. The index preserves missing type and layout information. Symbols with incomplete signatures can still be looked up. Supported indexed signatures use scalar, pointer and borrowed reference parameters and results. The generated views.hpp contains read-only accessors for supported fixed-offset fields, and the manifest lists omitted fields. --generated is optional. The preparer can regenerate the checked C++ from the index.

The prepared package embeds its declarations and accessors. A callback can use them directly. This example reads a scalar field from the borrowed argument.

cpp
template <> class Interceptor<int(const demo::Packet&)> {
public:
  long long pre(const Call& call) {
    return tracer_recovered::demo::PacketView::value(call.argument<0>());
  }
  long long post(const Call& call) { return call.result<int>(); }
};

In the attached REPL, validate and inject the package.

bash
%probe validate "demo::score(demo::Packet const&)" --callback observer.cpp --prepared prepared-score --prepared-mode require
%probe inject "demo::score(demo::Packet const&)" --callback observer.cpp --prepared prepared-score --prepared-mode require

The native C++ API uses the same index and preparation workflow.

cpp
auto index = tracer.open_module_index("libdemo.so.tracer.sqlite");
auto score = index.find_symbol("demo::score(demo::Packet const&)");
auto packet = index.find_type("demo::Packet");
index.prepare_probe(score.id, {}, "prepared-score");

Standalone C++ callers can include <tracer/module_index.hpp> and link tracer_module_index. Use tracer_module::ModuleIndex::build with tracer_module::ModuleSource::file(elf_path) to build an index or ModuleIndex::open to reuse one.

Start and attach

On Linux x86-64 with the native server and agent installed:

sh
clang-tracer-repl --attach 12345
# Optional explicit build-tree server:
clang-tracer-repl --server /path/to/build/clang-tracer-server --attach 12345

The console creates a private endpoint, starts its server in a separate process session, waits for readiness, and attaches before returning to the prompt. Agent discovery is performed by the server; --agent PATH is an override. Server lookup checks an adjacent executable and then PATH.

For an existing server:

sh
clang-tracer-repl --endpoint 127.0.0.1:50051 --attach 12345

An explicit endpoint, including CLANG_TRACER_ENDPOINT, connects to that service and never silently starts a replacement. The PID belongs to the server host. The existing tracing service's permissions and target/ABI restrictions apply. The macOS client connects to a Linux server; it cannot start a Linux backend locally.

With an owned local Linux server, --process NAME matches executable paths. %attach without a PID opens the process picker; multiple matches require choosing a displayed PID. The picker shows each candidate's executable and Linux start time and checks the selected identity at attach. %processes --filter TEXT lists the same local candidates. In scripts, use %attach PID --start-time TICKS to attach only when the PID still has the displayed start time. Remote process enumeration is not in the service API, so remote attach uses an explicit PID.

Launch a local application

Build the application with the installed C++17 <tracer/launch.hpp> header and add a checkpoint at the start of main, before starting threads or calling the code you want to trace. It returns immediately on an ordinary run. Treat a failed checkpoint as a startup failure.

cpp
#include <tracer/launch.hpp>

int main() {
  if (!tracer::launch::wait_for_resume())
    return 125;
  return run_application();
}

Use these commands in the native REPL on Linux x86-64. With the REPL's private server, only that server may attach to the launched application. With any other endpoint, including CLANG_TRACER_ENDPOINT, the server must run on the same host as the REPL, and the launched application accepts any tracer the host's tracing policy allows. %launch selects the attached session and holds the application at the checkpoint while you install probes.

bash
%launch ./app --arg "example input" --env MODE=test --cwd ./work --stdin ./input.txt --timeout 5
%probe inject "app::start()" --callback observer.cpp
%resume
%terminate

The earliest traceable work is the first eligible call after the checkpoint. The loader, global constructors, and any earlier application code have already run. Repeat --arg for arguments and --env NAME=VALUE for overrides to the inherited environment. Relative paths are resolved from the REPL's working directory. Standard input defaults to /dev/null. Use --stdout NEW_FILE and --stderr NEW_FILE to choose output files. The REPL reports the paths and otherwise creates private log files. Existing files are protected from overwrite.

--timeout bounds the wait for the checkpoint in seconds. It defaults to the REPL timeout, which also applies separately to attach. Setup or attach failure and readiness timeout terminate and reap the child. %resume [PID] and %terminate [PID] use the selected target when PID is omitted. %terminate kills and reaps the launched child whether paused or resumed. The REPL retains ownership after detach and terminates any remaining owned children on exit. Use %status to list owned targets and reap any that have already exited. Only the launched process is managed.

If an attach reply fails or times out, the operation may still finish on the server. The console reports the endpoint, PID and newly observed candidate session IDs, blocks automatic retries for that PID, and reconciles again on %status and exit. Inspect %sessions and explicitly %detach SESSION when appropriate. Candidates are never assumed to belong to this console on an external server; recovery information is retained until explicitly resolved.

Call a registered function in the paused target

Register each callable at the startup checkpoint. The application compiler checks the function pointer's argument and result types. The name is an exact match to the name you register and can distinguish overloads.

cpp
#include <tracer/launch.hpp>

double scale(int value, double factor) { return value * factor; }

int main() {
  using tracer::launch::named_call;
  if (!tracer::launch::wait_for_resume(named_call("app::scale", &scale)))
    return 125;
  // Continue normal application startup.
}
bash
%launch ./app
%call app::scale --arg 6 --arg 1.5
%resume

The result line shows the type and value, such as type=double value=9. Registered functions accept up to eight arguments drawn from bool, 32-bit and 64-bit signed and unsigned integers, float, and double. The same types and void are available for results. Enter decimal integers, finite decimal floating-point values, and true or false. Wrong argument counts and invalid values are rejected before execution. Pointers, references, objects, variadic functions, and functions with an implicit receiver are outside this interface.

Calls run one at a time on the thread that entered the checkpoint, before %resume. Choose functions that are ready to run at that point in startup. Their side effects remain in the target, and an escaping C++ exception is reported as a failed call. Returned scalars are copied into the REPL's reply. Calls require a target launched by this REPL with a registered checkpoint.

Use --timeout SECONDS to bound how long the REPL waits. Timeout or interruption leaves the call pending and it may continue running. Use %call-result [--timeout SECONDS] to collect its reply. A pending call blocks another call, resume, or probe changes on that target. %terminate still kills the owned target if it cannot finish.

Browse a local C++ target

bash
%threads
%modules --filter libdemo.so --details
%symbols --filter Calculator --addresses
%symbols --address 0xADDRESS --mapping TOKEN

%threads shows thread IDs, names and start times for the selected process. %modules lists application module paths from the selected attached process. --filter TEXT matches a case-sensitive substring of the full path. Add --details for file-backed executable address ranges, file offsets, device and inode, and the ELF build ID when the backing file can be verified. The mapping token describes the session's full snapshot, including when the display is filtered.

Use the C++ API at the prompt or in a REPL script.

cpp
auto paths = tracer.modules("libdemo.so");
auto module = tracer.module_info(paths.at(0));
for (const auto& entry : module.mappings) { std::cout << entry.begin_address << ' ' << entry.build_id << '\n'; }

Call tracer.modules() to list all application module paths. Its ModuleList result supports iteration, size(), empty(), and at(). The paths are also available as a vector in .paths. Pass an exact path from the list or a unique exact filename to tracer.module_info(). Missing or ambiguous names throw std::invalid_argument. The result includes path, mapping_token, and mappings. Each mapping has begin_address, exclusive end_address, file_offset, device, inode, and build_id.

%symbols --addresses shows runtime and ELF entries for supported C++ callables when there is a unique verified mapping. For reverse lookup, copy a runtime address and the mapping= token from the same session. Addresses inside a supported callable also work. If the mappings or backing files change, take a new snapshot before using an address. The token checks observed mapping identity. An unload and reload of the same image at the same address between snapshots can produce identical observations.

Capture local syscalls or CPU samples

Attach to a running Linux x86-64 target using the REPL's own local server, then choose a capture:

bash
%syscalls --timeout 2 --count 256
%sample cpu --timeout 2 --count 256

%syscalls reports separate entry and exit records with the syscall number and the raw kernel return value on exit. %sample cpu reports user-space instruction addresses at roughly one sample per 10 ms of scheduled CPU time. Each record carries the process ID, thread ID, and a monotonic nanosecond timestamp on the same clock as probe events. Use a current mapping snapshot and %symbols --address to look up a sample address.

Each capture snapshots and verifies up to 64 existing target threads. Threads created after that snapshot and child processes are outside the capture. The command releases its kernel resources before printing records in timestamp order. It stops on timeout, the record limit, Ctrl+C, or the exit of all monitored threads. The defaults are two seconds and 256 records, with ceilings of 60 seconds and 8192 records.

The summary reports kernel loss, throttle notifications, and samples discarded at the requested limit separately. Kernels with a perf loss counter include loss still pending at shutdown. On older kernels, loss_accounting=records counts loss notifications the kernel wrote to the ring. Collection boundaries, loss, and the record limit can leave individual syscall entries or exits without a partner. These pilot records are printed by their capture command.

Syscall capture reads the raw syscall tracepoint IDs and formats from tracefs and opens the events through perf for each target thread. It needs tracefs read access and permission to open those events. CPU sampling uses a user-space perf task-clock event and can work under a policy that denies syscall tracing. Both modes report permission failures directly. Perf events allow the target threads to continue running. A syscall-stop backend based on ptrace would stop them at each syscall boundary and compete with the injector for ptrace ownership. Linux event tracing · Perf permissions · perf_event_open · ptrace

Preview a bulk trace

bash
%trace preview --module 'libapp*' --include 'app::*' --exclude 'app::detail::*' --save trace.textproto
%trace preview --exact "Calculator::multiply(int, int) const"
%trace preview --manifest trace.textproto

Run the preview after attaching to a local Linux x86-64 C++ application. Repeat --module to match any executable module by basename or path. --include and --exact combine their selections, then --exclude removes matches. Globs are case-sensitive and support *, ? and bracket patterns. They match either qualified names or full signatures. Use --exact to choose an overload by its full C++ signature. Quote patterns at the REPL.

The dry run reads executable mappings, ELF symbols and DWARF, including matching separate debug files. It reports a live entry when one can be verified. DWARF_SUPPORTED means the entry passed static ABI checks. Callback compilation and installation checks run separately. PREPARED_REQUIRED identifies a concrete virtual implementation that needs a compatible prepared package. Unsupported entries and ambiguous selections show a reason. Narrow a duplicate signature with --module.

The capacity line shows retained slots and whether the DWARF-supported selection fits. It is a snapshot and reserves no slots. The preview runs without installing probes, stopping target threads or executing code inside the target. --save creates a new versioned text-protobuf file with selection rules. Reusing it resolves against the current session and mappings.

Apply and remove a bulk trace

bash
%trace apply --manifest trace.textproto
%trace apply --manifest trace.textproto --callback observer.cpp
%trace remove BATCH_ID

Apply re-resolves the manifest against the selected session. The default Clang JIT observer records typed PRE and POST events. With --callback, the same C++ source is compiled for each matched function. Every match must be DWARF-supported and fit in the available retained slots. Ambiguous or unmatched selections, entries requiring prepared packages, and entries with active probes block installation.

The REPL prints the batch ID before applying and reports the status of each entry. If an install fails, the server restores this batch's probes in reverse order. Use the same batch ID with %trace remove to retry entries reported as RESTORE_PENDING or to check a batch after an interrupted command. Removal is repeatable for a retained batch in its original session. Removal and rollback restore entry bytes. The agent still retains compiled slots until the target exits.

Read and scan mapped memory

bash
%memory maps
%memory read 0xADDRESS --mapping TOKEN --count 32
%memory read 0xADDRESS --mapping TOKEN --type i64
%memory scan 0xADDRESS --mapping TOKEN --count 4096 --pattern "48 8? ?? ff" --limit 16

Run these commands after attaching to a local Linux x86-64 target. Copy the token after memory mapping= and use an address from one of the listed ranges. Ranges include anonymous and file-backed mappings, with permissions shown as reported by Linux. The memory token is specific to the attached session and its memory map.

Use --count for a hex and ASCII dump of 1 to 65536 bytes. Use --type for one little-endian u8, u16, u32, u64, i8, i16, i32, i64, f32 or f64 value. Reads can cross page and mapping boundaries when the entire span is readable. A gap, inaccessible page, or short kernel read fails the request at the first affected address and returns no bytes.

The server checks the mapping snapshot and target identity around each read or scan. Run %memory maps again after any mapping or permission change. The target keeps running during inspection, so bytes can change while they are copied. An unmap and remap with identical visible metadata between checks can produce the same snapshot.

Scans accept 1 to 1048576 bytes and patterns of 1 to 256 bytes. Separate hex bytes with spaces. Use ?? for an entire wildcard byte, or 8? or ?f for a wildcard nibble. To choose individual bits, append a colon and a same-length hex mask, as in "13 37 : 1f ff". A bit participates only if the explicit mask enables it and the bit belongs to a non-wildcard nibble.

Matches are reported in ascending address order and can overlap or cross adjacent readable mappings. The default match limit is 64 and the maximum is 1024. truncated=true means the scan found at least one more match. A scan fails without returning matches if any part of its requested range is unreadable or the snapshot changes during inspection. The scan uses the configured operation timeout and supports Ctrl+C.

Preview a verified function entry

bash
%memory maps
%probe entry "Calculator::multiply(int, int) const" --mapping TOKEN
%probe entry --module /absolute/path/to/app --elf-address 0xELF_VA --abi linux-x86-64-sysv --mapping TOKEN

Use the token from the attached session's memory snapshot. A named entry uses DWARF. The explicit form requires the exact mapped module path and a link-time ELF virtual address. It accepts an exact function symbol start or an exact .eh_frame range start in a stripped image. The ABI label in that form is supplied by the caller. The preview verifies executable mapping identity and compares the live bytes with the ELF file, which must be a readable regular file of at most 128 MiB.

The preview disassembles up to 64 verified entry bytes and follows direct branches within that window. Call targets are reported without following them. Indirect targets are shown as unresolved. patch_size shows the instruction-aligned window accepted by the current copy-only detour policy. If the policy rejects the entry, the preview shows the reason. It performs no installation or writes.

Probe a short getter

%probe inject uses the auto backend by default. It keeps the verified entry jump when the overwrite window and relocation fit. The installed probe reports its backend, selection reason, and patch address.

bash
%probe inject "demo::Circle::get_radius() const" --backend auto --caller "demo::call_radius(const demo::Circle &)" --stack-depth 6
%record getter.db --sqlite --phase POST --probe PROBE_ID --count 4 --timeout 30
%detach

For a supported short integer getter, --caller selects a named function in the same module. The call-site backend requires one verified five-byte direct call to the getter and an executable relay within rel32 range of the next instruction. It traces calls through that site. Use --backend entry to require an entry jump.

When auto has no verified caller or no reachable relay, the trap backend copies the complete getter and installs one INT3 at its verified entry. The server redirects owned traps to the normal wrapper, leaving the application's return address on its stack. The initial supported body is a 32-bit load from the receiver followed by ret. An existing ENDBR64 stays in place and selects the trap path. The trap owns execution control for its session and restores its byte at stop, detach, or a thread or process creation stop. Remove a fallback probe before replacing it.

Trace object lifetimes and state in a prebuilt binary

Use the full Linux build on x86-64 or AArch64, with the REPL, server, and agent from the same build. Supply the existing ELF and its matching DWARF, either embedded or in a matching separate debug file. The watch installs patches in process memory. The application executable and source files stay intact.

On c++17, use that branch's preparation tools to generate typed adapters and object watch plans from the existing binary and its original compile commands. Regenerate typed adapters created on main before preparing a watch on c++17.

The plan records the capture mode you select during preparation.

  • Individual writes. Select one --field and a writer with --code. Use --backend code-cache to run supported stores in the target without a ptrace stop for every write. --backend ptrace is the default and steps verified stores for diagnostic runs. By default, the watch samples values and reports changes. Start a saved write plan with --no-values to record FIELD_WRITTEN for each completed admitted store, including same-value stores, without field samples. The backend is part of the saved plan.
  • Method snapshots. Use --on with the original header and compile command to compare the receiver at verified entry and return boundaries. A snapshot delta describes the net change during one call. Supply the synchronization policy that protects the sampled state. See method snapshots.

Run a scalar write watch on x86-64

From the repository root on Linux x86-64, use a full build in build with tests enabled. Build the demonstration fixture once and start it in the first terminal. It prints its PID and waits for input.

sh
cmake --build build --target repl-object-plan-target
sh -c 'printf "PID=%s\n" "$$"; exec "$1"' _ ./build/repl-object-plan-target

From the same directory in a second terminal, open the REPL. Use a fresh package directory and SQLite path for each run.

sh
./build/clang-tracer-repl --server ./build/clang-tracer-server --agent ./build/libclang_tracer_agent.so --fail-fast

Prepare the plan before attaching. Then replace PID with the printed PID and check that preview reports binding=same-build and a verified store site. Start installs the redirects and prints the watch ID.

bash
%object prepare demo::PlanRecord --module ./build/repl-object-plan-target --field value --code "demo::write_value(demo::PlanRecord &)" --backend code-cache --output ./record-watch
%attach PID
%object preview --plan ./record-watch
%object start --plan ./record-watch --stack-depth 4
%record object-writes.db --sqlite --name object.trace --probe WATCH_ID --count 2 --timeout 30

Replace WATCH_ID with the ID printed by start. While %record is waiting, enter g in the first terminal. The fixture prints value=23. The recorder should report received=2 and complete=true for the creation and the write from 17 to 23.

bash
%object status WATCH_ID
%object stop WATCH_ID
%detach
%events open object-writes.db --as saved
%events list saved
%events show saved --index 1
%events stack saved --index 1

Stop restores the verified instruction bytes. Check active=no and restoration_pending=no before detaching. If restoration is pending, retry stop using the same ID. Replay works after detach, including in a fresh REPL. Enter q in the first terminal to exit the fixture. To repeat with --no-values, restart the fixture, reuse the write plan, add the flag to %object start, and use a fresh recording path. The two events are still creation and a store, with the store shown as FIELD_WRITTEN.

Read coverage and cleanup status

  • Review the resolved fields, writer sites, and binding status in preview. Preview is read-only. A same-build restart resolves fresh live addresses. A compatible rebuild requires verifiable field and code bindings. Missing or mismatched evidence can prevent a watch from starting.
  • Lifecycle events require observable, unambiguous construction and teardown. An out-of-line copy of an inline constructor or destructor can provide the boundary if its ABI is verified. A fully inlined or optimized-away call can leave a partial timeline. --first-seen can scope a supported standalone write watch to one verified writer invocation when construction is unavailable.
  • On x86-64, a short lifetime boundary can use verified alignment NOPs after the function. A short destructor return can also jump through the relocated entry window. If the mapped ELF lacks a safe redirect for a required entry or exit, use --backend ptrace for the lifetime trace.
  • When completion must be observed after a direct call, a tail jump into the lifetime boundary requires a verified continuation. Preview and start reject unverified tail callers because they can bypass the return hook.
  • Ptrace can observe stores in a writer that ends in an indirect call or jump when every block in the writer is decoded and any gaps contain only alignment NOPs. It observes the selected writer's stores. An indirect jump with unverified blocks, such as an unresolved jump table, is refused.
  • When the complete and base constructors share an entry, a verified direct call from outside constructor and destructor frames can identify a complete construction. When a known derived type can initialize its base as an aggregate, these shared entries remain uncertain unless stronger evidence is available.
  • On x86-64, scalar watches admit verified 32-bit integer arithmetic, bitwise and shift updates. For locked atomic instructions without a returned old value, code-cache records the write and reports that the values could not be verified. Ptrace can sample the values while target peers are parked.
  • Collection and pointee watches require verified mutation boundaries and supported identities. Unverified inline paths can leave coverage gaps. Tagged-union decoding requires a verified unsigned 32-bit discriminator and supported 32-bit alternatives. Untagged union observations carry storage bytes.
  • Native capture covers admitted code and threads. Generated helper windows can leave signal or stack gaps, including AArch64 scalable signal records that exceed the fixed Linux signal frame. Shared-file identity correlates recordings across processes, where ordering can remain partial.
  • Use %object status to check drops, unsupported sites, coverage gaps, and capture limits. Use %object stop or %detach to retire the watch and restore patches. See the verification record for the exercised cases and limits.

Prepare an object watch for method snapshots

Prepare from the original headers and compile command. The package contains the generated adapter and the verified ELF entry. Declare the synchronization that protects the receiver and any storage the adapter follows. Use thread-confined when that graph is accessed from a single thread. Use caller-lock when the caller holds the application's lock over the method and both samples. Use stable-at-boundaries when the application establishes safe entry and return samples, for example by joining a child writer before return. For the Portfolio commands below, run the rebalance while %record is waiting and substitute the PID and watch ID from your run.

bash
%object prepare demo::Portfolio --module ./portfolio --include ./portfolio.hpp --policy ./snapshot-policy.hpp --compdb ./compile_commands.json --translation-unit ./portfolio.cpp --on "demo::Portfolio::rebalance()" --field legs --field risk --key legs=id --key risk=key --synchronization thread-confined --output ./portfolio-watch --emit-source ./generated
%attach PID
%object preview --plan ./portfolio-watch
%object start --plan ./portfolio-watch --stack-depth 8
%record portfolio.db --sqlite --name object.trace --probe WATCH_ID --count 2 --timeout 30
%object stop WATCH_ID
%detach
%events open portfolio.db --as saved

Snapshot deltas describe the interval between a method's entry and return. Fields select the reported paths. The generated receiver codec reads the receiver and the pointees authorized by the preparation policy. A failed sample yields a coverage gap. A missing return yields a coverage gap when the probe retires. Set --max-elements, --max-string-bytes, --max-depth, --max-snapshot-bytes, and --max-instances to bound capture and observation.

Choose method snapshots for changes to strings, private nested records, containers, variants, or registered pointees. For example, the Portfolio watch pairs entries by leg ID and map key and can report a leaf change such as risk_["AAPL"].limits_[0]. An added or removed map entry or keyed vector element includes its captured record or sequence on the corresponding side of the delta. Use %events show saved --index N to inspect the typed values, or %events export saved --format json --output changes.json to export them. In JSON, snapshotBefore and snapshotAfter carry recursive children for composite values, with fieldName on record children. The capture limits also apply to values replayed from SQLite. When no key identity is available, the watch retains both captured entry sequences in the coverage gap and withholds individual adds and removals.

Method snapshots support up to 65,536 encoded bytes per value, 65,536 elements, and a depth of 64. The default byte and element budgets are 4,096 and the default depth is 32. The element budget is shared by the captured containers in each value. A field selection captures the selected top-level receiver members and their contents. A nested path filters which changes to report within its selected member.

For method snapshots, --max-instances limits receivers with an outstanding sample. Completed calls release their receiver slots. The watch detects overlapping calls on a receiver and relies on the declared synchronization policy across separate invocations.

For constructor-based watches, --max-instances limits live observed objects. Retirement releases the slot. The watch retains each observed address's generation counter until the watch ends so that address reuse remains distinguishable in replay.

A compatible rebuilt ELF can reuse a prepared method watch when DWARF confirms the receiver layout and the original void, scalar, or pointer signature. Pass --module to preview and start if the rebuilt image has a new name.

On AArch64 the native agent samples the receiver at a verified entry and at each verified return instruction. The original method executes in its application mapping, and CFI stack capture starts at its original entry. An exception that leaves the method can produce a missing-return gap when the watch retires.

An AnyPayloads<Record> specialization can register named record payloads for a direct std::any field. Name the field with a type alias to a tuple of the admitted types. The typed projection appears as extension_snapshot for the example below.

cpp
namespace tracer_snapshot {
template <class Record> struct AnyPayloads;
template <> struct AnyPayloads<demo::Portfolio> {
  using extension = std::tuple<demo::RiskState>;
};
}

Follow logical collection entries during writes

bash
%object start --type demo::Portfolio --field quantity --vector legs --element-key id=12 --code "demo::Portfolio::rebalance()" --mutation _ZNSt6vectorIN4demo3LegESaIS1_EE7reserveEm

The watch validates the writer's first receiver argument and the selected libstdc++ vector layout from DWARF. It binds a unique element by its 32-bit unsigned key and suspends that address during the selected mutation. A verified return can admit a new storage generation. Add --backend code-cache --synchronization thread-confined to translate the admitted fragments of a nonleaf writer and its selected mutation. On either backend, use --first-seen for a standalone scalar receiver whose constructor was inlined, absent, or ran before attaching. The provisional identity lasts for one writer invocation.

Repeat --mutation when the writer uses more than one storage-changing function. Each selected function must accept the verified container as its first argument. Native capture verifies direct calls and their return continuations. For an inlined function, the watch verifies the receiver and the control-flow edges into and out of its matching DWARF ranges. An inline instance can span disjoint ranges. With declared synchronization and value capture, RANGE_BOUND includes the verified value at binding. A rebind includes the prior value when it was sampled safely before suspension.

Use --map risk --map-key AAPL --field exposure.limit to follow a nested field in a std::map entry. For std::unordered_map<int, T>, use a numeric key such as --map-key "-7". Both containers require a verified libstdc++ layout and default key equivalence. Use --field value when the mapped value is itself numeric. Select a mutation such as insert, erase or rehash that takes the map as its first argument. The watch suspends the old binding and verifies the new generation on return, even when the matching node keeps its address. Rehash alone emits no field change. Missing, duplicate or unreadable keys and exhausted traversal budgets produce coverage gaps.

Individual field watches can capture admitted stores to integers, booleans, enums, floats and doubles within private records, vectors, maps and pointees. Preview reports the verified encoding and the admitted writer sites. For exact writes, replay identifies the store instruction and its source line. Structural changes to containers and changes to strings, variants and std::any can be inspected with typed method snapshots at verified boundaries.

Trace a Shape through Image

Build the fixture once with a Linux x86-64 GCC 8.5 compiler and matching embedded DWARF. Run it in one terminal and leave it at READY.

sh
"$GXX85" -std=c++17 -O2 -g -fno-omit-frame-pointer -fcf-protection=none \
  -fPIE -pie -pthread -Wl,--build-id=sha1 tests/fixtures/repl_object_watch.cpp -o shapes
./shapes

Attach from the native REPL and start the watch. Enter g in the target terminal while the REPL is recording. The fixture builds, mutates, and removes two Circles in the same allocation slot.

bash
%attach PID
%object start --type demo::Circle --base demo::Shape --owner demo::Image --field radius --collection _shapes --snapshot-field _description --code borrowed_write --stack-depth 5
%record shapes.db --sqlite --name object.trace --count 15 --timeout 30
%object stop
%detach
%events open shapes.db --as shapes
%events list shapes --limit 15
%events stack shapes --index 4

The diagnostic backend admits existing target threads and one writer function in the main executable. It uses ELF linkage for the complete constructor and destructor and the add, get, remove, and set_description boundaries. It verifies the mapped build ID, live instruction bytes, DWARF layouts and RTTI. The supported layout uses a verified fixed base offset, an int32 field, the libstdc++ C++11 string ABI and a vector of default-sized unique pointers. The remove boundary checks the watched entries against the verified membership after return. Use --owner-add, --owner-get, --owner-remove, and --owner-snapshot to select differently named methods with the supported ABI. The default selectors use add, get, remove, and set_description on the declared owner or base. Preview verifies the receiver and callable shape.

The server owns the breakpoints until stop or detach. It parks peers while the writer steps each admitted instruction. The effective destination must equal the selected field of a live generation. An interrupted store emits a coverage gap. A successful retry can produce a fresh delta at the same PC. Enter f instead of g and record 16 events to exercise that path. The string delta comes from the verified setter boundary. Stack depth defaults to zero. Enabled write stacks walk available frame pointers in the main executable. Use --max-elements and --max-string-bytes to set snapshot limits.

Add --no-values to record FIELD_WRITTEN for every completed store, including a same-value store. This skips pre/post value reads and omits value samples from lifecycle and fault records. Status shows values=off. The default captures value changes and verified boundary snapshots.

Coverage is partial. Stores outside the selected function, unsupported instructions and optimized-away lifetime boundaries are outside this draft. New threads in the same process can enter the diagnostic watch. An exec or fork boundary that changes the observed process reports partial coverage. Use %object status for counts and restoration state. Unsupported sites, reported gaps, or dropped observations mark coverage partial. If restoration needs a retry, the watch keeps its ID and the target remains stopped. Use --tid to select the thread whose stores are reported. The diagnostic backend restores its patches when --max-events or --timeout is reached. Native code-cache and method watches cap observations at those limits and keep their patches until stop or detach. Set --event-buffer to size the native code-cache event queue. The default is 4096 observations. When the queue fills, --overflow drop counts and drops the new observation. --overflow stop ends capture at the first overflow and reports that reason. Application stores continue in either mode.

For a standalone scalar with all its writers covered by the code-cache watch, set --serialize-wait-us N to serialize the observed stores and event publication for each field address. The wait is bounded by the supplied number of microseconds. If writers overlap after the wait or tracing is interrupted by re-entry, the event reports unavailable ordering and withholds the old value. A mismatch between consecutive value samples reports an intervening change outside the observed store sequence. The default uses concurrent capture.

Use --shared-file PATH on each process's native std::atomic<int> watch to correlate writes to a writable shared file mapping. A scalar watch can also use this option when the application protects the field with a process-shared lock and the watch declares --synchronization caller-lock. The server holds the file open, and the agent checks the live device, inode and byte offset. Recordings expose those three values as sharedStorage across overlapping watches on the same host. An atomic read-modify-write can report its own previous value. Coverage remains partial because other writers and their ordering are unknown. Both capture modes retain the shared storage identity.

Use --pointee "routes.head->node" --field state.quantity to follow a pointer path within a verified writer invocation. Dots select embedded members and arrows follow raw data pointers, verified libstdc++ default-deleter std::unique_ptr, and verified libstdc++ std::shared_ptr. Supply --mutation for the owner operation that changes the path and declare thread-confined or caller-lock synchronization. Each successful rebind starts a storage generation, even when the final address repeats. A null or unreadable path suspends write attribution and produces a coverage gap.

Trace a direct integer assignment

To find direct writes in source during preparation, pass --discover-writers, --compdb, and one or more --translation-unit arguments. The command saves source candidates with the ELF plan and can select their verified writer functions. Repeat --code to select additional verified writers, including writers that reach the field through aliases.

Build the tests/fixtures/person sources as separate translation units with -O2 -g and LTO disabled. Run the prebuilt fixture until it prints READY. The standalone watch binds a signed 32-bit field using the record layout from the writer's DWARF and a verified constructor return.

bash
%attach PID
%memory maps
%probe entry "demo::update(demo::Person &)" --mapping TOKEN
%memory read PC --mapping TOKEN --count SIZE
%object start --type demo::Person --field age --code "demo::update(demo::Person &)" --stack-depth 4
%memory maps
%memory read PC --mapping PATCHED_TOKEN --count SIZE
%record age.db --sqlite --name object.trace --count 2 --timeout 30
%detach
%attach PID
%memory maps
%memory read PC --mapping RESTORED_TOKEN --count SIZE
%events open age.db --as ages
%events show ages --index 1
%detach

Use the address and instruction size of the store shown by %probe entry. Enter g in the fixture terminal while recording to construct the Person with age 42 and assign 1 twice. The watch records the original writer PC and DWARF source line. With --no-values, record three events to include the constructor and both writes. After verifying the restored instruction, enter r to read the live value. After the last detach, enter v to run the assignment again, then q to exit.

Trace atomic integer updates

For a DWARF-verified libstdc++ std::atomic<int> field, the watch admits 32-bit mov, lock xadd, and lock cmpxchg in the selected function. With values enabled, a store takes its new value from the source operand and displays old=unavailable. Fetch-add uses the returned old value and the input increment. Compare-and-exchange emits a write only when the post-instruction zero flag is set, including in --no-values mode. The diagnostic backend steps the complete instruction, including LOCK. At detach it restores the full original bytes and rewinds any owned trap that has yet to execute.

Decode a tagged union write

Pass --union-tag FIELD and a --union-case TAG=MEMBER for each admitted alternative. Use a direct member path such as --field payload.integer to identify the four-byte storage, and declare --synchronization thread-confined or caller-lock to protect the tag and storage during both samples.

bash
%object prepare tagged_test::State --module ./fixture --field payload.integer --code _ZN11tagged_test10write_bitsERNS_5StateEj --union-tag kind --union-case 1=integer --union-case 2=real --synchronization thread-confined --backend code-cache --output watch

The plan checks the tag offset and each alternative against DWARF. A tag can be an unsigned 32-bit field or an enum with that underlying type. Signed integers, unsigned integers, and floats are supported as 32-bit alternatives. Unknown or unreadable tags retain raw storage bytes. --no-values skips both the discriminator and storage reads.

Trace writes in the native code cache

bash
%object start --backend code-cache --type demo::Person --field age --code person_write_many
%object status
%record age.db --sqlite --name object.trace --count 4000 --timeout 30
%detach

ptrace is the default. Select code-cache to translate verified leaf functions or independently verified writer fragments into executable memory in the target. Standalone signed 32-bit fields and std::atomic<int> use complete constructor and destructor boundaries in the main executable. On x86-64, a standalone leaf writer with a visible function pointer or virtual entry uses a verified entry redirect. This covers direct calls, function pointers, and vtable dispatch into that writer. Use --writer-entry to require this coverage for every selected leaf, including with repeated --code. An entry redirect needs a verified overwrite window. Short leaves can use verified alignment padding. A symbol export alone allows a fallback to direct call sites when no entry window verifies. Preview and status report partial coverage for direct call sites alone. For a shared writer, --module takes a unique mapped ELF basename or absolute path. A shared leaf that uses an entry redirect needs a verified nonfaulting overwrite window. Native watches capture virtual destruction at the destructor entry, including deleting destructors that inline the complete destructor. A watch fails to start if its virtual destructor has no verified redirect. When code-cache capture relies on direct calls or return continuations, preview and start reject unverified call sites, including sites behind unresolved jump tables. Supported ELF exception tables let the planner verify calls in cleanup blocks, including direct branches into a matching cold partition. The diagnostic backend rejects writers with an unresolved indirect branch, such as a jump table. Inlined lifetimes, forked children, and unadmitted store instructions are outside coverage.

Application threads run the original store encoding once in the translated function. The agent reads the effective address and operands around that instruction and publishes to a shared event queue. --no-values skips value sampling and still checks the outcome of compare-and-exchange. %object status reports each redirect, the number of completed translated store instructions, and event drops. The store count includes failed compare-and-exchanges and stores to untracked addresses.

Events use the original application PC. For a synchronous SIGSEGV, SIGBUS, SIGFPE, or SIGILL on a copied instruction, a chained application handler sees that PC and can retry or skip the instruction. If the signal takes its default action and the original instruction is covered by a redirect or cannot be verified, the kernel delivers the fault at the translated PC. Keep fault signal dispositions stable during tracing. Use --async-signal N for a signal with an existing application handler. At a copied application instruction the handler sees the original PC and can resume or select another original instruction. The x86-64 and AArch64 hooks defer these signals during supported capture callbacks and runtime call resolution when system calls are unfiltered. The handler sees the original callee and caller return address after ordinary and tail call resolution. For AArch64 scalable state that fits the fixed Linux signal frame, the agent restores the spilled SVE or SME records before invoking the handler. Delivery in an uncovered helper window records a coverage gap. Optional stacks use available application frame pointers. The hooks use application stack space to save registers and extended processor state. --stack-cfi with --stack-depth N unwinds from the saved application registers and original store PC. The emitted stack reports whether CFI reached the root, hit the depth limit, or stopped at a missing rule. Unwinding directly through generated helper code remains unavailable.

Stop or detach restores the complete redirect instructions and drains queued observations. The agent releases retired translated bodies after active executions have drained. Stable entry and exit stubs and the associated signal metadata remain available for delayed execution. When the process replaces its executable image, status closes the watch with a mapping-change coverage gap after confirming the old redirects and translated code are absent.

Trace scalar writes on Linux AArch64

Use the normal REPL with the AArch64 object server. Offline preparation, preview, lifecycle and scalar write events, SQLite recording, and replay use the same commands and event types as on x86-64. The diagnostic backend uses four-byte breakpoint instructions. The code-cache backend installs four-byte branches to relocated instructions and releases ptrace control after arming.

bash
%attach PID
%object start --type arm_test::Record --field value --code arm_write_value --backend code-cache
%record writes.db --sqlite --name object.trace --count 10 --timeout 30
%object stop

Live installation selects an application thread at a verified idle sleep or a userspace rendezvous. For a rendezvous, pass --rendezvous SYMBOL and select an existing main-image function where the thread can safely enter the loader. Threads created after installation can execute the redirects. The backend supports 32-bit STR/STUR, release stores, LSE fetch-add with a returned prior value, and LSE compare-and-exchange. An admitted writer in a loaded shared library can be selected with --module. CFI capture follows saved link registers, including signed return addresses. In-process capture preserves SVE vector, predicate, and first-fault registers. Injection and capture also preserve SME streaming state, ZA, TPIDR2 and, on SME2, ZT0.

Follow live callees

bash
%object start --type demo::Record --field value --backend code-cache --code dispatch --follow-calls

The selected executable or mapped shared-library scope supplies the call sites. A verified direct or indirect call enters a native gateway with its original return address. Calls already covered by lifetime boundaries retain those redirects. Verified direct edges can extend the selected scope to nested functions in the same image that keep executing at their original PCs. A runtime gateway checks live targets against their ELF bytes and translates supported leaf instructions and tail calls. For a discovered nonleaf scope, the controller verifies and installs its call and store redirects before the first covered execution. Its original call sites keep their return PCs. Ordinary stores run without controller stops. Stores match the watched address and lifetime even when the callee receives it through an alias. Replayed stores include the mapped ELF identity and the runtime module generation. A shared library can load after arming and unload between calls.

Use --runtime-limit N to bound nested scope discovery and retained translations. The default is 1,024. When a callee exceeds the limit or its code cannot be verified and translated, the original call runs and the watch records a coverage gap. Stopping restores the redirects and closes entry to cached callees. The agent releases each retired callee mapping after its active executions have drained. A shared scope selected with --module keeps a loader reference through patch restoration and drain. %object status reports runtime translation and release counts.

Observe startup before main

clang-tracer-object-watch launch definition.json ./target [ARGS...] starts a selected prebuilt ELF under the diagnostic backend and arms the watch at the Linux exec stop. The definition is a JSON object watch request with concreteType, field, and codeSymbol. The command emits JSON event lines and the exec-stop coverage marker to stdout. The target's output goes to stderr and its stdin reads EOF. SIGINT requests live detachment and exact patch restoration.

For a native code-cache definition, run clang-tracer-object-watch launch --agent ./libclang_tracer_agent.so definition.json ./target [ARGS...] with the agent built for the target architecture. This arms at the verified ELF executable entry after the dynamic loader transfers control. The executable-entry marker identifies the start of coverage, which includes constructors run by the executable startup code and main.

On an eligible glibc target, add --loader-ready after the agent path to arm after relocation and before preinit and dependency constructors. The launcher verifies the loader mapping and its consistent-state notification. Set codeModule in the JSON definition to select a shared library already present in the initial loader link map.

Use --syscall-output --synchronization thread-confined on a diagnostic scalar watch to observe read and pread when the destination is the exact 32-bit field. A short, overlapping, or unreadable output records a coverage gap and withholds the values. These events identify the verified syscall instruction and its mapped image.

Trace a virtual write through a borrowed reference

bash
%object start --backend code-cache --type demo::Circle --base demo::Shape --owner demo::Image --collection _shapes --field radius --caller borrowed_resize --module libct-shapes-gcc85.so --code "demo::Circle::resize(int)"
%record radius.db --sqlite --name object.trace --count 2 --timeout 30
%object status
%detach

The named main-executable caller must call the leaf getter directly, then reach one register- or memory-indirect near call along a straight-line path with a stable stack pointer and no intervening stores. The call executes in place and resolves its target normally. A verified entry jump at the selected writer preserves the original call frame and any ENDBR64 landing instruction. Other targets execute through their original entries.

The watch starts before construction. A verified return from the complete constructor registers a lifetime ID and advances the generation at its address. The constructor may use relocatable RIP-relative loads or address computations. A leaf Image::add returns the inserted pointer in RAX, and the agent confirms membership in the DWARF-verified vector of unique pointers. The getter and writer check that owner, the primary-base RTTI, and the live lifetime ID. Each operation also carries a borrow_id.

The deleting and complete destructor entries retire the lifetime before their original bodies continue. A deleting destructor that invokes the complete destructor produces one retirement. If the owner has already cleared the slot, the same boundary emits OWNER_REMOVED. The fixture uses unique_ptr::reset for that ordering and a class allocator that reuses one aligned slot. Each lifetime has its own ID even when the object address and name repeat.

The verified lifecycle path covers a concrete type with an unambiguous complete-constructor entry, including aliases for a final type. It needs a leaf constructor and add, safe entry windows, and a stable owner during the borrowed operation. Ambiguous base construction, inlined boundaries, arbitrary owner mutations, and string snapshots are outside coverage. Destruction reports its start. The fixture independently checks completed deallocation and reuse.

The loader pins the selected shared image at its verified load bias for the lifetime of the retained translation. Patch installation and restoration verify the live file-backed mappings while the target threads are stopped. This supports uniquely mapped, loader-managed ELF images in the base namespace. Manual unmapping, alternate loader namespaces, and indirect tail jumps at the borrow site are outside coverage.

Interceptor upload

bash
%server status
%sessions
%modules
%symbols --filter Calculator --limit 20
%probe resolve "Calculator::multiply(int, int) const"
%interceptor load method.cpp --as multiply_hook
%interceptor show multiply_hook
%interceptor validate multiply_hook --target "Calculator::multiply(int, int) const"
%interceptor upload multiply_hook --target "Calculator::multiply(int, int) const" --stack-depth 16
%probes

load reads the file on the console machine. upload sends its source by value through ResolveProbe/AddProbe and reports success only for an active probe. The draft remains available after deployment errors. Use --stack-depth full --stack-application-only false to capture through the thread root and include runtime and JIT frames. A numeric depth caps the unwind at that many frames before filtering. For large shared events, pass --context-event-bytes 25165824 --context-transport-memory-bytes 234881024 to the REPL at launch or to %server start for 24 MiB events. Pass the same options to clang-tracer-server when starting an external server. For REPL collections, --buffer-bytes controls how much space is available for the retained event and its projected stack. The short equivalent is:

bash
%probe inject "Calculator::multiply(int, int) const" --callback method.cpp

Omit --callback to use the built-in observer for event capture, including receiver snapshots when class layout is available.

Use %interceptor edit NAME for a multiline draft, .end to save, and .cancel to discard. %probe validate SELECTOR --callback FILE requests validation. Resolution/deployment options include --include, --compdb, --module and repeatable --compile-option. Headers and compilation-database paths refer to the server host. Source files are limited to 4 MiB. Uploaded interceptors are compiled by the server/agent; local REPL variables, pointers and lambdas are not implicitly transferred into the target.

Probe working directory

Add --cwd DIRECTORY to any %probe subcommand or to %probes. Relative paths for that command use the specified directory on the REPL host. This includes callbacks, prepared packages, supplemental include paths, and preparation inputs and output. Backtick expansions also run in that directory. For server-side headers, databases and translation units, the resulting paths must be accessible on the server host. Paths inside raw --compile-option arguments follow the compiler's working directory. A plain module name still works as a filter. Later commands use their own working directory.

bash
%probe prepare "demo::compute(int)" --include src/compute.cpp --output prepared --cwd /work/demo
%probe inject "demo::compute(int)" --callback hook.cpp --prepared prepared --cwd /work/demo

Preparation looks for compile_commands.json in the command's working directory by default. With either a database file or a directory supplied through --compdb, it prefers a unique recorded command for the first include. If the include has no entry, it uses the first source beside it. Use a unique --translation-unit or a narrower database when the included source has multiple commands.

Supplemental probe compiler arguments

Use --extra-arg for one compiler argument and --extra-args for a list. Backticks run a command on the REPL host and split its stdout into arguments. A failed shell command stops the probe command.

bash
%probe prepare "Calculator::multiply(int, int) const" --include calculator.hpp --output multiply --extra-args `my-conf --cxxflags`
%probe inject "Calculator::multiply(int, int) const" --callback method.cpp --prepared multiply --extra-args "-I/opt/project/include -DTRACE_EXTRA=1"

Set defaults for preparation and agent compilation at REPL startup.

bash
clang-tracer-repl --attach 12345 --extra-arg=-DTRACE_EXTRA=1
clang-tracer-repl --attach 12345 --extra-args "$(my-conf --cxxflags)"

Supplemental -I, -isystem, and -idirafter directories are searched after the selected toolchain and compilation database directories. Supplemental -D accepts new object-like macros and rejects names defined or undefined by the compilation database. The clang-cl spellings /I and /D are also accepted. The selected driver, language standard, target, sysroot, and ABI remain authoritative. Preparation extras apply while reading the original headers. Pass callback-specific extras to injection or at startup. Relative supplemental include paths are resolved from the probe command's working directory, which defaults to the REPL's working directory. These paths must be visible to the agent during callback compilation.

Attach checks the loaded agent's bootstrap protocol and ELF build ID against the server and its configured agent file before accepting the session. Use %sessions to see the process start time and target JIT runtime profile. The reported libstdc++ header release and C++11 ABI flag describe the agent build defaults. Probe-specific flags and target signature ABI checks still apply. Successful installs report resolve, target JIT compile and patch durations in nanoseconds when the server supports them.

Reload an observer

bash
%probe reload PROBE_ID --callback observer-v2.cpp

Use the ID of the active probe. Reload keeps its target binding, ABI and deployment options. The agent prepares the new observer before switching the entry. A rejected callback or a switch that rolls back leaves the existing observer in place. Cancellation is checked up to the entry switch. Use %probes to identify the current generation if the reply is interrupted.

The entry switches directly to the new wrapper. Calls that already entered the previous wrapper finish there, with both PRE and POST tagged by the previous probe ID. A successful reload reports the new ID and retained capacity. The 32-slot process limit includes retired wrappers, which stay resident for safe late arrivals. Remove the active generation to restore the original entry. Removing a superseded generation drains it while leaving the successor in place. Detach drains all generations.

Borrow target pointers and references only during the callback. Use owned snapshots for REPL inspection and replay.

Opt in to scalar overrides

Mark an eligible free-function definition in the application and build it with Clang and DWARF. The marker declares the ordinary Linux x86-64 SysV ABI. Use it on functions that follow the standard register preservation rules. The agent verifies the marked ELF section, mapped entry, calling convention, and complete scalar signature before installing a detour.

cpp
#include <tracer/override_target.hpp>

TRACER_SCALAR_OVERRIDE_TARGET int compute(int input) { return input * 2; }

In the callback, request an argument change in pre() or a return change in post(). Indexes start at zero.

cpp
struct Interceptor {
  void pre(const Call &call) {
    if (call.arg<int>(0) == 10)
      call.override_argument(0, 12);
  }
  void post(const Call &call) {
    if (call.result<int>() == 24)
      call.override_result(25);
  }
};
bash
%probe validate "compute(int)" --callback override.cpp --allow-arg-overrides --allow-result-override
%probe inject "compute(int)" --callback override.cpp --allow-arg-overrides --allow-result-override

Each flag enables only its corresponding hook operation. Overrides require a local Unix control socket and a DWARF binding. Use --prepared-mode off if a prepared package would otherwise be selected. Supported values are bool, signed 32- and 64-bit integers, unsigned 64-bit integers, float, and double. Match the slot's type and width exactly. A void function can use argument overrides.

The original function runs with the committed arguments. An escaping hook exception discards its staged writes. An exception from the original function propagates to its caller without running post(). Overrides apply per call, including recursion, and preserve the original function's errno behavior. PRE events show the incoming arguments. POST events show the arguments used by the function and its original return value. Reload retains the permissions of the active generation. Removing the probe or detaching restores the function entry.

Collect and inspect

Missing semicolons inside loops or conditionals are syntax errors. They are rejected by the isolated checker before the live interpreter parses the cell; earlier variables, sessions and background collectors remain usable. Bare top-level void calls retain their optional trailing semicolon. Temporary collections can be inspected directly, including live.snapshot().size().

C++17 event ranges

Synchronous collection waits for the count, timeout (30 seconds by default), or Ctrl+C, then returns an iterable snapshot range:

cpp
auto captured = tracer.events(session, 100, 10);
for (const auto &event : captured) tracer.print(event);

Background collection returns immediately so the prompt remains usable:

cpp
auto live = tracer.events_async(session, 100, 10);
// Enter other REPL commands while collection continues.
auto data = live.snapshot();
for (const auto &event : live) tracer.print(event);
live.running();
live.error();
live.stop();

Iteration streams. Each loop starts at the oldest retained event, then waits for later ones and yields each as the agent sends it. The loop ends when the collector finishes (count, timeout, stop() or a stream error) or on Ctrl+C, which leaves the collector running. Iterating a finished range visits its retained events without waiting, and no loop consumes events, so later loops can include the same ones. A range with neither count nor timeout is iterated until Ctrl+C or stop(). snapshot() never waits; it returns a Collection of the currently retained events with received/evicted counters and completion, cancellation and timeout flags.
