Stream failures appear in error() in either mode; partial results remain inspectable. events_async(session, 100, 10) stops at 100 events or 10 seconds; zero count/timeout means no corresponding limit. Synchronous counts and timeouts must be positive. Both modes use C++17, without coroutines or C++20 ranges.

A range reserves the remaining shared event-count and byte budget. While it is retained, another capture may have no room; release all copies of the range (for example, with %cpp reset) to free that reservation. Snapshots can retain their owned events beyond that point. The oldest events are evicted at the budget limit. Stopping preserves the range and its reservation. The last range copy's destruction, session detach, disconnection and console shutdown cancel and join its worker. Workers never execute user C++ or print into the prompt. The controller/facade remains a foreground API; use these range handles rather than calling the facade from user-created threads.

Use %help api EventRange for the range API. Existing tracer.collect(...) and named collection commands retain their behavior.

C++17 collection adaptors

Use %help api adaptors for an overview, or look up an individual operation with %help api drop, %help api filter, or any other adaptor name.

take, drop, filter, take_while, drop_while, transform, stride, enumerate, reverse, to_vector, and first are available directly in the REPL. They also work with Collection values from collect, batch, and snapshot:

cpp
auto events = tracer.events(session, 100, 10);
for (const auto& e : events | take(10)) tracer.print(e);
auto is_post = [](const auto& e) { return e.phase() == "POST"; };
for (const auto& e : events | filter(is_post) | take(10)) tracer.print(e);
for (const auto& e : events | drop(5) | take(10)) tracer.print(e);
auto early = [](const auto& e) { return e.sequence() < 50; };
for (const auto& e : events | take_while(early)) tracer.print(e);
auto first_post = events | filter([](const auto& e) {
  return e.phase() == "POST";
}) | first();
if (first_post) tracer.print(*first_post);
auto names = events | transform([](const auto& e) {
  return e.function_name();
}) | to_vector();
for (const auto& [index, e] : events | stride(2) | enumerate()) {
  std::cout << index << ": " << e.function_name() << std::endl;
}
auto newest_first = events | reverse();
auto tail = events | drop_while([](const auto& e) {
  return e.sequence() < 50;
}) | to_vector();

take(n) returns at most the first n events; drop(n) skips the first n; filter(predicate) keeps matching events; take_while(predicate) stops at the first non-match. first() is a terminal adaptor returning an owned std::optional<Event>, empty when there is no match. Counts must be nonnegative. Predicates are evaluated lazily during iteration, and pipe order matters: filter(p) | take(10) takes ten matches, while take(10) | filter(p) tests only the first ten events. take(0) does not evaluate predicates.

Declare predicates before using them in a top-level REPL loop, or store the pipeline in a variable first. Clang Interpreter can crash while mangling an inline lambda inside a top-level loop; ordinary compiled C++ accepts it.

drop_while(p) skips only the initial matching prefix. transform(f) lazily projects each event into an owned value, such as its name, sequence or typed argument. stride(n) selects every nth element, starting with the first; n must be positive. enumerate() pairs each element with a zero-based index in the current pipeline. to_vector() materializes the selected values into an owned vector; reverse() materializes a vector in reverse order. These two operations evaluate their input immediately. Materialized results and views can be piped into further adaptors. Exceptions from predicates/projections propagate on the foreground thread.

Views own their input: lvalue collections are copied and temporaries are moved, so stored pipelines remain valid. An event-range view retains its collector handle and streams from the oldest retained event at each loop's start, without consuming events. Thus live | take(10) yields ten events, waiting for those that have not arrived yet, and returns as soon as the tenth is read; it does not limit background collection. Use live.snapshot() | take(10) to inspect only currently retained events, and tracer.events_async(session, 10, 5) to limit collection itself. Other C++ code can include event_ranges.hpp and use the tracer_repl namespace explicitly.

Console commands

bash
%events
%collect --as live
%collect --count 100 --timeout 10 --as batch
%events list batch --limit 20
%events show batch --index 0
%events stack batch --index 0
%events calls batch
%events stats batch
%record capture.pb --count 1000
%record capture.db --sqlite --count 1000
%events open capture.pb --as saved
%events open capture.db --as stored
%events stats saved
%events export saved --format json --output events.json
%events clear saved

%events, %collect, and %record run until Ctrl+C when no count is supplied. Ctrl+C cancels the stream, returns to the prompt, and leaves probes and the server running. Counted streams default to a 30-second total timeout; explicit --timeout overrides it. Partial batches survive cancellation, timeout, or a service error and report their completion state and last cursor.

Filter with --probe ID, --phase PRE|POST, repeatable --name SELECTOR, --session ID, --all, and --after CURSOR. Selection defaults to the current session. Name/session/sequence filters go to the service; probe and phase filters are applied locally, and counts refer to matching events.

All named collections share the configured event-count and Protobuf resident allocation budget (defaults: 4096 events, 64 MiB, plus bounded container overhead). A collecting ring evicts its oldest events when full and reports local evictions separately from agent/server loss counters. Existing named collections reserve their capacity; clear them to make room. C++ snapshots keep their own shared references and can retain events after the console releases them. Collecting again under the same name releases that collection before receiving new events. Offline replay requires an unused name or an explicit %events clear first, so a corrupt recording cannot overwrite an existing capture.

Detail inspection shows typed arguments/results, receiver fields, stack frames, and raw metadata. %events stack NAME --index N prints the capture status and each retained stack frame directly, including frames from replayed events. In C++, event.stack() returns an owned vector of frames in capture order. It is empty when the event has no stored frames.

cpp
auto event = tracer.batch("batch").at(0);
for (const auto& frame : event.stack()) { std::cout << frame.pc << ' ' << frame.function << '\n'; }

Shared-state payloads are decoded with their attached schema when available. Native PRE/POST pairing includes server lifetime, session, probe, thread and call identity, and marks missing halves. Shared-context invocation/task identities remain available in event details. Loss statistics sum the latest observed cumulative agent counter per probe and server counter per server lifetime, without counting repeated samples twice. Unknown native phases remain inspectable and are counted outside PRE/POST pairs.

%events stats NAME uses the same summary for captured and replayed collections. Each function row counts distinct observed calls for a probe in its process and session. A call with just one phase contributes to missing_pre or missing_post. Only a pair with one unambiguous timestamp per phase and a nonnegative interval contributes to timed and the histogram. Histogram labels are inclusive nanosecond ranges, with empty buckets omitted and a final bucket for one second or longer. Durations measure the elapsed interval between the two trace timestamps, including tracing overhead.

Caller edges count calls with evidence of the direct native caller in either phase's entry stack. Caller labels use the function and module when available, then the module offset or native PC. caller_unknown counts calls whose stack does not establish that edge. Enable stack capture with --stack-depth 8 when installing a single probe. For a bulk manifest, pass this observer with %trace apply --manifest trace.textproto --callback observer.cpp to capture the stack on PRE and retain both phases for timing.

cpp
struct Interceptor {
  void pre(const Call& call) { call.capture_stack(8, false); }
  void post(const Call&) {}
};

Agent and server loss counters are cumulative samples from retained events. They and local buffer evictions are reported separately from incomplete calls.

By default, %record uses four-byte little-endian lengths and Protobuf TraceEvent frames, with a 32 MiB per-frame limit. Framed recording and export create new files exclusively. %record FILE --sqlite creates or appends to a SQLite recording and deduplicates events by server instance and sequence. Replay rejects truncated headers/bodies and invalid messages. A failed recording keeps its partial file. Offline loading retains the configured bounded window.

Query a recording offline

Open the native console without attaching to a process. To browse a SQLite recording from clang-tracer drain --sqlite, use the same commands as for a framed Protobuf recording.

bash
%events open capture.db --as saved
%events list saved --limit 10
%events show saved --index 0

Use tracer.replay to filter the recording before loading a collection.

cpp
tracer_repl::EventQuery query;
query.names = {"demo::compute(int)"};
query.phase = "POST";
query.count = 20;
auto matches = tracer.replay("capture.db", query);
for (const auto& event : matches) std::cout << event.result_as<int>() << '\n';

Set pid or session_id to narrow a capture that contains multiple processes or sessions. Names match exact function selectors or custom event names. A list of names matches any of them, and the other filters are combined. A positive count reads up to that many matches in recording order. Zero reads all matches and retains the latest events that fit the memory budget. received and evicted show how much of the query was retained. Replay opens SQLite read-only and works after the target and tracing server have exited. The results support the same typed accessors and C++ adaptors as live events.

The native SQLite recorders (%record FILE --sqlite, tracer.record(), clang-tracer events --sqlite, and clang-tracer drain --sqlite) save the standalone C++ type bundle for prepared probes with custom state. Opening the database or calling tracer.replay makes those types and their generated mappings available at the next prompt. A fresh REPL can reconstruct the recorded C++ value without access to the application headers:

text
tracer_repl::EventQuery query;
query.names = {"account.adjusted"};
query.count = 1;
auto matches = tracer.replay("capture.db", query);
auto reading = matches.at(0).state_as<prepared_demo::Reading>();

Earlier recordings and recordings without a standalone type bundle still support state_snapshot() and explicit C++ imports. Replay checks the saved declarations before loading them. If a declaration is unsupported or conflicts with a type already loaded in the REPL, the recorded fields remain inspectable.

To record from C++, call tracer.record while attached.

cpp
tracer_repl::RecordOptions options;
options.names = {"account.adjusted"};
options.count = 12;
options.timeout_seconds = 15;
auto saved = tracer.record("capture.db", options);

This creates or appends to the SQLite recording. By default it uses the selected session. Set options.session to another session handle or options.all_sessions to record from all sessions. The filters also include phase, probe_id, and after_sequence. saved.complete reports whether the requested count was reached. Use saved.received, saved.cursor, saved.cancelled, and saved.timed_out to inspect the outcome. See %help api tracer.record for the native REPL topic.

Analyze in C++

Discover the API from the prompt before writing analysis:

bash
%help
%help probe inject
%help api
%help api tracer
%help api Event
%help api tracer.events_async
%complete "tracer."

The command index groups commands by task. Look up a command or subcommand for its usage, options, and examples. The C++ API index lists types and operations. Individual API topics explain when to use them and show C++ examples. Type topics also show the public signatures from the loaded declarations. Shortcuts such as %help Event still work. Help uses syntax highlighting on color terminals and plain text for redirected output or when NO_COLOR is set.

Tab completes commands, subcommands, options, known option values, help topics, and C++ keywords and members. For example, %collect --ph completes to --phase, and %collect --phase PO completes to POST. In a path argument such as %cpp load ./ or %probe prepare "demo()" --cwd ./, Tab lists local matches. Directories end in / so you can continue completing the path. Quoted C++ includes also complete local paths.

Press Tab after #incl, if, for, while, %cpp load, or %probe prepare to insert a template. Type to replace the current placeholder and press Tab or Shift+Tab to move between placeholders. Use Alt+/ to complete a value while editing a placeholder. For %probe inject, Tab moves from the selector to an optional arguments field. Type %probe inject --callback or %probe inject --prepared before Tab to start with a path placeholder. The editor closes brackets and quotes as you type, and Enter indents continued C++ input. Inside an empty brace pair, Enter opens an indented line between the braces.

Member completion for expressions such as tracer., data., and data.at(0). uses Clang and the session's accepted inputs. %complete "data.at(0)." prints the same candidates when data has been declared. Completion parses code without executing it or issuing tracing operations. It runs on Tab, rather than on each keystroke; longer sessions can increase completion time. %cpp reset clears that session. Declarations remain discoverable after an execution exception. After a C++ parse error, use %cpp reset to restore synchronized completion and bare expressions; tracing commands, API help and statements terminated with ; remain available. Ambiguous bare input reports recovery guidance instead of silently dropping a call.

Use %type SYMBOL to inspect a declaration in the current C++ session. The command accepts simple names, qualified names such as ns::function, and members such as tracer.events_async. It lists function overloads and shows readable types such as std::string and std::map<std::string, int>. It looks up declarations without evaluating C++ expressions.

Color terminals distinguish preprocessor directives, include headers, C++ keywords, strings, numbers, operators, percent commands, options, and comments. The prompt, help examples, and %type output share the palette.

Ordinary C++ checks retain accepted syntax in a separate, syntax-only compiler process. Each new input is checked in a disposable fork, so rejected declarations and macros cannot corrupt the retained state or execute initializers. Later inputs avoid reparsing the API and earlier cells; first use still initializes both compilers. %cpp reset releases this checker along with the local C++ state. Cancellation and the existing 15-second check deadline terminate only the owned checker process group. Completion and header generation use separate helpers.

cpp
auto data = tracer.batch("batch");
data.size()
data.at(0).argument(0)
std::cout << data.at(1).result() << std::endl;
tracer.print(data.at(0))
tracer.print(data)
int argument = data.at(0).argument_as<int>(0);
for (const auto &event : data) { if (event.has_result()) std::cout << event.result_as<int>() + argument << std::endl; }
for (const auto &event : data) tracer.print(event);
auto captured_session = session;
auto more = tracer.collect(captured_session, 100, 10);
more.complete
more.timed_out

argument_as<T>(index) and result_as<T>() return owned C++ values for live and replayed events, including shared-context events. For a function with a captured boolean argument/result:

cpp
bool input = event.argument_as<bool>(0);
bool output = event.result_as<bool>();
if (output && input) std::cout << "both true" << std::endl;

Bool access requires a captured BOOL; integral access requires INT32, INT64, or UINT64; floating access requires FLOAT32 or FLOAT64. Integer conversions check the destination range, including signed/unsigned boundaries. Floating conversions check range and round to the requested precision; NaN and infinity are preserved. Mismatched types, missing/invalid payloads and void throw std::invalid_argument. Addresses without a captured snapshot cannot become a string or local object. Out-of-range numeric conversions and argument indices throw std::out_of_range. A missing result throws std::runtime_error; use has_result() to check presence before accessing it. Native PRE events normally have no result.

result_value() and argument_value(index) return a ScalarValue, defined as std::variant<bool, std::int64_t, std::uint64_t, double>, for generic analysis with std::get, std::get_if, or std::visit. The existing result() and argument(index) methods remain text formatters. Inspect a complete event with tracer.print(event) or %events show batch --index 1.

Strings and class/struct values

New captures copy string and record contents while the target objects are alive. argument_as<std::string>(index) and result_as<std::string>() return owned strings, preserving empty strings, embedded NUL and arbitrary bytes. Reference/value arguments are snapshotted at entry; POST events retain that entry snapshot even if the function mutates or frees the original contents. Return objects are captured at return, before leaving their valid lifetime.

For a raw pointer to a record with layout metadata, add --snapshot-return-pointee to %probe inject. The built-in observer copies the fields immediately after the function returns. Use a type declaration that matches the target build and ensure each non-null pointer refers to a live object whose fields are stable during capture. Read the fields with event.result_snapshot() or decode an owned T with event.result_as<T>() after importing a mapping for T. event.result() still shows the address, including 0x0 for null returns.

For a polymorphic pointer return, preparation discovers eligible implementations from the matching source inputs. RTTI selects a prepared concrete layout during capture. Other live objects use the declared base layout. Pass an implementation's .cpp with --include if its definition is in that file. For typed local decoding of a polymorphic snapshot, supply an EventCodec<T> for the value you want to construct.

For source-prepared probes, Clang also discovers the raw pointer and reference members of every captured record (arguments, receivers, and results, including members declared by public non-virtual bases) and follows them. A field such as _imp holds the original address and _imp_snapshot holds the copied fields of the live pointee; a reference member is captured the same way. For a polymorphic pointee the admitted layouts are the declared class, when it is concrete, and concrete derived classes available from the supplied source, and a checked RTTI read selects the matching layout. A non-polymorphic pointee is captured by its exact static type, so no policy is needed, provided everything the capture must read is checkable: scalars, enums, arrays, strings, vector, array, optional, pair, tuple, variant, smart pointers to such types, and records of those. A pointee holding anything else (list, map, set, unordered_*, deque, std::any, std::function, weak_ptr) is followed automatically only when it is polymorphic and its RTTI matches a derived class, or the declared class of an owner-held implementation pointer; otherwise it stays address-only unless a FollowPointers policy names it. Because there is no RTTI to check, only the pointer's alignment and the readability of the whole object are verified, and the target must keep the pointee valid and stable through POST. A char pointer is captured as a bounded (--string-bytes, longer text is truncated), readability-checked C string and a pointer to an arithmetic or enum value as one element; both are stored as <field>_snapshot. The same rules apply to the pointer and reference members of every captured pointee, of records held by value inside a captured record, and of the pointees of std::unique_ptr and std::shared_ptr members, to --follow-depth levels. A link back to an object that is already captured above it is not followed again, and a link cut by the depth bound stays address-only. Null, unreadable, unmapped, abstract, incomplete, std:: and function pointees remain address-only, and pointers stored inside standard containers are not followed. All roots are encoded before any followed member, shallowest members first, so a member that does not fit the per-thread snapshot storage is dropped and never displaces a root. Smart pointer members (std::unique_ptr, std::shared_ptr) are captured inline as their address plus a copy of the pointee. Pass --no-automatic-members to %probe prepare or to clang-tracer-prepare-injectors-native, or set TRACER_PREPARE_AUTOMATIC_MEMBERS=off in the environment of the prepare tool, to follow no members automatically. If a package cannot be built with the fuller captures, preparation falls back to narrower ones and reports each step on stderr. The agent, the REPL, and the prepare tool must come from the same build: an older REPL cannot read nested member snapshots and an older agent lacks the readability checks a newer package calls. Followed members are encoded in a checked mode: strings are copied out with a checked read, a vector's storage and a smart pointer's pointee must be wholly readable first, and a shared pointer's control block is never read, so a pointer the target left stale makes that member address-only instead of crashing the target. This relies on process_vm_readv; a seccomp filter that kills that call would kill the target. Policy-named members get the same checks, but a FollowPointers policy on a type the checks cannot cover (node-based containers, std::any, std::function, virtual bases, custom encoders) is your own assertion that the pointee is valid. Records with virtual bases, pairs and tuples with reference elements, vector<bool> and weak_ptr are never followed automatically. A pointee that needs a custom tracer_snapshot::encode is followed automatically only when its RTTI matches. Every limit on this capture is an option (see Followed-member limits); none is hard-coded. A pointer or reference to a private nested implementation class (class Widget { class Impl; Impl *impl_; };) is followed too, because the prepared adapter republishes nested class names. If the capture code that follows members does not compile, the probe is built without them and the validation report says so; setting TRACER_TEST_BREAK_FOLLOWED_MEMBERS in the target's environment forces that fallback for testing. In a followed member a weak_ptr is always recorded as expired, and a smart pointer whose pointee was left out by the checks or the read budget looks the same as one with no pointee.

Prepared packages of probes that share application types each declare those types. One REPL session keeps the first declaration of a type and drops the repeats from later packages, reporting them as reused imported types: ..., so several prepared probes on the same classes can be injected in one session.

A reusable record policy can follow specific raw pointer or reference fields wherever that record is captured as an argument, receiver, or result. Define the policy in a C++ header and supply it through the existing %probe prepare --include option alongside the matching application definitions. An explicit policy selects the member set for that record and can include non-polymorphic records.

cpp
namespace tracer_snapshot {
template<class Record> struct FollowPointers;

template<> struct FollowPointers<HFW::Item> {
  static constexpr const char* fields[] = {"_imp", "_other"};
};
}

Each configured field must refer to a live object with stable fields at the capture point. The record snapshot keeps its address field and adds an owned snapshot named <field>_snapshot for each captured pointee. For example, event.result_snapshot().field("_imp_snapshot") reports its concrete type from cpp_type(). A null member or a type absent from the prepared package has only the address. Pointer returns use --snapshot-return-pointee at injection. Reference returns already capture the referenced object.

Followed-member limits

Every bound on followed-member capture is an option. Nothing is hard-coded: the defaults below live in one place (SnapshotLimits in src/snapshot_limits.hpp), each option is validated against the same table, and when a limit cuts something the event or the prepare output says which option to raise.

Option Environment variable Set with Default Range Meaning
--follow-depth TRACER_PREPARE_FOLLOW_DEPTH prepare tool, %probe prepare, %probe inject 3 0-40 Levels of pointees followed below a captured record; 0 follows none.
--follow-members TRACER_PREPARE_FOLLOW_MEMBERS prepare tool, %probe prepare, %probe inject 48 0-4294967295 Followed members per probe, policy-named ones first. Each adds about 160 bytes of stack to the generated wrapper.
--record-members TRACER_PREPARE_RECORD_MEMBERS prepare tool, %probe prepare 32 0-4294967295 Pointer members discovered automatically per record.
--nested-depth TRACER_PREPARE_NESTED_DEPTH prepare tool, %probe prepare 2 0-4294967295 Levels of by-value records and smart pointers searched for pointer members.
--string-bytes TRACER_PREPARE_STRING_BYTES prepare tool, %probe prepare, %probe inject 4000 0-65536 Bytes kept of one string (char * or std::string) in a followed member. At most the slice minus 96 bytes of framing.
--vector-elements TRACER_PREPARE_VECTOR_ELEMENTS prepare tool, %probe prepare, %probe inject 4096 0-4294967295 Elements of a std::vector in a followed member; a larger vector is left out. The captured bytes must also fit --snapshot-slice (5000 int elements need --vector-elements 5000 --snapshot-slice 32768).
--checked-reads TRACER_PREPARE_CHECKED_READS prepare tool, %probe prepare, %probe inject 256 1-4294967295 Checked memory reads (system calls) one followed member may spend.
--snapshot-reserve TRACER_PREPARE_SNAPSHOT_RESERVE prepare tool, %probe prepare, %probe inject 8192 0-4294967295 Bytes of the per-thread storage that members captured at entry leave for the roots encoded later (a result, nested calls).
--snapshot-arena TRACER_PREPARE_SNAPSHOT_ARENA prepare tool, %probe prepare, %probe inject 16384 16384-4294967295 Per-thread storage for all snapshots of a call. Never shrinks: the largest request of any installed probe wins. At least one slice.
--snapshot-slice TRACER_PREPARE_SNAPSHOT_SLICE prepare tool, %probe prepare, %probe inject 4096 4096-65536 Bytes of one snapshot payload. Never shrinks: the largest request wins.

Besides these, --no-automatic-members (prepare tool flag, %probe prepare option, or TRACER_PREPARE_AUTOMATIC_MEMBERS=off) follows no member automatically, and TRACER_REPL_DERIVED_CANDIDATES (environment of the REPL, default 15) sets how many derived records are tried per polymorphic pointer when the REPL builds its local mappings; a pointer with more candidates is reported in the mapping notes.

A value is a number, unlimited (the largest value in the Range column) or, where the range starts at 0, off (0). A value outside the range is refused with the range, for example --follow-depth must be between 0 and 40 (or unlimited): 99. A prepare-time option shapes the package, so %probe inject can only lower what the package discovered; the other options can be given at either step, and the one given at %probe inject wins. The three maxima that are not "as large as the option holds" are forced by something else:

  • --snapshot-slice 65536 and, through it, --string-bytes: a payload is one string field of the event, which the event writer bounds at 64 KiB (limits.string_bytes in src/context_capture.cpp). The whole event is also bounded by the server's --context-event-bytes (default 256 KiB).
  • --follow-depth 40: every followed level nests two protobuf messages in the event, and the protobuf parser refuses more than 100 levels when the server and the REPL read it. Measured end to end, a chain arrives up to 49 levels in a result and 48 in an argument and the event is lost beyond that; 40 keeps eight levels of slack for the receiver and state roots that were not measured.
  • --snapshot-arena and --snapshot-slice have the built-in sizes as their minimum because the per-thread storage only grows.
  • --snapshot-arena accepts up to 4294967295 bytes, but the storage is one anonymous mapping per thread of the target, so unlimited asks every thread for 4 GiB of address space. If a mapping fails the storage keeps its size and the capture reports no snapshot storage was left for a followed member.

Tune them where the data lives. The depth and the char * size, for the handle example (examples/prepared-injectors/handle):

bash
%probe prepare "HFW::HfwManager::getItem(int)" --include item.hpp --include item-impl.hpp --output prepared --follow-depth 5
%probe inject "HFW::HfwManager::getItem(int)" --prepared prepared --prepared-mode require --string-bytes 6000 --snapshot-slice 8192 --snapshot-arena 65536

or TRACER_PREPARE_FOLLOW_DEPTH=5 in the environment of the REPL or of clang-tracer-prepare-injectors-native.

What you see when a limit cuts something:

Cut Where Text
Pointer members of a record are beyond --follow-depth (prepare) prepare stderr, once per record prepare: pointer members of NAME are address-only: it is N levels below a captured record (--follow-depth, TRACER_PREPARE_FOLLOW_DEPTH)
More pointer members than --record-members (prepare) prepare stderr, once per record prepare: NAME has more followable members than --record-members (N); the rest stay address-only
Pointer members nested deeper than --nested-depth (prepare) prepare stderr, once per record prepare: NAME has pointer members nested more than --nested-depth (N) levels inside it; they stay address-only
Derived records beyond TRACER_REPL_DERIVED_CANDIDATES mapping notes of the REPL derived records of NAME beyond N are not tried (TRACER_REPL_DERIVED_CANDIDATES)
A member's own pointer members were not followed (--follow-depth) field <field>_snapshot_cut of the parent its pointer members were not followed: raise --follow-depth
Members dropped by --follow-members below a member field <field>_snapshot_cut of the parent some of its pointer members were not followed: raise --follow-members
Members dropped by --follow-members at a root field snapshot_cut of the root N pointer members were not followed: raise --follow-members
String shortened (--string-bytes, or the slice bounds it) field <field>_snapshot_cut a C string was shortened: raise --string-bytes (and --snapshot-slice, which also bounds it) (a string was ... for a std::string)
Vector larger than --vector-elements field <field>_snapshot_cut a vector was left out because it is larger than the limit: raise --vector-elements
Checked reads ran out field <field>_snapshot_cut the checked reads of a followed member ran out: raise --checked-reads
Member does not fit the slice field <field>_snapshot_cut a followed member does not fit the snapshot payload: raise --snapshot-slice or --snapshot-arena
No storage left for a member field <field>_snapshot_cut no snapshot storage was left for a followed member: raise --snapshot-arena or lower --snapshot-reserve
Member does not fit the event (shared-context events) field <field>_snapshot_cut the followed member did not fit the event: raise --context-event-bytes of the server

<field>_snapshot_cut is a string field next to <field>_snapshot, so event.result_snapshot().field("_chain_snapshot_cut") reads it; a cut inside a nested member sits in that member's record.

To choose the captured fields for one implementation, pass a C++ file with --callback to %probe inject. Define an overload of tracer_snapshot::encode for that concrete type. The probe encodes the returned record using the same bounded snapshot codec and reports the original implementation type. Other implementations use automatic field capture.

cpp
namespace tracer_snapshot {
struct ItemV2Fields { int revision; };

ItemV2Fields encode(const HFW::ItemV2& item) noexcept {
  return {item.revision};
}
}

The encoder executes in the target process and takes the live implementation by const reference. It must be noexcept and return a named record by value. An encoder-only file can be injected directly. If the file also defines an invocation-scoped Interceptor, it needs a post() hook.

Inspect a record without declaring a local C++ type:

cpp
auto value = event.argument_snapshot(0);
value.cpp_type()
int id = value.field("id").as<int>();
std::string name = value.field("name").as<std::string>();
auto fields = value.fields();
auto samples = value.field("samples").as<std::vector<int>>();

Import application headers to generate mappings from Clang's AST, including nested records and record types inside standard containers:

bash
%cpp options add "-I/path/to/application/include" "-DAPP_FEATURE=1"
%cpp options
%cpp import "application/types.hpp"

After collecting events, event.argument_as<application::Order>(0) constructs a local C++ object. Standard strings, vectors, arrays, lists, deques, maps, sets and optionals decode recursively without registrations. The header is parsed with the same local compiler options as ordinary C++ input. At startup, repeatable --cpp-arg ARG remains available; for example clang-tracer-repl --cpp-arg -I/path/to/include --cpp-arg -DAPP_FEATURE=1.

Bulk import maps eligible non-system application records visible after the include. Use %cpp import HEADER --type application::Order to select a type; repeat --type for more roots. Nested dependencies are generated automatically, including named, nondependent template instantiations and aliases. Existing explicit EventRecord<T> and EventCodec<T> definitions are preserved. Structurally unsupported records are reported and skipped; an explicitly selected unsupported type rejects the import. Generated conversions are checked in the disposable helper before entering the live interpreter. Header/generation errors retain previous variables and tracing sessions. An accepted header has normal C++ semantics, including execution of its static initializers.

The native REPL applies Clang's -fno-access-control to all local C++ input, checking, and mapping generation. This lets you inspect private and protected members directly and lets generated decoders include them. Pass -fno-access-control when compiling a generated header with non-public members outside the REPL.

The REPL can generate a factory when Clang can map every argument of a unique constructor to a captured field. It recognizes direct member initialization and forwarding through supported base constructors. The factory constructs the value and copies any remaining assignable fields. This also covers const fields initialized by the constructor. A prepared adapter can retain the verified initializer list. Constructor code that transforms values or depends on application state needs a custom EventCodec<T>. The factory requires usable local lifetime definitions and does not reconstruct raw-pointer ownership from captured addresses.

Eligible derived records decode inherited fields as well as their own fields. Use DeclaringType::field for field names shared by multiple base or derived declarations. A shared virtual base contributes its fields once. Polymorphic records need locally usable construction, destruction, and virtual function definitions. With the REPL's own local Linux x86-64 server, a prepared probe can resolve an out-of-line destructor from a shared library already mapped in the target. With a server the REPL did not start, the library is used only when the target is a process on this host, owned by the REPL's user, whose /proc/PID/maps confirms the reported mappings; otherwise the record is rebuilt field by field, as described below. The REPL checks the mapped ELF identity and requires one library exporting the required C++ ABI symbols. It loads that library into the REPL process and binds those symbols before generating the typed decoder. No additional probe options are required. Library initializers run in the REPL when the loader opens the library.

A record that cannot be constructed locally is decoded as tracer_repl::Reconstructed<T>; use -> to reach the record. This covers records with raw pointer or reference members, records whose constructor, virtual functions, or destructor are unavailable or cannot be inferred, and records that contain such a record by value or through a std::unique_ptr. Records that map normally keep doing so. A reconstructed record's fields are rebuilt without running its constructors or destructor and its vptr is null, so read fields and call non-virtual members only. A pointer member refers to a local copy of its captured pointee, which is itself rebuilt the same way, so a captured chain of pointers can be followed with ->. It is null when the pointee was not captured or its captured type is neither the declared pointee nor one of the imported application records derived from it (at most 15 derived records are considered); a captured pointee that fails to decode raises the decode error. A char pointer points at a copy of the captured string and a pointer to a scalar at a copy of the value. A reference member needs its referent: decoding throws std::runtime_error naming the record and field when it was not captured. Smart pointer members point at the local copy of the pointee, or are empty when it was not captured. Other raw pointers are null. Do not move, copy, assign or destroy the reconstructed record itself; it owns the pointees, so do not move from, reset or assign its std::unique_ptr members either, because those only view the copies. Records with virtual bases cannot be reconstructed. Define your own EventCodec<T> before first use to replace the generated reconstruction.

Use result_snapshot() for field inspection when only the captured layout is available. If additional definitions are needed for a typed result, prepare the package in one session, then import the application definitions and inject the saved package in a fresh session.

If a generated decoder fails to compile (for example, a set element lacks its required comparison operator), the entire import is rejected without changing live state. Retry with --type to select supported roots; no partial mappings are installed from the failed import.

Configure options before the first accepted C++ cell. Help/completion alone do not lock them; %cpp options clear restores the default profile at that point. After C++ input, changing options is rejected without dropping variables. An explicit %cpp reset clears C++ variables and unlocks configuration while retaining tracing sessions. Local options do not change remote probe settings: --include, --compile-option and --compdb still refer to the server.

Use tracer.prepare with a header path, a braced list, or a std::vector<std::string>. Put the probed function's declaration header first, followed by headers for types used by the callback.

cpp
tracer.prepare("demo::compute(int)", {"demo.hpp", "state.hpp"}, "prepared");

Successful injection with a typed package prepared in the same REPL imports eligible mappings from its standalone adapter. For tracer.inject(...), the mappings become available at the next input after the call. The import uses the local compiler profile. If the mapping import fails, the probe stays installed and snapshots remain available. For a package reused from another session, %cpp import can load its exported generated/adapter.hpp.

Named tracer::Context events expose their state as owned C++ values. event.state_snapshot(index) returns an EventValue for field inspection. event.state_as<T>(index) uses the same conversions and record mappings as argument_as<T>. The index defaults to the first state. Select the custom event with %collect --name NAME. See the prepared method example for a nested record captured from typed arguments.

Save and reuse generated wrappers

%cpp import saves its generated EventRecord<T> mappings and prints the header's absolute path. Independent imports reuse an unchanged mapping across sessions. The default directory is $XDG_CACHE_HOME/clang-tracer/repl/mappings, or ~/.cache/clang-tracer/repl/mappings when XDG_CACHE_HOME is unset. Cache keys include the include name, selected types, compiler profile, working directory, generator binary and compiler include-path environment settings. Checksums cover the generated source and all physical headers seen by the AST, including transitive dependencies. Include-search lookups are also recorded, so newly created higher-priority headers and changes to __has_include results invalidate reuse. Changed or missing dependencies cause regeneration; unusual header-map/framework lookups that cannot be represented reliably are regenerated. Imports after user C++ declarations generate against the live declaration history and save a session-specific mapping. Such imports may depend on earlier C++ declarations. Use generate for a self-contained mapping header based on the application include alone. Profiles with forced includes, precompiled headers, modules or VFS overlays are regenerated rather than taking a potentially stale automatic cache hit.

Generate an entire include without loading it into the interpreter:

bash
%cpp options add "-I/path/to/application/include" "-DAPP_FEATURE=1"
%cpp generate "application/types.hpp" --output "application-events.hpp"

Omit --type to generate every eligible application record in the include; repeat --type QualifiedType to select roots. --output also works with %cpp import. Generation uses only Clang's syntax-only AST helper: it does not start a JIT, link application symbols, run static initializers or execute user constructors. Headers containing declarations of unavailable application functions can therefore be analyzed. Structural eligibility and generated decoder bodies are still checked by the compiler. generate ignores live C++ variables and declarations; import honors them.

The saved header includes the resolved application header and the local event API. Reuse it with #include "/absolute/path/application-events.hpp" in a later REPL session with compatible compiler settings. Ordinary C++ loading and decoding still require any function definitions they actually use. Automatic cache lookup verifies dependencies; explicitly including a saved header has normal C++ include semantics. Writes replace generated headers atomically; unrelated existing files and application dependencies are never overwritten.

Shell output and compilation databases

bash
%shell "pkg-config --cflags some-library"
%cpp options add `pkg-config --cflags some-library`
%cpp options add `cat ./compiler-flags.txt` "-DLOCAL_FEATURE=1"
%cpp options compdb "/path/to/build/compile_commands.json" --file "/path/to/app/types.hpp"

Backticks must occupy a complete argument to options add. Their stdout is split into compiler arguments with quoted paths and escaped characters preserved; it is never evaluated as a second shell command. Stderr is displayed separately. %shell takes one quoted command and displays captured stdout and stderr. Commands run locally with closed stdin, a ten-second deadline and a 64-KiB limit per output stream. Cancellation, timeout, malformed flag quoting, or a nonzero exit leaves compiler options unchanged. Remaining background children of a shell command are stopped when that command finishes.

options compdb accepts a database file or its containing directory and replaces the local user compiler profile. It first selects an exact file entry. If none exists, it chooses a C++ source entry in the requested file's same directory, reporting the source selected. Multiple fallback files are ordered by normalized filename; multiple exact entries use database order. There is no fallback to another directory. Relative paths use the selected entry's working directory. Source inputs, compiler launchers, output, dependency-generation, language-action and linker arguments are removed; defines, include paths, language-standard and other compile settings remain. Compiler commands in JSON are parsed, never executed. Response-file arguments must be expanded before loading the profile. Invalid profiles retain the previous options; the existing before-first-C++-cell configuration rule applies.

Automatic mappings require accessible default/move construction and destruction, public assignable supported fields, and no inheritance, unions or bit-fields. Generation is bounded to 128 records, 128 fields per record and 60 KiB of source; select fewer roots with --type when necessary. Use %help cpp for commands.

Manual mappings remain available when you want explicit control:

cpp
struct Order { int id; std::string name; std::vector<int> samples; };
template<> struct tracer_repl::EventRecord<Order> {
  static constexpr const char* type_name = "Order"; // canonical target type
  static auto fields() {
    return std::make_tuple(
      tracer_repl::event_member("id", &Order::id),
      tracer_repl::event_member("name", &Order::name),
      tracer_repl::event_member("samples", &Order::samples));
  }
};
Order order = event.argument_as<Order>(0);
Order returned = event.result_as<Order>();

The mapping checks the remote record name, required field names, field kinds, and numeric ranges. For classes with constructor-only/const members, specialize EventCodec<T> with static T decode(const EventValue&) and return an object from your constructor or factory. This custom conversion runs locally.

Automatic target capture uses complete ABI-validated layouts and serializable fields, including nested records and supported STL members. Prepared layouts can include private and protected fields. Unions, bit-fields, volatile data, arbitrary raw pointees and wide/custom-character strings are unavailable for general automatic record capture. There is a 4-KiB payload limit per value, a 16-KiB thread-local capture arena, and bounded schema/item/depth limits. Missing, unsupported, truncated, malformed or over-budget snapshots throw; partial objects are never returned as complete. Older recordings containing only object addresses need a new capture to supply contents. The old scalar variant/text APIs remain available.

Snapshots survive detach, target exit, collection clearing and recording replay. Both native and shared-context event envelopes carry the same owned data. Use %help api EventValue for the loaded inspection API and Tab on event.argument_snapshot(0). for its methods. Install the server and agent together so their bootstrap protocols match.

The prelude provides tracer and a selected-session reference named session. Copying session makes a handle that retains that server/session identity; later selection changes do not redirect it. Detached/stale handles fail before tracing operations. The facade also provides attach, inject, and detach. The interpreter initializes only for C++ input, so command-only startup does not initialize Clang.

tracer.print(event) writes the full event immediately. tracer.print(collection) prints its retention/completion summary and every retained event, including a visible summary for an empty collection. Bare void calls work with or without a trailing semicolon; the console works around Clang's void value-printing behavior without executing calls twice. For text returned by describe() or the text accessors, use std::cout << value << std::endl to display its contents consistently across LLVM versions. Typed getters also decode owned string, container and mapped record snapshots as described above.

Enter continues an unfinished C++ block, parenthesis, bracket, string, or block comment in the multiline editor. Ctrl+C discards the entire pending input; earlier variables and tracing sessions remain available. Ctrl+J always inserts a newline; %cpp load FILE submits a multiline source file.

End a % command line with \ between arguments to continue on the next line. The final line submits the command. The same syntax works in piped input and --startup files.

bash
%module index \
  --file ./app

Every submitted C++ cell is checked in a disposable clang-tracer-repl-check process before the live interpreter parses or executes it. The checker parses the accepted cells in their original order without executing them, preserving macro state and incremental source context. A rejected cell cannot change live variables or macros, and completion and expressions remain available without %cpp reset. The checker stops at the first compiler error. Ctrl+C cancels a pending check; analysis also has a 15-second deadline and a 64-KiB output limit. Tab completion runs in the same isolated, bounded helper. Install the helper alongside clang-tracer-repl (CMake installs both).

Checks require the session's working directory and previously included headers to remain unchanged. If either changes, input is rejected before live parsing: restore those inputs to keep using the existing variables, or explicitly reset to adopt the new compilation context. After C++ itself changes the working directory, reset adopts that directory. Other compiler inputs, including header search results and conditional include availability, must also remain stable; the file checks detect ordinary size/timestamp changes to loaded headers.

%cpp reset explicitly destroys C++ declarations and values while preserving the tracing controller and sessions; it is no longer routine error recovery. Executed native C++ still runs in the console's process: runtime side effects cannot be rolled back, and arbitrary native loops or crashes do not have guaranteed interruption. Ctrl+C also cancels tracing operations. Completion covers command names and local C++ declarations/members. Dynamic completion of remote tracing symbols remains follow-up work.

Cleanup and scripted use

bash
%probe remove 1
%detach
%server stop
%quit

Use the actual returned probe ID. Removing a probe reports restoration status. EOF/quit detaches sessions this console created and stops only its owned server. Selecting a pre-existing session does not transfer ownership. %server stop waits for server restoration and is unavailable for an external service. A shutdown timeout preserves the PID, endpoint and private directory for recovery; the console never force-kills a restoring server. On Linux, the owned server also receives a graceful termination signal if its console dies unexpectedly, allowing it to restore hooks before exiting.

Piped input returns a nonzero status if any command or C++ input fails. --fail-fast stops at the first failure and still performs cleanup. The parser requires full-input acceptance and rejects malformed quotes, trailing garbage, duplicate/conflicting options, integer overflow and invalid limits before dispatch. Console commands use %; C++ input uses Clang's parser.

Regenerate the grammar

The lexer/parser and visitor interfaces are generated from src/repl/TracerCommands.g4 with ANTLR 4.13.2. Generated sources ship with the repository, so neither Java nor Python is needed to run the console.

sh
scripts/regenerate-repl-parser.sh /path/to/antlr-4.13.2-complete.jar
scripts/regenerate-repl-parser.sh /path/to/antlr-4.13.2-complete.jar --check

The script verifies the jar's SHA256 eae2dfa119a64327444672aff63e9ec35a20180dc5b8090b7a6ab85125df4d76. Set TRACER_REPL_JAVA to a Java executable when it is not on PATH. The generated parser builds a typed command; semantic validation precedes execution. Generated grammar actions never perform target operations.

Validation

The native client was built and tested on macOS with LLVM 22.1.8 and on Linux x86-64 with LLVM 21.1.8. All six client CTests pass on both hosts. A separate real Linux integration check covers owned-server startup, PID/name attach, interceptor deployment, live event collection/inspection, local C++ analysis, recording/replay, probe restoration and cleanup. Typed-value tests cover bools, integers, floating values, type/payload errors and range boundaries. The Linux check also verifies native bool arguments/results and typed recording replay. Terminal tests exercise the user's bare tracer.print(data.at(0)) spelling, batch printing, actual Tab insertion for methods/fields, and in-prompt API help. Staged installations on both hosts evaluate C++ through the installed facade header. See NATIVE_REPL_PROGRESS.md for evidence and the exact validation scope.

Event retention and SQLite storage

Configure retained history

sh
clang-tracer-server --listen 127.0.0.1:50051 \
  --event-history-limit 16384 \
  --context-history-limit 512 \
  --context-history-bytes 67108864

In the console, enter the following on one line:

text
server start --event-history-limit 16384 --context-history-limit 512 --context-history-bytes 67108864

The server retains a bounded shared history. This change keeps its defaults and adds startup flags --event-history-limit, --context-history-limit, and --context-history-bytes (serialized context bytes, not total process RAM). All limits are positive integers; lowering a context limit must not block tracing. An event larger than the context-byte budget is dropped. This can include PRE/POST events from a context-enabled probe. Limits apply to the shared server history, not separately to each session, and cannot be changed on a running server.

Save or drain

sh
# Save without consuming retained history.
clang-tracer events 12345 --sqlite capture.db --count 100 --timeout 30
# Drain the current retained snapshot for every session.
clang-tracer drain --sqlite capture.db
# Continuously save and consume events for one PID.
clang-tracer drain 12345 --sqlite capture.db --listen --timeout 60

In the native REPL, save without consuming retained history:

bash
%record capture.db --sqlite --name account.adjusted --count 12

Python console commands:

text
record capture.db 100 --sqlite --timeout 30
drain capture.db
drain capture.db --listen --count 1000 --timeout 60

The console uses the selected session by default; without a selection it drains all sessions. --session ID, --pid PID, --name NAME, and --after CURSOR narrow the capture. Ctrl-C returns to the prompt. Native drain defaults to all sessions and supports PID and after filters. --listen polls every 100 ms when the snapshot is empty; it is a foreground operation.

clang-tracer drain --sqlite capture.db saves a snapshot of retained events and acknowledges exactly those events after SQLite commits. --listen repeats this until interrupted; --count and --timeout bound the operation. An optional PID narrows the drain. The console supports drain capture.db [--listen] [--count N] with the existing session, PID, name and after filters. record capture.db N --sqlite and native events PID --sqlite capture.db save without consuming.

Reads never reserve or delete events. Acknowledgements carry a random server lifetime identity and exact sequence IDs. Snapshot continuation pins that same identity. Concurrent drains are idempotent in one database, but different databases may both save a batch read before either acknowledgement. Storage failures do not acknowledge events. An acknowledgement failure may leave a committed batch; retrying into the same database deduplicates it. Draining consumes history for every client; stale watchers receive OUT_OF_RANGE. Existing overflow and transport loss remain possible; recording does not provide lossless capture.

SQLite format and failure handling

Both writers use trace_events with full Protobuf payloads and queryable identity, process, thread, phase, function and drop-counter columns. Unsigned 64-bit values are decimal TEXT, avoiding SQLite signed-integer overflow. The primary key is (server_instance_id, sequence); server restarts must not collide. Each bounded batch commits before acknowledging. SQLite stays on the client host and can grow until storage is full. WAL uses FULL synchronous commits. The database path must name a persistent file; empty paths and :memory: are rejected. Both writers create a missing database and append to an existing one.

Open the recording from the native REPL with %events open capture.db --as saved. Use tracer.replay("capture.db", query) to select events by function or custom event name, phase, process, or session before reading them. See Query a recording offline for examples.

Verification

Acceptance: validate CLI limits; exercise ordinary/context eviction under small limits; finite snapshots terminate during production; filtered acknowledgement preserves unrelated events; persisted Protobuf replays exactly; database failure never removes events; retries deduplicate; restart IDs prevent stale acknowledgements; continuous capture stops cleanly; both CLI and console reach the same behavior.

Verified on 2026-11-01 in an isolated Linux x86-64 build with LLVM 21.1.8: 173 Python/native tests passed, plus all three native server/client CLI compatibility CTest checks. The macOS client suite passed 160 tests with 13 Linux-only skips. Ruff, strict mypy, and Python wheel/source builds passed. The native CLI also rejected :memory: before connecting to a server.

Reproduce with .venv/bin/python -m pytest python/tests (set CLANG_TRACER_NATIVE_BUILD to the Linux build directory for native tests), and CTest grpc_native_integration, grpc_client_integration, and grpc_friendly_client_integration after building their fixtures.

Shared context

For a commented, runnable introduction, start with the two-probe worker example.

Shared context lets independently compiled class interceptors keep typed C++ state and publish a snapshot with Call::context().event(). The stream carries descriptor-backed values, so the CLI can decode fields across schema revisions without a user-maintained JSON schema.

Declare and use state

Include the public tracer/context.hpp header in callback sources that declare context types. Mark each state with its scope and inject it through the interceptor constructor:

cpp
#include <string>
#include <vector>
#include <tracer/callback.hpp>
#include <tracer/context.hpp>

struct RequestScope {};

struct RequestState : tracer::shared_state<RequestScope> {
  std::string request_id;
  std::vector<std::string> items;
};

struct Interceptor {
  Interceptor(tracer::State<RequestState>);

  void pre(const tracer::Call&, RequestState& state) {
    state.request_id = "request-42";
    state.items.push_back("book");
  }

  void post(const tracer::Call& call) {
    auto& state = call.context().get<RequestState>();
    call.context().with<RequestState>([](RequestState& value) {
      value.items.push_back("shipped");
    });
    call.context().event("request.completed");
  }
};

State<T> declares a constructor dependency; the engine constructs and binds the state before the hook and can inject T& into a hook parameter. Use get<T>() for direct typed access or with<T>(visitor) for a scoped visitor. shared_state<Scope> identifies state shared by compatible calls and probes; state<Scope> identifies ordinary scoped state. Synchronization for ordinary state remains the callback author's responsibility. Shared state access follows the engine's guarded access rules; do not retain references beyond the hook or visitor call.

Generated owner construction can initialize a payload from the source hook's root call with T(const tracer::ScopeInit&); init.root_call() exposes that call only during initialization. For generic declarations, use call.context().init_scope<Scope>(), the typed-payload overload init_scope<Scope>(payload), and end_scope<Scope>(). Scope initialization and teardown are runtime-managed; they do not require a user token or global map.

Call event(name, max_items) to publish a complete snapshot of the visible state. The default item cap is 100; the accepted range is 0 through 4096. The serialized event payload and its metadata have a 256 KiB capture limit. Descriptor sets are admitted separately, with a 1 MiB limit per descriptor set; they do not consume that event-payload limit. Admission is atomic: if the event or any required descriptor cannot fit its respective bounded budget, the event is dropped rather than partially published.

Thread propagation

When a supported pthread_create call happens in an active application hook, the native adapter captures the full eligible context-task chain and attaches it to the new thread. This also covers libraries that create threads through pthread_create; callbacks do not need to wrap the call or pass a token. Accepted child work retains its state and probe leases until it completes, so removing the last related probe may wait for that work to drain. Propagation is limited to application execution. The adapter fails open to the original pthread_create call when it cannot safely admit propagation, and records a bounded diagnostic. Native pthread_create detouring is supported only when the target's CET status is verified inactive for all threads; active or unverified CET configurations are rejected for this propagation mode.

Events and field queries

Context events are included in the regular events and WatchEvents output. The viewer discovers the union of field paths present in retained descriptors for a state family by default. Select one or several dotted paths with --context-field; a path missing from a particular revision is shown as <missing> rather than converted to a different field:

sh
./build/clang-tracer events "$PID" --count 20
./build/clang-tracer events "$PID" --count 20 \
  --context-field request_id,items.sku

The output labels each value with its state family and schema revision. Event arguments and results remain hidden unless the callback's print options request them. A requested native entry stack is retained and displayed with the same Watch event.

Package lineage

The engine assigns each recognized callback owner package a random 16-byte lineage UUID and persists it in engine-managed package metadata. Callback files in the same recognized package reuse that lineage; edits and file renames do not derive a new identity from source text, path, type spelling or build ID. The package root is located from existing retained metadata or the nearest .git / compile_commands.json root, with the callback directory as the standalone fallback. Imported definitions are associated with their defining package. The UUID is internal; there is no public source-origin UUID option.

If a package cannot be verified or its metadata cannot be retained, the engine isolates that source with a distinct lineage and reports a diagnostic. This prevents unrelated or unverifiable packages with identical C++ names from sharing state. The package metadata is separate from callback contents and is created only during probe setup.

Build and recording

Shared context is supported by the Linux x86-64 build profile. It requires the matching static libstdc++.a and libgcc_eh.a selected by the build compiler. CMake packages that exact standard-library runtime in the sealed libclang_tracer_context_stdlib.so support image. Runtime admission checks its ABI, object layouts and archive identity before activating state callbacks; unsupported or mismatched profiles are rejected. TRACER_JIT_FLAGS still selects callback compilation options, but it does not replace the sealed runtime profile.

Context streaming uses bounded in-memory, best-effort delivery by default. To enable durable, resumable producer and collector journals, give the server a private directory that can retain its contents across restarts:

sh
./build/clang-tracer-server \
  --agent "$PWD/build/libclang_tracer_agent.so" \
  --listen "unix:///tmp/clang-tracer/control.sock" \
  --context-durable-dir /var/lib/clang-tracer/context

The server creates per-recording collector journals in stable hashed subdirectories and per-process producer journals under this directory. Each recording/sink pair has an independent durable checkpoint. Keep the directory across restarts to resume those recordings; deleting it starts new recordings. The ordinary trace API remains available when durable recording is not enabled.

Acceptance source

The unchanged nested-state fixture exercises constructor injection, nested containers, mutation in PRE/POST and typed event publication. The live CLI integration is in class_interceptor_integration.py.

Lesson 16: capture polymorphic items and their containers

Reference: Polymorphic items tutorial and advanced capture.

Earlier lessons captured integers and one flat record. Here the traced functions work with Item, a handle whose data lives behind an interface pointer. The factory picks one of three implementations, and each stores more than the last: inherited fields, a vector, a map, and nested containers. The lesson shows that a probe captures the implementation the pointer really refers to, with everything it stores.

File Purpose
item.hpp Item: the public handle. Its private impl points to an ItemInterface.
item_interface.hpp ItemInterface: the abstract base with description() and encode().
item_v1.hpp ItemV1: a label string and a revision number.
item_v2.hpp ItemV2: derives from ItemV1 and adds tags (vector) and attributes (map).
item_v3.hpp ItemV3: parts (vector of records), stock (map of vectors), history (list of vectors).
item_factory.hpp ItemFactory::create: builds an Item and chooses the implementation by version name.
target.cpp Creates and encodes a v1, v2 and v3 item each time you press Enter.
report.cpp Prints every created item with its fields, for part 1.
encoded.cpp Prints which implementation served each encode call, for part 2.
Makefile Builds target and writes compile_commands.json for this directory.

Run make with the compiler from the tracer build profile (set CXX for SDK builds), start ./target, then start clang-tracer-repl in this directory.

Part 1: the items the factory returns

ItemFactory::create returns an Item*. %probe prepare reads the headers, so the probe knows Item, the interface, and the three implementations. --snapshot-return-pointee copies the returned Item instead of keeping only its address.

bash
%attach 12345
%probe prepare "ItemFactory::create(const std::string&) const" --include item_factory.hpp --translation-unit target.cpp --output prepared-create
%probe inject "ItemFactory::create(const std::string&) const" --prepared prepared-create --prepared-mode require --snapshot-return-pointee
%collect --count 3 --timeout 30 --phase POST --as items

Injection from a package prepared in the current REPL also imports the item classes, which is why Item and ItemV3 are usable below. If you restart the REPL and inject from the existing prepared-create directory without preparing again, import them yourself first with %cpp import item_factory.hpp.

Press Enter once in the target terminal while %collect waits, then:

bash
%events list items
%cpp load report.cpp

Expected: %events list shows three POST events whose result is only an address. The report prints what was behind each address:

text
item 1: ItemV1
  label=basic widget revision=4
item 2: ItemV2
  label=tagged widget revision=7
  tags: blue fragile
  attributes: shelf=3 weight=12
item 3: ItemV3
  title=assembled widget
  part frame 40x25.5 batches: 101 102
  part cover 41x26 batches: 201
  stock north: 5 8 13
  stock south: 21
  change: created by:ana
  change: resized by:ben width:40

%events show items --index 2 prints the same snapshot without any C++.

You can also rebuild a captured Item as a local C++ object and walk it like the original, private members included:

cpp
auto item = tracer.batch("items").at(2).result_as<Item>();
item->id
auto v3 = static_cast<ItemV3*>(item->impl);
v3->parts.at(1).size.height

Expected: 3 and 26.

Part 2: the item a method is called on

Item::encode is one function, but each call is dispatched to a different implementation. The probe captures the receiver (this), so each event says which implementation ran. You can stay in the session of part 1 (skip %attach) or start a new one. In the same session the REPL already has the item classes from the first injected package, so it keeps them and prints reused imported types: Item ItemInterface ... for the second.

bash
%attach 12345
%probe prepare "Item::encode(const std::string&) const" --include item_factory.hpp --translation-unit target.cpp --output prepared-encode
%probe inject "Item::encode(const std::string&) const" --prepared prepared-encode --prepared-mode require
%collect --name "Item::encode(const std::string&) const" --count 3 --timeout 30 --phase POST --as encoded

--name keeps the events of the part 1 probe out of this collection. Press Enter once in the target terminal, then:

bash
%cpp load encoded.cpp
%detach

Expected:

text
item 1 (ItemV1) encode(text) = text:basic widget#4
item 2 (ItemV2) encode(text) = text:tagged widget#7 +blue +fragile shelf=3 weight=12
item 3 (ItemV3) encode(text) = text:assembled widget [frame x2] [cover x1] warehouses=2 changes=2

In this part the Item is the receiver, not the result: encode returns a std::string, so result_as<Item>() fails with event record type mismatch: std::basic_string<char>. Decode the receiver instead:

cpp
auto call = tracer.batch("encoded").at(0);
auto item = call.receiver_snapshot().as<Item>();
item->id
static_cast<ItemV1*>(item->impl)->revision
auto text = call.result_as<std::string>();

Expected: 1 and 4, and text holds text:basic widget#4.

How the capture works

  • Item has a raw pointer member, impl. A prepared probe follows it and stores the copy as the field impl_snapshot, next to the address in impl.
  • impl is declared as ItemInterface*. The probe reads the object's run-time type and copies the matching implementation, so impl_snapshot.cpp_type() is ItemV1, ItemV2 or ItemV3. An implementation is only recognized if a header passed to %probe prepare defines it.
  • ItemV2 reports label and revision as well as its own fields, because inherited fields are captured with the derived class.
  • Read one field with field("name").as<T>(), where T can be a standard container such as std::map<std::string, int>. report.cpp does this for ItemV2.
  • Decode a whole implementation with as<ItemV3>(), or the whole handle with result_as<Item>(). These classes are rebuilt field by field without running their constructors, so use -> to reach the fields and do not call their virtual functions. report.cpp does this for ItemV3.

Things to try

  • Add an ItemV4 in its own header with another container, for example std::vector<std::map<std::string, double>>, and return it from the factory for "v4". Run make clean and make, restart the target, and repeat part 1.
  • Ask the factory for an unknown version. The item has a null impl, no impl_snapshot field, and the report prints no implementation captured.
  • Move one implementation's definition out of the headers given to %probe prepare. Its items keep the impl address but lose the snapshot.

Run make clean before repeating the lesson so prepared-create and prepared-encode can be created again.

Basic PRE and POST callbacks

interceptor.cpp reads the first integer argument in PRE and the original integer result in POST. Each invocation gets one interceptor object shared by its two hooks.

Use the small target from C++ objects. From a configured Linux repository build, with an installed tracer:

bash
cmake --build build --target cpp-interceptors-target

Start the server and target, then attach using the manual startup commands. With that shell's target_pid and CLANG_TRACER_ENDPOINT:

bash
clang-tracer trace "$target_pid" 'add(int, int)' \
  --callback "$PWD/examples/basic-callbacks/interceptor.cpp"
clang-tracer events "$target_pid" --count 10 --timeout 10
clang-tracer detach "$target_pid"

PRE returns first_argument * 100 + 17 as the callback value; POST returns the application's original result. Stop the demo target and server when finished.

Legacy entry-only callback

callback.cpp uses the older TraceContext interface. It reads the first signed integer argument and returns argument * 100 + 17 as a callback value. It runs on entry, on the application's calling thread.

After starting the C++ example target and attaching to its PID:

bash
clang-tracer trace "$target_pid" 'add(int, int)' \
  --callback "$PWD/examples/legacy-callbacks/callback.cpp"
clang-tracer events "$target_pid" --count 10 --timeout 10
clang-tracer detach "$target_pid"

Use basic callbacks to learn the PRE/POST class API.

Complete native C++ interceptor example

The target below uses ordinary C++ declarations, with no compiler attributes. LLVM reads the running binary's DWARF; Clang constructs a checked receiver type so call.self() reads object fields without target source or a copied class. Control and events remain gRPC and binary Protobuf; the CLI displays readable events.

Run on Linux x86-64 with a configured tracer build. The existing example target uses -g and -O0 in CMake, without enabling executable symbol exports. Debug information is required; source files and compilation databases are not. DWARF supplies the relocated entry even when the function is absent from both ELF symbol tables. Inlined calls and functions without a patchable concrete entry are outside this example's coverage.

target.cpp

The target prints its PID, arguments, member fields, and original results.

cpp
#include <cerrno>
#include <csignal>
#include <cstdio>
#include <ctime>

#include <unistd.h>

namespace {
volatile std::sig_atomic_t keep_running = 1;
int initialization_count = [] {
  std::puts("INITIALIZER fired");
  std::fflush(stdout);
  return 1;
}();

void stop_target(int) { keep_running = 0; }
} // namespace

int add(int left, int right) {
  volatile int saved_left = left;
  volatile int result = saved_left + right;
  return result;
}

class Calculator {
public:
  int bias = 7;
  mutable int calls = 0;

  int multiply(int value, int factor) const {
    ++calls;
    volatile int saved_value = value;
    volatile int result = saved_value * factor + bias + calls;
    return result;
  }

private:
  int hidden = 99;
};

int main() {
  std::signal(SIGINT, stop_target);
  std::signal(SIGTERM, stop_target);

  const Calculator calculator;
  int iteration = 1;
  std::printf("TARGET pid=%ld\n", static_cast<long>(::getpid()));
  std::fflush(stdout);

  while (keep_running != 0) {
    const int left = iteration;
    const int right = 10 + iteration;
    const int factor = 2 + iteration;
    const int sum = add(left, right);
    const int product = calculator.multiply(left, factor);
    std::printf("CALL init=%d left=%d right=%d add=%d value=%d factor=%d bias=%d calls=%d multiply=%d\n",
                initialization_count, left, right, sum, left, factor,
                calculator.bias, calculator.calls, product);
    std::fflush(stdout);

    iteration = iteration == 5 ? 1 : iteration + 1;
    timespec delay{0, 200'000'000};
    while (keep_running != 0 && ::nanosleep(&delay, &delay) != 0 &&
           errno == EINTR) {
    }
  }

  std::puts("TARGET stopped");
}

method.cpp

The method interceptor reads bias and calls before and after multiply runs.

cpp
// Clang constructs the receiver type from binary DWARF; no target source is
// needed.
class Interceptor {
public:
  void pre(const Call &call) {
    call.argument<int>(0);
    call.argument<int>(1);
    call.field(call.self()->bias);
    call.field(call.self()->calls);
  }

  void post(const Call &call) {
    call.argument<int>(0);
    call.argument<int>(1);
    call.field(call.self()->bias);
    call.field(call.self()->calls);
  }
};

call.self() is a const-qualified Calculator pointer reconstructed from DWARF. pre() sees calls before the method increments it; post() sees the new value. Argument 0 is value, argument 1 is factor; their names come from debug data. call.field(call.self()->bias) infers bias from the callback's Clang AST. There are no string labels in these interceptors. POST carries the original result automatically. Private/protected fields remain inaccessible.

free_function.cpp

The free-function interceptor captures both add arguments and its original result.

cpp
// Parameter names come from DWARF and values are carried in Protobuf.
class Interceptor {
public:
  void pre(const Call &call) {
    call.argument<int>(0);
    call.argument<int>(1);
  }

  void post(const Call &call) {
    call.argument<int>(0);
    call.argument<int>(1);
  }
};

Run the normal CLI

Use one shell in the Linux repository root so the endpoint and PID variables stay available. The following commands build only the requested executables and use the public CLI.

Build the target, server, client, and agent:

bash
cmake --build build -j4 --target \
  clang-tracer-server clang-tracer clang_tracer_agent cpp-interceptors-target

Start the server with a private endpoint:

bash
run_dir=$(mktemp -d /tmp/clang-tracer-demo.XXXXXX)
export CLANG_TRACER_ENDPOINT="unix://$run_dir/control.sock"

./build/clang-tracer-server \
  --agent "$PWD/build/libclang_tracer_agent.so" \
  --listen "$CLANG_TRACER_ENDPOINT" \
  --timeout 30 >"$run_dir/server.log" 2>&1 &
server_pid=$!

for attempt in $(seq 1 100); do
  ./build/clang-tracer list >/dev/null 2>&1 && break
  sleep 0.1
done
./build/clang-tracer list

Start the target and attach by PID:

bash
./build/cpp-interceptors-target >"$run_dir/target.log" 2>&1 &
target_pid=$!

sleep 1
./build/clang-tracer attach "$target_pid"

Install both interceptors by their C++ names:

bash
./build/clang-tracer trace "$target_pid" \
  'Calculator::multiply(int, int) const' \
  --callback "$PWD/examples/cpp-interceptors/method.cpp"

./build/clang-tracer trace "$target_pid" \
  'add(int, int)' \
  --callback "$PWD/examples/cpp-interceptors/free_function.cpp"

Read 20 events, then compare with the target's own output:

bash
./build/clang-tracer events "$target_pid" --count 20 --timeout 10
tail -n 5 "$run_dir/target.log"

Detach while leaving the target running:

bash
./build/clang-tracer detach "$target_pid" &&
  kill -0 "$target_pid" &&
  echo "Detached; target is still running."

After successful detach, optionally stop the demo processes:

bash
kill "$target_pid" "$server_pid"
wait "$target_pid" "$server_pid"

No target source, build database, or include is needed to attach or trace. An optional --include /absolute/target_header.hpp can provide richer receiver declarations, still checked against the binary's debug layout. Missing or unsupported DWARF produces an explicit error. This version uses embedded DWARF and simple scalar/pointer receiver layouts; external/split debug files, inheritance, virtual layout, bitfields, and aggregate fields are unsupported. The Linux host must permit attaching to the target.

Recorded normal CLI run

The recorded output was collected with the target source and compilation database temporarily unavailable, and without optional includes. Both interceptors produced named arguments and inferred field labels. Both entries were restored on detach; the target continued running with TracerPid=0. No integration tests were run.

For the same lifecycle with automatic startup and cleanup, run:

bash
./examples/cpp-interceptors/run.sh

That helper uses the normal CLI, then stops the processes it started after detach. Its optional first argument selects a different configured build directory.

DWARF-typed class-instance arguments
