call.argument<Index>() exposes any supported argument position using the type resolved from DWARF. No Order/Coupon declaration or target header is needed in the callback. This example mixes two different class types, a by-value Order, references, a pointer, an integer, and a double.

Index in total Target type Callback access
0 Order& const auto& order = call.argument<0>()
1 double auto fee = call.argument<1>()
2 const Coupon& const auto& coupon = call.argument<2>()
3 Order const auto& sample = call.argument<3>()
4 int auto count = call.argument<4>()

Views of class arguments are const-qualified. Reference and pointer views refer to the actual argument object; POST sees its updates. A by-value argument exposes the wrapper's entry snapshot, which remains unchanged in POST even if the callee modifies its own copy. call.result<T>() exposes the original result in POST.

Field paths are inferred from the originating argument, such as order.quantity and sample.quantity; the callback's local alias need not match the target name. Local scalar captures infer their labels too. Transport remains gRPC/Protobuf.

order.hpp (target-owned, optional for tracing)

cpp
#pragma once

struct Order {
  int quantity;
  double unit_price;
};
struct Coupon {
  double amount;
  int uses;
};

target.cpp

cpp
#include "order.hpp"

#include <cerrno>
#include <csignal>
#include <cstdio>
#include <ctime>
#include <unistd.h>

// The tracer obtains these argument types solely from the binary's DWARF.
double total(Order &order, double fee, const Coupon &coupon, Order sample,
             int count) {
  volatile double saved_fee = fee;
  const double result = order.quantity * order.unit_price + saved_fee -
                        coupon.amount + sample.quantity * sample.unit_price;
  order.quantity += count;
  sample.quantity +=
      10; // A local by-value copy: the caller's sample stays unchanged.
  return result;
}

double pointer_total(Order *order, int extra) {
  volatile int saved_extra = extra;
  if (!order)
    return 0;
  const double result = order->quantity * order->unit_price + saved_extra;
  order->quantity += extra;
  return result;
}

namespace {
volatile std::sig_atomic_t running = 1;
void stop(int) { running = 0; }
} // namespace
int main() {
  std::signal(SIGINT, stop);
  std::signal(SIGTERM, stop);
  std::printf("TARGET pid=%ld\n", static_cast<long>(::getpid()));
  std::fflush(stdout);
  int calls = 0;
  int failures = 0;
  while (running) {
    Order order{3, 12.50};
    const Coupon coupon{2.0, 1};
    Order sample{2, 3.50};
    const double result = total(order, 1.25, coupon, sample, 2);
    const int after_total = order.quantity;
    const double pointer_result = pointer_total(&order, 3);
    if (result != 43.75 || after_total != 5 || order.quantity != 8 ||
        sample.quantity != 2 || pointer_result != 65.5)
      ++failures;
    std::printf("CALL calls=%d order_before=3 order_after_total=%d "
                "order_after_pointer=%d sample=2 fee=1.25 coupon=2 count=2 "
                "total=%.2f pointer=%.2f failures=%d\n",
                ++calls, after_total, order.quantity, result, pointer_result,
                failures);
    std::fflush(stdout);
    timespec delay{0, 200'000'000};
    while (running && ::nanosleep(&delay, &delay) != 0 && errno == EINTR) {
    }
  }
}

interceptor.cpp

cpp
// No Order/Coupon definition or target headers are needed here.
class Interceptor {
  static void capture(const Call &call) {
    const auto &order = call.argument<0>();
    const auto fee = call.argument<1>();
    const auto &coupon = call.argument<2>();
    const auto &sample = call.argument<3>();
    const auto count = call.argument<4>();
    call.field(order.quantity);
    call.field(order.unit_price);
    call.field(coupon.amount);
    call.field(coupon.uses);
    call.field(sample.quantity);
    call.field(sample.unit_price);
    call.field(fee);
    call.field(count);
  }

public:
  void pre(const Call &call) { capture(call); }
  void post(const Call &call) { capture(call); }
};

pointer.cpp

cpp
class Interceptor {
  static void capture(const Call &call) {
    const auto *order = call.argument<0>();
    const auto extra = call.argument<1>();
    if (order) {
      call.field(order->quantity);
      call.field(order->unit_price);
    }
    call.field(extra);
  }

public:
  void pre(const Call &call) { capture(call); }
  void post(const Call &call) { capture(call); }
};

Run using the normal CLI

On Linux x86-64, in a configured repository checkout:

bash
cmake --build build -j4 --target \

The helper uses only normal CLI attach/trace/events/detach commands, verifies PRE/POST from both probes and progress after detach, then stops its demo processes. No integration tests are invoked. The example build uses -g and -O0, without enabling executable symbol exports; the target has no attributes. DWARF supplies the concrete entry and its ASLR relocation. For individual commands in one shell:

bash
run_dir=$(mktemp -d /tmp/clang-tracer-order-demo.XXXXXX)
export CLANG_TRACER_ENDPOINT="unix://$run_dir/control.sock"
./build/clang-tracer-server --agent "$PWD/build/libclang_tracer_agent.so" \

for attempt in $(seq 1 100); do

target_pid=$!
sleep 1

No source, compilation database or include options are used by tracing. The recorded output was captured with the target source and compilation database temporarily unavailable. total showed order.quantity 3 -> 5, sample.quantity 2 -> 2, fee 1.25, coupon.amount 2, count 2, result 43.75; pointer_total showed order.quantity 5 -> 8 and result 65.5. Both entries restored, TracerPid became 0, the target continued, and its result-failure count stayed 0.

Optional headers and compile_commands.json

The commands above work without the target's headers, sources or build database. When a target header is available, Clang can use its original declarations:

bash
./build/clang-tracer trace "$target_pid" \
  'total(Order&, double, const Coupon&, Order, int)' \
  --callback examples/order-arguments/interceptor.cpp \
  --include examples/order-arguments/order.hpp --compdb build

--compdb accepts a directory or a compile_commands.json file. Clang infers the header's command from source entries using filename and directory similarity; the CLI prints which entry it selected. It uses the command's flags and working directory to parse a synthetic header-only translation unit. The selected .cpp does not need to exist. Without --compdb, the CLI searches parent directories of the first header for a database; if none exists, standalone headers use C++20. All supplied headers share the first header's inferred command. The resulting class layout and ABI must still match the binary's DWARF before patching.

Supported boundary

Up to eight explicit arguments and 16 named arguments/fields per hook. Flat named class/struct types must have complete embedded DWARF and matching ordinary layout with supported scalar/builtin-pointer members. The agent constructs all argument record declarations with Clang APIs and checks type, access, size and every member offset. Any conflicting layouts fail before patching.

By-value classes require explicit DWARF pass-by-value calling-convention evidence; Clang then performs the native aggregate ABI lowering. Nontrivial/unsupported passing conventions, inheritance, virtual layout, bitfields, nested aggregate members, class results, and missing/incomplete debug information are rejected. Callback-side class construction/copying and method invocation remain rejected; the generated native wrapper may copy only the validated by-value argument. Keep views within the invocation and obey the target's object-lifetime and synchronization rules. Optional headers are not required.

Native bootstrap ABI is 13; Protobuf adds OBJECT=8 for by-value snapshot addresses. The event protocol remains version 2 and named member values remain typed scalars.

Generate and inject from the native C++ REPL

Build and launch the example on Linux x86-64 from the repository root:

bash
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DTRACER_BUILD_REPL=ON
cmake --build build --target clang-tracer-repl clang-tracer-server clang_tracer_agent prepared-injectors-target
./examples/prepared-injectors/run-native.sh

The launcher prints the example directory and target PID, attaches automatically, and presents the native tracer[PID]> prompt. Paste the commands below into that prompt. Keep each % command on one line.

1. Generate the package from the header

bash
%probe prepare "prepared_demo::compute(int)" --include demo/calculator.hpp --output prepared

The launcher links the build's compilation database into the current directory. %probe prepare uses ./compile_commands.json by default. Pass --compdb FILE to select another database.

Preparation prefers the first header's recorded compile command. If that header has no entry, it uses the first eligible source entry in the same directory. Pass --translation-unit FILE to select an entry explicitly.

The selector chooses the integer overload declared in the header. Clang parses the headers with the selected flags and records the symbol and ABI. This can run before the target is built. Pass --module ELF during preparation if you want to pin the package to a particular build.

The newly created package contains:

text
prepared/
  prepared.pb
  generated/
    adapter.hpp
    adapter.cpp

The native runtime consumes prepared.pb. A typed package embeds the generated declarations and the standard library headers they need. Preparation uses the application headers to extract and verify the adapter. Injection uses the adapter from the package. Use --metadata-only to save just prepared.pb, including the embedded adapter. The optional adapter files remain separate from the interceptor. Use a new output directory each time.

2. Validate against the running application

bash
%probe validate "prepared_demo::compute(int)" --callback demo/interceptor.cpp

Expect success: true and prepared_used: true. Validation checks the prepared contract against the mapped executable and compiles the callback without installing a hook.

The entire example interceptor is:

cpp
template <> class Interceptor<int(int)> {
public:
  long long pre(const Call &call) { return call.arg<int>(0) * 100 + 17; }
  long long post(const Call &call) { return call.result<int>(); }
};

The callback observes arguments and results. The target still computes value * 3 + 7; for input 1, its result is 10.

3. Inject and collect

bash
%probe inject "prepared_demo::compute(int)" --callback demo/interceptor.cpp --print-arguments --print-result
%collect --count 4 --timeout 15 --phase POST --as captured

Injection reports installed probe=...; retain that number for removal. Expect a collection containing four POST events. Then enter ordinary C++ at the same native prompt:

cpp
auto captured = tracer.batch("captured");
captured.size()
tracer.print(captured.at(0))
for (const auto& e : captured) { std::cout << e.argument_as<int>(0) << " -> " << e.result_as<int>() << '\n'; }

For background capture, type tracer.events_a and press Tab to complete tracer.events_async. After injecting, start capture with auto live = tracer.events_async(session);. Run live.snapshot().size() to see how many events are retained and live.stop(); to stop capture.

4. Restore and exit

bash
%probe remove PROBE_ID
%quit

Replace PROBE_ID with the number reported during injection. Removal reports restored=true. Quitting detaches and stops the server owned by this console; the launcher stops its example application. Generated files and target.log remain in the directory printed at startup. Use %quit to leave the native prompt.

Equivalent native C++ API

In a fresh example session, these calls perform preparation and injection without the %probe commands:

cpp
tracer.prepare("prepared_demo::compute(int)", "demo/calculator.hpp", "prepared_cpp");
auto hook = tracer.inject(session, "prepared_demo::compute(int)", "demo/interceptor.cpp");
auto events = tracer.collect(session, 4, 15);
tracer.print(events);

Use %quit to restore and detach after this variant, or %probe remove with the probe ID reported during injection.

Modes and scope of this draft

  • require: use the prepared package or report why it could not be bound.
  • prefer: attempt prepared resolution, then fall back to DWARF if it fails.
  • off: use the ordinary DWARF resolution path.

The REPL automatically tries the latest package it generated for the selector and falls back to DWARF when it cannot use the package. Pass --prepared DIRECTORY to select a package in another directory or from another REPL session. Fallback happens during resolution, before the hook is installed.

Prepared packages support concrete Linux x86-64 free functions and methods. For virtual dispatch, select the override, such as Derived::run(int) const. Calls through a base pointer are captured when dispatch reaches that implementation, including calls through an adjusting thunk. A selector installs one hook at its executable entry. Typed packages retain the declared C++ signature and header layout. The declarations and build flags must describe the running function's ABI. Injection binds the package to the symbol in the mapped ELF image and checks the adapter's ABI and layouts before compiling the callback. If multiple modules define the symbol, pass --module PATH to select one.

Regenerate version 3 typed packages to obtain the standalone adapter. Generated record declarations support layout and value inspection. The current adapter generator supports namespace-scope records, enums, polymorphic bases, concrete class template specializations, and supported standard library types. Preparation checks virtual base layout and rejects types whose ABI it cannot reproduce.

Use explicit template arguments and the concrete parameter list to prepare template functions and methods, for example twice<int>(int), Handler::convert<double>(double) const, or Box<int, 5>::apply(int) const. The preparer resolves the concrete declaration without building the target. Injection requires the instance to have an executable symbol and a safe patch window in the target.

The concrete demo prepares Handler::scale(int), Handler::shift<int>(int), Handler::Nested::adjust(int), and Handler::Nested::adjust<int>(int) with the prepared_concrete:: qualifier. The native_repl_prepared_concrete test injects all four static methods after removing the application header and checks that they return 12, 6, 13, and 14 for input 4. For nested static methods, the package preserves the original symbol and callable signature. Argument and result types follow the same adapter rules as other prepared probes.

For records with application-defined copy, move, or destruction code, the standalone adapter preserves the lifetime declarations and lets the target perform those operations. Reference and by-value snapshots can capture fields from those records. For a raw pointer, the callback decides when to read the pointee and can publish an owned field payload. Use --compile-option "-fno-access-control" on injection if the callback itself names protected or private fields. Automatic snapshots already include those fields. If the adapter cannot reproduce a pointee layout, the probe can still capture the pointer address.

To run the same workflow automatically through the native REPL:

bash
./examples/prepared-injectors/run-native.sh --smoke

Expect NATIVE_EVENT_COUNT=4, NATIVE_RESULTS=1, and detached session=.... This variant restores its hook by detaching through tracer.detach(session).

Set CLANG_TRACER_PREPARED_BUILD to use a different CMake build directory.

Automatic snapshots for returned pointers

Build and run the Linux x86-64 pointee example:

bash
cmake --build build --target clang-tracer-repl clang-tracer-server clang_tracer_agent prepared-pointee-target
./examples/prepared-injectors/run-native.sh --pointee

At the native prompt, prepare the declared return type and inject with the opt-in pointee snapshot flag:

bash
%probe prepare "prepared_pointee::HfwManager::createItem(int)" --include demo/pointee/item.hpp --output prepared
%probe inject "prepared_pointee::HfwManager::createItem(int)" --prepared prepared --prepared-mode require --snapshot-return-pointee
%collect --count 4 --timeout 15 --phase POST --as captured
auto captured = tracer.batch("captured");
auto event = captured.at(captured.at(0).result() == "0x0" ? 1 : 0);
auto item = event.result_as<prepared_pointee::HfwItem>();
auto snapshot = event.result_snapshot();
std::cout << item.label << " " << item.base_id << " " << snapshot.field("details").field("revision").as<int>() << std::endl;
%quit

The target alternates between returning an HfwItem* and nullptr. For non-null returns, result_snapshot() includes id, label, nested details, and the protected base_id inherited from the polymorphic HfwBase. The prepared package imports the mapping automatically. Clang identifies the constructor arguments, including the protected const base_id forwarded to HfwBase, so result_as<prepared_pointee::HfwItem>() constructs an owned copy. receiver_snapshot() contains the manager's fields. Null returns display 0x0. Run the same capture as a smoke test with this command.

bash
./examples/prepared-injectors/run-native.sh --pointee --smoke

The corresponding CTest is native_repl_prepared_pointee.

Polymorphic pointer returns

Build prepared-polymorphic-pointee-target and start the example.

bash
./examples/prepared-injectors/run-native.sh --polymorphic-pointee

The launcher prints the commands in inspect.repl. The target returns a Base* to a Child whose base subobject sits at a nonzero offset. Source preparation discovers Child and captures Child::x as 42 without a type-specific command option. The example also reads x through result_as<ChildFields>() with a local decoder. Add --smoke to check the child, base and null cases.

PImpl return snapshots

Build the C++17 PImpl fixture and run either return form in its own native REPL session:

bash
cmake --build build --target clang-tracer-repl clang-tracer-server clang_tracer_agent prepared-pimpl-target
./examples/prepared-injectors/run-native.sh --pimpl-pointer
./examples/prepared-injectors/run-native.sh --pimpl-reference

The public Item declaration keeps its pointer fields private and forward-declares ItemImp. The internal header defines ItemV1, ItemV2, and ItemV3. The pointer and reference demos prepare from the two application headers without a pointer policy; source discovery follows the polymorphic _imp and _other members and captures each concrete implementation. The complete non-polymorphic _stamp record is captured by its exact static type after a readability check, so it needs no policy either. The pointer probe uses the existing --snapshot-return-pointee opt-in, while the reference probe captures its Item directly.

Both sessions inspect private and nested fields for all three known implementations. For example, call event.result_snapshot().field("_imp_snapshot").as<HFW::ItemV1>() on an event with an ItemV1 implementation. The generated factory builds the concrete value. The demos also exercise a custom projection with result_as<LocalFields>(). The fourth implementation is defined only in item.cpp, so the snapshot keeps its _imp address. An _unreadable member points to a PROT_NONE page and the guarded lookup leaves its address in the snapshot. Both sessions check null members. Pointer mode also checks a null outer result. The --pimpl-custom and --pimpl-roles examples use the explicit FollowPointers policy to select the followed members of the record.

Run the automated cases with:

bash
./examples/prepared-injectors/run-native.sh --pimpl-pointer --smoke
./examples/prepared-injectors/run-native.sh --pimpl-reference --smoke
./examples/prepared-injectors/run-native.sh --pimpl-roles --smoke

CTest registers these as native_repl_prepared_pimpl_pointer and native_repl_prepared_pimpl_reference; native_repl_prepared_pimpl_roles checks that the same policy also captures arguments and receivers. Separate sessions avoid re-importing the same application declarations into one REPL process.

The --pimpl-custom mode demonstrates a user encoder for ItemV2. It replaces the automatic ItemV2 fields with a single summary projection while preserving the HFW::ItemV2 result type; ItemV1 and ItemV3 remain automatic. Its callback has no PRE or POST hook:

bash
./examples/prepared-injectors/run-native.sh --pimpl-custom
./examples/prepared-injectors/run-native.sh --pimpl-custom --smoke

CTest registers this as native_repl_prepared_pimpl_custom.

Handle return with a private implementation pointer

The handle example returns HFW::HfwItem &, whose only data member is a private HfwItemImpl *_impl. The base class ngd::HeapObject defines its destructor in a shared library, and the implementation class is complete only in item-impl.hpp. The record cannot be constructed locally, so result_as<HFW::HfwItem>() rebuilds it field by field as a Reconstructed<HFW::HfwItem> whose _impl points at the locally decoded implementation. The implementation is also readable from the _impl_snapshot field. Build the REPL tools, then run it with the REPL's own server or with a server started separately:

bash
./examples/prepared-injectors/handle/run.sh build
./examples/prepared-injectors/handle/run.sh build --external-server

Add --plain to build a non-polymorphic implementation. It needs no policy: the pointee's static type is exact, so it is captured after a readability check (the target must keep it valid). Both modes should print:

text
ROOT type=HFW::HfwItem fields=2
IMPL type=HFW::HfwItemImpl revision=827 label=implementation label
TYPED revision=827 label=implementation label
HANDLE revision=827 label=implementation label

item.hpp can instead hold the implementation through a reference (HANDLE_REFERENCE), a std::unique_ptr (HANDLE_UNIQUE), a std::shared_ptr (HANDLE_SHARED), or a pointer declared by a base class (HANDLE_BASE_MEMBER). HfwManager::makeItem returns the record by value and HfwManager::inspectItem takes it as an argument. HANDLE_DEEP adds a C string member, a pointer to an int, a pointer inside a nested record, a ring of nodes, a second level (_impl to a detail record that points back), a pointer to a std::string and a pointer to unmapped memory: the ring stops at the depth bound, the back link is cut because its target is already captured, and the std:: and unmapped pointers stay address-only. HANDLE_BUDGET adds a function whose four large arguments fill the snapshot storage; every root keeps its snapshot. CTest builds each variant and captures it as a result, a by-value result, and an argument in native_repl_prepared_handle_return; the FollowPointers policy remains available to restrict or select the followed members.

HANDLE_LIMITS adds a chain of 64 nodes, a vector and a few strings to show the capture limits at work. How far members are followed, how long a char * is kept and the rest are options, not constants; the table of every option, its environment variable, default and range is in Followed-member limits. With the defaults the chain is captured to three levels and a next_snapshot_cut field beside the third names --follow-depth. To follow five levels, prepare with a deeper limit; to keep a longer char *, raise the string and the slice when injecting:

bash
%probe prepare "HFW::HfwManager::getItem(int)" --include item.hpp --include item-impl.hpp --output prepared --follow-depth 5
%probe inject "HFW::HfwManager::getItem(int)" --prepared prepared --prepared-mode require --string-bytes 6000 --snapshot-slice 8192 --snapshot-arena 65536

TRACER_PREPARE_FOLLOW_DEPTH=5 in the environment does the same as --follow-depth 5. native_repl_prepared_handle_return runs each option in both directions (for example depth_default, depth_five, string_default, string_raised).

Typed method example

Build prepared-methods-target and launch with --methods. The method demo target has no DWARF. The launcher prints the commands and full selector from methods/try.repl and starts the native C++ REPL.

The method declaration and fields are in methods/account.hpp. The callback in methods/interceptor.cpp specializes Interceptor<Signature> with the method’s concrete argument and result types. Preparation and injection use the same selector. The REPL finds the package registered by %probe prepare.

The event accessors return owned snapshots of supported arguments, results, and receiver fields. e.receiver_snapshot() captures the declaring class and its bases at method entry. PRE and POST events for the same call share that entry snapshot. Fields at every access level use their short names when unique. For hidden fields, use the qualified name, such as e.receiver_snapshot().field("prepared_demo::Audit::account_id").as<int>().

The method example exercises strings and string views, a vector by value, optional values, a nested user record, a pair, a tuple, an array, a signed bit-field, and fields inherited through private and protected bases. It also passes owning and weak smart pointers and a variant as typed method arguments. The inherited fields exercise a non-null and a null unique pointer, a shared pointer, live and expired weak pointers, and variants holding duplicate types and std::monostate.

An owning smart pointer snapshot exposes address and an owned copy under value when it points to a supported object. A null pointer has address zero. Array, opaque, and non-owning aliasing pointers are captured by address. A weak pointer records expired without acquiring ownership. A variant records its index and the matching alternative_N. For decodable alternatives, argument_as<std::variant<...>>() reconstructs an owned variant. A valueless variant retains its std::variant_npos index in the snapshot. Pointer values and variants use the same bounded capture budget as the other fields.

Variadic and virtual methods, constructors and destructors, ambiguous repeated non-virtual base subobjects, unions, and private reference members are outside this example's automatic capture support. Unique pointers with custom deleters and recursive pointee graphs also report unavailable snapshots.

Run ./examples/prepared-injectors/run-native.sh --methods --smoke to check the prepared binding and the field values through the native REPL.

Typed custom event

Launch the example with --state. The launcher runs methods/setup-state.repl in the native REPL to prepare the package, install the probe, collect an event, and bind reading. Use the inspection commands in methods/try-state.repl at the prompt. The example prepares the method with --metadata-only and requires the package during injection. Omit --metadata-only to keep the separate generated C++ adapter files alongside the metadata.

The interceptor saves a copy of three typed arguments in a scoped prepared_demo::Reading and publishes account.adjusted on return. The public payload definition is in methods/reading.hpp. Additional --include inputs can supply callback payload types. After injection, the same REPL imports mappings from its generated adapter.

The --state --smoke run deletes the staged application headers and compilation database after preparation. It requires prepared validation and injection and checks the decoded Reading in the native REPL.

bash
%collect --name account.adjusted --count 1 --timeout 15 --as adjusted
auto event = tracer.batch("adjusted").at(0);
auto reading = event.state_as<prepared_demo::Reading>();
reading.parts.at(1)
reading.adjustment.delta

The label is deposit, the vector is {2, 5}, and the nested adjustment has delta 4 and limit 30. Use event.state_snapshot() for field access without a C++ mapping. Both forms read owned capture-time data. A truncated state reports an error.

Typed values in the native C++17 REPL

These examples attach to a real process, upload an interceptor, collect POST events, and read arguments and results as C++ values. Run them on Linux x86-64 with a matching native REPL and server. For a source checkout, use Clang 21 (clang++-21) or set CXX to a compiler targeting the server's runtime. The target and REPL examples use C++17. The existing Linux process-attach/ptrace permission requirements also apply.

From this directory:

sh
bash run.sh all

With the standard /usr/local installation (including linux-dev), run from any directory:

sh
bash /usr/local/share/clang-tracer/examples/native-repl-values/run.sh all

The runner starts a small target with debug information and runs seven demonstrations. The installed example includes a target built against the matching runtime. From a source checkout, the runner compiles the target. Each prints the actual values and example passed: NAME after checking them. It detaches and stops its own server after each case, then stops its target on exit. It uses a temporary build directory, so the installed examples directory can be read-only. It needs no Python. Only target.cpp is compiled as a program; the other .cpp files are REPL cells loaded by %cpp load, without a main() function.

Run individual categories:

sh
bash run.sh user
bash run.sh simple
bash run.sh sequences
bash run.sh associative
# Or run a single associative type:
bash run.sh map
bash run.sh unordered_map
bash run.sh set
bash run.sh unordered_set

For an interactive prompt with Tab completion:

sh
bash run.sh user --interactive

Enter each printed command separately and press Enter before entering the next; the editor treats a multiline paste as one cell. After the user-type example finishes, data and event remain available for exploration, for example:

cpp
event.argument_snapshot(1).field("owner").as<std::string>()
tracer.print(data.at(0))

Use %help EventValue, Tab after event., or %quit to finish. Each category gets a fresh REPL so their example variable names do not conflict. The runner uses a 60-second operation budget for compiling the target's headers/codecs. Set CXX, CLANG_TRACER_REPL, or CLANG_TRACER_SERVER to use other matching compiler/runtime executables. CLANG_TRACER_VALUES_TARGET can reuse a prebuilt copy of this example's target instead of compiling it again; the runner still starts and stops its own process.

1. User-defined structs and classes

types.hpp defines a struct Address and a class Account with a nested Address, Box<int> and Box<double> fields. The target receives both by value and returns an updated Account by value. user.cpp compares the captured input with the returned object, calls a method on the reconstructed class, and inspects nested fields without converting to a user-defined C++ type.

cpp
auto address = event.argument_as<value_examples::Address>(0);
auto before = event.argument_as<value_examples::Account>(1);
auto after = event.result_as<value_examples::Account>();
std::cout << after.describe() << std::endl;
auto city = event.argument_snapshot(1).field("address").field("city")
                .as<std::string>();

The runner uses %cpp import "types.hpp" to generate EventRecord<T> mappings from the application header after configuring %cpp options add "-I/path/to/include". Nested Address, template specializations and std::vector<Address> reuse that mapping automatically; there is no manual field registration. mappings.hpp remains an optional manual-mapping reference. Automatic capture requires public serializable fields; the example class deliberately uses public fields. A local EventCodec<T>::decode(const EventValue&) factory is an alternative for local types that cannot be default-constructed/assigned; it does not expose private fields of a target class.

Expected output includes:

text
struct Address: Paris, 75001
class Account before: Ada #7 in London
class Account returned: Ada #8 in Paris
nested template fields: 5, 2
field inspection: Ada, London
example passed: user

2. Scalars and simple standard types

simple.cpp reads bool, int, double, std::string, and std::optional<int>, plus a std::string result. The optional alternates between a present zero and std::nullopt; the checks distinguish those cases. Standard types need no EventRecord mapping.

cpp
bool enabled = event.argument_as<bool>(0);
int count = event.argument_as<int>(1);
double ratio = event.argument_as<double>(2);
auto text = event.argument_as<std::string>(3);
auto serial = event.argument_as<std::optional<int>>(4);
auto returned = event.result_as<std::string>();

Expected lines include bool=true int=3 double=1.25 string=hello, both optional=0 and optional=none, and returned=hello-returned.

3. Sequence containers and nested records

sequences.cpp reads each of these argument types separately:

Index C++ type Example access
0 std::array<int, 3> coordinates.at(2) → 6
1 std::vector<Address> addresses.at(0).city → Paris
2 std::list<int> numbers.front() → 3
3 std::deque<std::string> messages.front() → queued
4 std::vector<std::vector<int>> matrix.at(0).at(1) → 2

The nested vector also contains an empty inner vector, which stays empty after capture and reconstruction.

4. Associative containers

Each example has its own function, probe, and source file. This keeps their combined DWARF metadata within the tracing service's existing bounds.

Source C++ argument type (index 0) Example access
map.cpp std::map<std::string, int> counts.at("apples") → 2
unordered_map.cpp std::unordered_map<int, std::vector<int>> groups.at(2).at(1) → 4
set.cpp std::set<int> ids.count(4) → 1
unordered_set.cpp std::unordered_set<std::string> labels.count("red") → 1

The unordered map also contains an empty mapped vector. The examples compare contents, not the iteration order of unordered containers.

Capture boundaries

Values are owned snapshots: arguments reflect entry values and results reflect return values. They remain readable after detach or target exit. These are examples cover the supported type families. Automatic target capture excludes private/protected fields, unions, bit-fields, raw pointees, wide/custom strings, smart pointers, std::tuple, and std::variant. Existing snapshot size/schema limits still apply; see docs/native-repl.md.

Capture native C++ call stacks

The target calls worker_loop -> run_iteration -> library_dispatch -> StackCalculator::multiply -> stack_add on three threads. The last three functions live in libcall-stacks-calculator.so. The executable uses optimized callers with omitted frame pointers; the library also omits frame pointers. There are no target instrumentation attributes or agent dependencies.

Stacks show application frames by default: four method frames and five nested-function frames in this example. Standard templates in the executable, runtime libraries and the tracer's JIT bridge are hidden from both Call::stack() and CLI events. To see the complete native stack, pass --stack-application-only false to trace, or call call.capture_stack(24, false) inside a hook. An ordinary call.capture_stack(24) inherits the probe's default-true option. Use stack.application_only, stack.hidden_frames and stack.captured_depth to inspect the view and raw unwind depth. The depth limit applies before filtering, so hidden frames still count toward it; unwind completeness is unchanged. Names in application-owned frames may remain unavailable.

To compare using the helper:

sh
# Default application-only output from both native hooks and CLI:
STACK_METHOD_CALLBACK=examples/call-stacks/symbolized.cpp \
STACK_FUNCTION_CALLBACK=examples/call-stacks/symbolized.cpp \
STACK_FUNCTION_CAPTURE=callback \
bash examples/call-stacks/run.sh /tmp/stacks-application-only complete

# Same callbacks, full native/JIT/runtime stacks:
STACK_APPLICATION_ONLY=false \
STACK_METHOD_CALLBACK=examples/call-stacks/symbolized.cpp \
STACK_FUNCTION_CALLBACK=examples/call-stacks/symbolized.cpp \
STACK_FUNCTION_CAPTURE=callback \
bash examples/call-stacks/run.sh /tmp/stacks-full complete

See actual filtered PRE/POST and CLI output and ../../stack-capture-results/2026-10-30-application-only/report.md (local recording). call-stacks-filter-target is a separate demo with an application caller taking std::vector arguments; that caller stays visible. Its standard thread-invoker frames are still hidden.

From the project root on Linux x86_64, using the existing configured build:

sh
cmake --build build -j4 --target clang-tracer clang-tracer-server \
  clang_tracer_agent call-stacks-target
bash examples/call-stacks/run.sh

The script uses ordinary attach, trace, events and detach commands. It starts an independent target before attaching, arms both probes, then releases its optional demonstration start gate with SIGUSR1. The normal target runs immediately when started without --wait. It captures 24 events, detaches both probes, verifies continued target calls and checks unchanged executable/library hashes. Output and exact commands remain in the printed log directory.

To type the commands yourself:

sh
run_dir=$(mktemp -d /tmp/clang-tracer-call-stacks.XXXXXX)
export CLANG_TRACER_ENDPOINT="unix://$run_dir/control.sock"
./build/call-stacks-target --wait > "$run_dir/target.log" &
PID=$!
./build/clang-tracer-server --agent "$PWD/build/libclang_tracer_agent.so" \
  --listen "$CLANG_TRACER_ENDPOINT" --timeout 30 > "$run_dir/server.log" 2>&1 &
SERVER=$!
# Wait until this succeeds:
./build/clang-tracer list
./build/clang-tracer attach "$PID"
./build/clang-tracer trace "$PID" 'StackCalculator::multiply(int, int)' \
  --callback examples/call-stacks/method.cpp --stack 24
./build/clang-tracer trace "$PID" 'stack_add(int, int)' \
  --callback examples/call-stacks/function.cpp
kill -USR1 "$PID"
./build/clang-tracer events "$PID" --count 24 --timeout 15
./build/clang-tracer detach "$PID"
tail -3 "$run_dir/target.log"
kill -TERM "$PID" "$SERVER"
wait "$PID" "$SERVER"

method.cpp reads call.self()->bias and calls in PRE and POST, and reads the automatic snapshot through call.stack(). function.cpp independently requests capture in both hooks with call.capture_stack(24) and records its frame count. The callback sees bounded structured native addresses and frame kinds; Protobuf events carry those frames plus LLVM symbolization. Each callback frame also exposes function, module, file (immutable C strings) and line, resolved before the hook reads call.stack(). Empty strings and line 0 mean unavailable. POST uses the entry caller stack, while member fields and the original result reflect the completed call.

Measured overhead

The runnable benchmark.cpp / benchmark.sh compare unattached execution, normal tracing without capture, and application-only stacks using the same existing calculator library. Both traced modes use the no-output automatic.cpp callback; symbolized.cpp would request capture even without --stack. See the ../../stack-capture-results/2026-10-30-overhead/report.md (local recording).

The ../../stack-capture-results/2026-10-30-optimized/report.md (local recording) used the identical benchmark: median no-stack tracing fell from 12.317 to 7.415 us per call, and application-stack tracing from 339.749 to 125.678 us. No-stack event drops fell from 7.66% to 5.31%; stack event drops remained zero. These figures exclude text printing and describe the tiny nested-call workload.

The ../../stack-capture-results/2026-10-30-buffered/report.md (local recording) received all 57,600 benchmark events with zero transport loss. No-stack median was 7.992 us/call and application-stack median 127.269 us/call. A bounded queue lets the caller return while a background sender handles congestion; full queues still count drops. transport-pressure.sh demonstrates completed calls while the server is stopped, followed by resume, immediate detach and event validation.

The ../../stack-capture-results/2026-10-30-stack-fast/report.md (local recording) lowered the stack-enabled median from 127.269 to 95.210 us/call (25.2% less time), with all 57,600 benchmark events received. Use PRESSURE_STACK_DEPTH=24 with transport-pressure.sh to exercise stack capture while its receiver is stopped.

The ../../stack-capture-results/2026-10-30-stack-profiled/report.md (local recording) measured 93.279 -> 89.162 us/call with application stacks, zero losses and identical frame metadata. It retains fresh mapping reads while reusing bounded procfs streams and decoded sparse CFI plans. A stopped receiver still allows the 1,500-call batch to complete, followed by delivery of all 3,200 events.

The ../../stack-capture-results/2026-10-30-mapread/report.md (local recording) reduced read syscall entries from 5 to 2 while retaining complete fresh streams. Fresh production medians were 92.094 -> 85.582 us/call, with all 57,600 events received per run. Short/interrupted reads, long records and fallbacks passed.

The ../../stack-capture-results/2026-10-30-positioned-maps/report.md (local recording) found no additional end-to-end speedup and restored the original source/agent exactly. Its interleaved current/candidate medians were 88.179 / 89.403 us/call, with zero event losses; the experiment and all raw recordings remain available.

Optional PRE arguments and POST return value

The same symbolized.cpp callback optionally prints the traced function's named arguments before its PRE stack and its original result before its POST stack. Both are off by default. Enable either independently:

sh
./build/clang-tracer trace "$PID" 'stack_add(int, int)' \
  --callback examples/call-stacks/symbolized.cpp \
  --callback-print-arguments true --callback-print-result true

For a complete runnable demonstration from the configured Linux checkout:

sh
STACK_PRINT_ARGUMENTS=true STACK_PRINT_RESULT=true \
STACK_METHOD_CALLBACK=examples/call-stacks/symbolized.cpp \
STACK_FUNCTION_CALLBACK=examples/call-stacks/symbolized.cpp \
STACK_FUNCTION_CAPTURE=callback \
bash examples/call-stacks/run.sh /tmp/stacks-with-values complete

Use a fresh directory. Omit STACK_PRINT_ARGUMENTS/STACK_PRINT_RESULT for stack-only callback output, or set either to false. The helper translates them to the corresponding --callback-print-* options for both probes. The preferences do not change captured values in Protobuf or the existing CLI event display. call.print_options() is the read-only preference view; argument_count(), argument_name(i), argument_value(i) and POST-only result_value() provide generic typed snapshots. Existing compile-time typed accessors remain available. Pointer and object values are rendered as addresses; class contents require explicit supported typed field access.

See complete actual PRE/POST output and ../../stack-capture-results/2026-10-30-optional-values/report.md (local recording).

Read names, modules and source lines inside both hooks

symbolized.cpp prints every frame from PRE and POST. Run it against the same three-thread nested example with both automatic and callback-requested capture:

sh
STACK_HIDE_SOURCES=1 \
STACK_METHOD_CALLBACK=examples/call-stacks/symbolized.cpp \
STACK_FUNCTION_CALLBACK=examples/call-stacks/symbolized.cpp \
STACK_FUNCTION_CAPTURE=callback \
bash examples/call-stacks/run.sh /tmp/stacks-symbolized complete

The method's --stack 24 prepares metadata before PRE and retains it for POST; the function callback requests capture in each hook without that flag. Both then read call.stack().frames[i].function, .module, .file, and .line. Callback-printed text is in the resulting target.log; normal Protobuf/CLI events are in events.log. ../../stack-capture-results/2026-10-30-callback-symbols/report.md (local recording) compares every printed frame with the corresponding event. Strings belong to the agent and should be used within the invocation. Metadata is resolved from ELF/DWARF; source text does not need to be present. Missing debug names remain empty. Full-stack mode marks JIT bridges explicitly with no invented source line.

For additional runnable cases:

sh
STACK_HIDE_SOURCES=1 bash examples/call-stacks/run.sh /tmp/stacks-complete complete
bash examples/call-stacks/run.sh /tmp/stacks-two-frames truncated
bash examples/call-stacks/run.sh /tmp/stacks-missing-cfi partial
bash examples/call-stacks/run.sh /tmp/stacks-depth-64 maximum
bash examples/call-stacks/run.sh /tmp/stacks-disabled disabled

Use fresh directories. partial selects a real caller compiled without unwind tables; the event retains that caller and reports exactly where CFI ends. truncated requests two frames. maximum requests 64; these particular stacks reach the thread root sooner. disabled omits capture. Every case checks the CLI's rejection of depth 65 and detaches with live workers. The first command temporarily hides only this example's target sources/header and the generated compilation database, restoring them on exit; it supplies no includes.

The implementation needs supported .eh_frame rules and readable mapped ELF images to unwind beyond a caller. Missing debug names do not make a recovered stack partial. Source text is unnecessary. Signal frames, unavailable CFI registers/expressions and changed images stop with an explicit reason. No inline or removed functions are synthesized. In full-stack mode JIT crossings appear as JIT_BRIDGE; TARGET_ENTRY is the selected logical entry, and NATIVE frames are recovered return PCs. Depth bounds the native unwind before filtering.

See the recorded output and verification report under stack-capture-results/2026-10-30/ in the project root.

Shared context: one request, two probes, one worker

process_request(id) starts a worker that calls calculate_total(id), waits for it, then returns the worker's result plus one. Both functions use the same interceptor file, compiled separately for each probe. Their hooks see the same request state, including on the worker thread.

File Purpose
target.cpp Ordinary application code; no tracer dependency.
interceptor.cpp Commented state declaration and PRE/POST hooks.
example-output.txt Recorded worker and outer POST snapshots showing both APIs.

The outer PRE starts the state with calls = 1. The worker PRE changes it to 2. Each POST publishes a snapshot; the outer POST finishes the request scope. The next request starts with fresh state. std::thread uses pthread_create on this Linux profile, so propagation happens automatically.

The POST hook demonstrates two different operations:

API What it does here
call.field("hook_result", result) Adds one named scalar to this call's metadata.
call.context().event("request.step") Publishes a named snapshot of the visible request state.

The field is recorded before the snapshot. Both trace commands below enable --callback-print-arguments true, so the context event also carries the recorded hook_result field. The shared-state fields are captured by event().

Run manually

Use one shell in the repository root on Linux x86-64. The tracer must already be installed (clang-tracer and clang-tracer-server on PATH), and the repository must have a configured build directory. See the build instructions if needed. This example uses the supported matching C++ toolchain and requires the host to permit attachment.

1. Build and start

Set build_dir to your existing configured build directory:

bash
build_dir=build
cmake --build "$build_dir" --target shared-context-target -j2

run_dir=$(mktemp -d /tmp/clang-tracer-shared.XXXXXX)
export CLANG_TRACER_ENDPOINT="unix://$run_dir/control.sock"

clang-tracer-server --listen "$CLANG_TRACER_ENDPOINT" --timeout 60 \
  >"$run_dir/server.log" 2>&1 &
server_pid=$!

"$build_dir/shared-context-target" >"$run_dir/target.log" 2>&1 &
target_pid=$!

sleep 1
clang-tracer list

Wait for list to succeed before continuing. The installed server finds its agent and private shared-context runtime automatically.

2. Attach and install both probes

bash
clang-tracer attach "$target_pid"

clang-tracer trace "$target_pid" 'process_request(int)' \
  --callback "$PWD/examples/shared-context/interceptor.cpp" \
  --callback-print-arguments true

clang-tracer trace "$target_pid" 'calculate_total(int)' \
  --callback "$PWD/examples/shared-context/interceptor.cpp" \
  --callback-print-arguments true

The target was built with debug information and without optimization. The CLI finds the functions by their C++ names; no target header or compilation database is needed for these scalar signatures.

3. Read state snapshots

bash
clang-tracer events "$target_pid" --count 24 --timeout 20 \
  --context-field request_id,calls,last_result

tail -n 5 "$run_dir/target.log"

Look for request.step events. For request 2, the worker snapshot has calls = 2, last_result = 4; the outer snapshot has calls = 2, last_result = 5. The target prints request=2 result=5. Each event header also shows fields=[hook_result=int32:4] for the worker or fields=[hook_result=int32:5] for the outer call. This is the value recorded by call.field(), separate from the RequestState.last_result snapshot field. The recorded sample output shows this pair from the verified linux-dev run, including the complete headers and all three state fields. Early snapshots may have calls = 1 while only the first probe was installed. After both are active, each complete request visits both hooks.

The engine guards the injected shared state during each hook. Keep state references inside the hook; the target's own result remains unchanged.

4. Detach and stop

bash
clang-tracer detach "$target_pid"
kill -0 "$target_pid" && echo "Detached; target is still running."

kill "$target_pid" "$server_pid"
wait "$target_pid" "$server_pid" 2>/dev/null || true
echo "Logs: $run_dir"

The API guide covers get(), with(), container snapshots, scope control and durable recording once this basic example works.

Local JIT tracing in the native REPL

Run this on Linux x86-64 with a matching Clang Tracer REPL, server, and agent that support bulk tracing and observer reload.

sh
./run.sh

The runner starts the calculator example with DWARF. It previews a manifest for add(int, int), installs a typed bulk observer, prints live call and caller statistics, and records 12 events to SQLite. It then stops the target and opens the recording in a fresh REPL to check the original results. The run prints JIT_EXAMPLE_PASSED=3 and the recording path.

The installed runner uses the bundled target, REPL, and server. For a source checkout, set CXX to a compiler that targets the server's runtime and use CLANG_TRACER_REPL or CLANG_TRACER_SERVER to select the build. The manifest and recording are stored in the printed demo directory.

Inspect and reload interactively

Start with ./run.sh --interactive. The runner attaches to its calculator. Browse the selected process and locate the runtime entry for add.

bash
%threads
%modules --details
%symbols --filter "add(int, int)" --addresses
%memory maps
%probe entry "add(int, int)" --mapping MEMORY_TOKEN
%memory read ENTRY_ADDRESS --mapping MEMORY_TOKEN --count 16
%memory scan ENTRY_ADDRESS --mapping MEMORY_TOKEN --count 16 --pattern "55 48 89 ??" --limit 4

Replace MEMORY_TOKEN with the token printed by %memory maps and ENTRY_ADDRESS with the verified runtime address from the preview. The scan pattern illustrates wildcard nibbles. Use bytes from the preview if your compiler emits a different prologue.

Validate the callback, preview and apply the batch, then reload its active probe. Copy the probe and batch IDs from the output.

bash
%interceptor load observer.cpp --as observer
%interceptor validate observer --target "add(int, int)"
%trace preview --exact "add(int, int)" --save trace.textproto
%trace apply --manifest trace.textproto --callback observer.cpp
%probes
%probe reload PROBE_ID --callback observer.cpp
%collect --name "add(int, int)" --count 8 --timeout 15 --as after_reload
%events stats after_reload
%trace remove BATCH_ID
%quit

The reload reports a new probe ID. Both generations belong to the batch. The stack captured by the observer establishes the caller edges in the stats.

Validation and benchmark notes

The native backend supports Linux x86_64 and was exercised with LLVM/Clang 21.1.8. The source repository includes test fixtures, callback examples and output checkers. Generated build trees, process recordings and development progress notes are local artifacts and are excluded from version control. References elsewhere to *-results/ describe those local recordings.

Reproduce the checks

Configure and build as described in the root README. The repository's CMake configuration registers the integration checks for CTest:

sh
ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure

The callback examples can also be exercised through the public CLI:

sh
bash examples/cpp-interceptors/run.sh
bash examples/order-arguments/run.sh
bash examples/call-stacks/run.sh /tmp/clang-tracer-stacks complete

Use a fresh output directory for each run. These commands attach to their own fixtures and record results locally. Stack checks cover complete, partial, truncated and disabled capture, nested calls, multiple calling threads and restoration after detach. Additional scripts in examples/call-stacks/ compare frame metadata and optional callback values with the emitted events.

PIE detour regression checks

native_detour_relocation executes relocated global loads, stores, immediate stores, address calculations, scalar SIMD loads and instructions with multiple references. It checks positive and negative displacements, both signed-32-bit range boundaries, memory accesses straddling the patch window, unreadable page boundaries, failed preparation without partial publication, and RX trampoline permissions. Unsupported control transfers and addressing forms remain rejected.

grpc_native_pie_integration builds tests/fixtures/target.cpp with explicit -fPIE -pie and runs the complete native integration against it. The early global store in traced_void must be relocated. The integration replaces the probe in the same session, checks events and the target's global value, and exercises detach, reattach and server-shutdown restoration.

Verified on 2 November 2026 with Clang/LLVM 21.1.8 on Linux x86_64: 20/20 CTests passed in 390.88 seconds. The exact PIE binary that previously failed at traced_void also passed the complete native integration with its SHA-256 unchanged (de71b39aec9a05bc2bbefba0f843908508048d6b8703106e5aebb9e14c30b7da). The relocation execution tests passed with AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer; function-type instrumentation was disabled for the tests' deliberately generated machine-code entry points. Focused clang-tidy checks reported no findings in the changed source. Local evidence is retained under test-results/pie-detour-20261102/ and on linux-dev:/tmp/clang-tracer-pie-fix-20261102/.

These results cover base 60d85f8 plus this fix. During validation, main advanced to e985625 with separate event-storage changes. The full fix patch applies cleanly to that revision; the complete suite was run on the isolated base above.

sh
ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure \
  -R '^(native_detour_relocation|grpc_native_pie_integration)$'

Measured tracing overhead

Measurements on 30 October 2026 used an eight-vCPU Linux x86_64 VM, Clang21.1.8 and a RelWithDebInfo agent. The benchmark binary used -O2 -g -fno-inline -fomit-frame-pointer -fno-optimize-sibling-calls -fasynchronous-unwind-tables -fcf-protection=none, linked to the existing calculator fixture. The application call chain was main -> benchmark_iteration -> library_dispatch -> StackCalculator::multiply -> stack_add.

Both traced modes used the empty automatic.cpp callback. Stack mode requested 24 frames with application filtering; callback argument/result text was off. Each mode had nine rotated repetitions. Traced repetitions used 100 warmup plus 1,500 timed calls; unattached repetitions used five million timed calls. Target and its sender ran on CPU2; the server ran on CPU3. Setup, JIT compilation, warmup, text output and detach were outside the timed loop. Capture, event serialization and enqueue were included; transport draining was asynchronous.

An accepted mapping-read batching change produced the following fresh comparison:

Mode Before median/call After median/call Events lost before / after
Tracing off 9.56 ns 9.82 ns —
Tracing without stacks 6.968 us 7.268 us 0 / 0
Application-only stacks 92.094 us 85.582 us 0 / 0

Both versions received all 28,800 events per traced mode, including warmup. All 144,000 before/after application frame records matched. With the receiver stopped, the updated implementation completed 1,500 stack-enabled calls in 130.482 ms; all 3,200 events arrived after resume and immediate detach.

A subsequent positioned-read candidate was evaluated with three interleaved three-round chunks per version, preserving nine repetitions and the original mode rotation. Its stack-enabled median was 89.403 us/call versus 88.179 us for the retained implementation. Both versions again received all events. There was no reliable overall gain, so the candidate was reverted and the original source and agent restored exactly.

These are repetition averages for a small synthetic workload. Ranges overlapped and controls varied; they are neither individual-call latency percentiles nor a performance guarantee. The benchmark driver and its summary tool remain in examples/call-stacks/ for further measurements. Build benchmark.cpp against the calculator fixture with the flags above and an appropriate runtime library path before running the driver.

sh
BENCH_ROUNDS=9 bash examples/call-stacks/benchmark.sh /tmp/clang-tracer-benchmark
ruby examples/call-stacks/summarize-benchmark.rb /tmp/clang-tracer-benchmark
PRESSURE_STACK_DEPTH=24 bash examples/call-stacks/transport-pressure.sh \
  /tmp/clang-tracer-pressure 1500

CPU affinity can be adjusted with BENCH_TARGET_CPU and BENCH_SERVER_CPU for machines with fewer CPUs. Stack capture still performs synchronous fresh mapping reads and uses the LLVM metadata mutex. Event delivery and stream-pool ownership do not wait on capacity; the finite event queue explicitly counts overflow.

Optional Python client and console

Use this reference for Python automation or the Python console. For native tracing, use the native command reference and C++ developer guide.

Install the Python client

The Python client is installed separately. Use Python 3.12 or newer. Install from the repository or replace ./python with your distribution's wheel.

bash
python3.12 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install ./python
clang-tracer-console --help

Python client API

The package exports Client, EventStream, ServerProcess, ServerStatus, messages (Tracer Protobuf types), and context (context transport Protobuf types). Operations return generated messages unless the table specifies a different type. RPC failures raise grpc.RpcError; argument and local storage failures raise normal Python exceptions. The client applies deadlines without automatically retrying mutations.

Connection and lifetime

Method or type Behavior
Client(endpoint=None, *, timeout=30, channel=None) Open a gRPC client. Endpoint defaults to CLANG_TRACER_ENDPOINT or 127.0.0.1:50051. The default channel is insecure. A supplied gRPC channel keeps its own policy and ownership. timeout is the default unary deadline.
status(*, timeout=1) → ServerStatus Probe endpoint readiness. Read endpoint, running, owned, pid, and diagnostic detail.
start_server(executable="clang-tracer-server", **options) → ServerStatus Launch a local child and wait for its endpoint and the client channel. A child that starts but misses the client deadline can still be owned by the client.
shutdown_server(*, timeout=30) Request graceful stop of the owned child. On timeout it remains tracked so you can wait again.
close(), with Client(...) as client Shut down the owned server and close the owned channel. For a shared server, detach the session explicitly before closing.
ServerProcess(endpoint="127.0.0.1:50051") Own and manage a local server separately from a tracing client. pid and running describe the child.
ServerProcess.start(executable="clang-tracer-server", **options) → self Launch and wait for readiness on Linux x86-64. Refuses an endpoint that already serves a tracer.
ServerProcess.status(*, timeout=1) → ServerStatus Probe endpoint readiness and add child ownership information.
ServerProcess.diagnostics() → str Read the latest captured child diagnostics.
ServerProcess.shutdown(*, timeout=30), with ServerProcess(...) as server Request cleanup and wait for the owned process. A timeout can be retried.

Both start methods accept agent, readiness timeout=30, native operation_timeout=10, durable_directory, event_history_limit, context_history_limit, context_history_bytes, context_event_bytes, and context_transport_memory_bytes. Omitted paths and budgets use native server defaults. See the native server command for units.

Use a private Unix endpoint to run an owned server without reserving a TCP port.

python
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

from clang_tracer import Client, ServerProcess

with TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
    endpoint = f"unix://{Path(directory) / 'tracer.sock'}"
    with ServerProcess(endpoint) as server:
        server.start(event_history_limit=8192)
        with Client(endpoint) as client:
            print(server.pid, server.running, client.status().running)
            print(client.list_sessions())
        print(server.diagnostics())

Attach, discover, and inspect

Method Behavior
attach(pid) → Session Attach to a positive Linux PID. Use the returned id for later calls.
list_sessions() → list[Session] List server attachments and their probes.
detach(session_id) → Session Restore probes and detach a session.
list_modules(session_id) → list[str] Return eligible mapped application paths.
list_threads(session_id) → list[TargetThread] Return Linux TIDs, names, and start times.
list_symbols(session_id, *, query="", module="", page_size=None, page_token="") → ListSymbolsResponse Match case-sensitive selector or linkage-name substrings and optionally narrow modules. A positive page size returns a continuation token.
list_memory_mappings(session_id) → ListMemoryMappingsResponse Return mapped ranges, permissions, and a session-bound mapping token.
read_memory(session_id, address, size, *, mapping_token) → bytes Read a complete readable range of 1–65,536 bytes. Refresh the token if the mappings change.
scan_memory(session_id, address, size, *, mapping_token, pattern, mask, max_matches=0) → ScanMemoryResponse Search a readable range of up to 1 MiB. Pattern and mask have equal length. Set each mask bit that should match and clear each wildcard bit. Zero requests the server's default result limit.
preview_function_entry(session_id, *, mapping_token, selector=None, elf_address=None, module="", abi="") → PreviewFunctionEntryResponse Verify and disassemble an entry. Use a selector, or provide ELF address, module and ABI together. Inspect patch_size and patch_diagnostic before installing a probe.
python
maps = client.list_memory_mappings(session.id)
entry = client.preview_function_entry(
    session.id, selector="add(int, int)", mapping_token=maps.mapping_token,
)
entry_bytes = client.read_memory(
    session.id, entry.runtime_address, len(entry.entry_bytes),
    mapping_token=maps.mapping_token,
)
print(entry_bytes.hex(" "), entry.patch_size, entry.patch_diagnostic)

Resolve, validate, install, and restore

Method Behavior
resolve_probe(session_id, selector, **resolution) → ProbeSpec Resolve a selector using server-side DWARF. Return a spec you can inspect or extend.
validate_probe(session_id, selector, callback_source, *, level="compile", **resolution) → ValidationReport Check callback source without activating a probe. Use syntax for parsing only or compile for code generation and symbol checks. Inspect the returned report and diagnostics.
add_probe(session_id, spec) → Probe Activate an explicit resolved or ABI-described spec.
inject(session_id, selector, callback_source, **options) → Probe Resolve, compile, and install a callback in one call. Supports the resolution options below.
reload_probe(session_id, probe_id, callback_source) → ReloadProbeResponse Switch active observer generations. Calls already in progress finish with their original generation.
remove_probe(session_id, probe_id) → Probe Restore original target bytes and report probe status.
preview_bulk_trace(session_id, rules) → PreviewBulkTraceResponse List matches and report ABI eligibility and capacity before installation.
apply_bulk_trace(session_id, rules, batch_id, *, callback_source=None) → BulkTraceReport Install a batch with a unique caller-chosen ID and an optional observer override. Inspect the returned report for outcomes and restoration status.
remove_bulk_trace(session_id, batch_id) → BulkTraceReport Restore the probes belonging to the batch or retry restoration.

Resolution options are ordered include_headers=(), compilation_database="", ordered compile_options=(), module="", debug_max_entries=0, and debug_max_depth=0. Include and database paths refer to the server. Zero DWARF budgets are unlimited. Callback source is a string read or composed on the client.

Injection also accepts stack_depth=0 (positive integer or "full"), include_internal_stack_frames=False, print_arguments=False, print_result=False, and callback_package_path="" (a server path for shared-context lineage).

python
from pathlib import Path
from clang_tracer import Client

with Client("127.0.0.1:50051") as client:
    session = client.attach(12345)
    try:
        source = Path("hook.cpp").read_text()
        report = client.validate_probe(session.id, "add(int, int)", source)
        if not report.success:
            raise RuntimeError(str(report))
        probe = client.inject(session.id, "add(int, int)", source, stack_depth=16)
        print("Press Enter in the target terminal now")
        for event in client.collect_traces(2, session_ids=[session.id]):
            print(event.sequence, event.function_name, event.phase)
        client.remove_probe(session.id, probe.id)
    finally:
        client.detach(session.id)

To manage several probes together, preview a versioned rule set before applying it. Here the rules match a single selector.

python
from uuid import uuid4

from clang_tracer import messages

rules = messages.BulkTraceRules(version=1, exact_selectors=["add(int, int)"])
print(client.preview_bulk_trace(session.id, rules))
batch_id = uuid4().hex
try:
    print(client.apply_bulk_trace(session.id, rules, batch_id))
    # Trigger the target and collect events while the batch is active.
finally:
    print(client.remove_bulk_trace(session.id, batch_id))

Read, record, and acknowledge

The common filters are session_ids=(), pid=0, names=(), and after_sequence=0. Empty filters select all eligible events. Names are exact selector, linkage or custom context-event names. Matches within a filter are ORed and distinct filters are ANDed. Resume strictly after the last processed sequence from the same server lifetime.

Method or type Behavior
watch_events(session_ids=(), *, after_sequence=0, pid=0, names=(), timeout=None) → EventStream Return a cancellable live iterator. The optional deadline covers the whole stream.
EventStream(call, after_sequence=0, names=()) Wrapper normally created by watch_events. Iteration yields TraceEvent and updates after_sequence. close() or context exit cancels the call, including blocked reads.
collect_traces(count, **filters) → list[TraceEvent] Collect up to a positive count in memory, with default timeout=30. Cancels the stream at the limit or on error.
record_traces(path, count, **filters) → int Stream a positive count to a new framed Protobuf file. Default timeout=30. A partial file remains if capture fails.
record_sqlite(path, count, **filters) → int Append a bounded live capture to SQLite without consuming history. Default timeout=30. Returns the number received.
read_events(*, limit=256, through_sequence=0, server_instance_id="", timeout=None, **filters) → ReadEventsResponse Read retained history without removal. Use the returned server ID and upper sequence to pin subsequent reads to the same lifetime and window. None uses the unary deadline.
acknowledge_events(server_instance_id, sequences, *, timeout=None) → int Consume exact committed event IDs from that server lifetime and return the acknowledged count. Affects other readers.
drain_traces(path, *, listen=False, count=None, timeout=None, **filters) → int Write and commit retained events to SQLite before acknowledging. Default drains the initial snapshot. listen=True follows new events. Retry storage or acknowledgement failures against the same database.
python
with client.watch_events([session.id], timeout=30) as stream:
    event = next(stream)
    print(event.sequence, event.function_name)
    cursor = stream.after_sequence
# The stream is closed. Supply after_sequence=cursor to resume on this server.

Python console startup and server commands

bash
clang-tracer-console --endpoint 127.0.0.1:50051 --timeout 45 --color auto
python -m clang_tracer --help

--endpoint specifies a server and defaults to the environment or loopback. Omit it and use server start to create an owned server. --timeout sets a unary RPC deadline (default 30 seconds). --color auto|always|never selects a color policy. Auto respects terminal detection and NO_COLOR. --help and -h show startup options.

Command and example Options and behavior
server start --timeout 45 --event-history-limit 8192 Start a private local server. --executable PATH and --agent PATH select binaries. --timeout SEC sets the readiness deadline (default 30) and --operation-timeout SEC sets the native deadline (default 10, range 1–300). --durable-directory PATH enables durable context recording. Supports the five history and transport budget flags in the native server reference.
server status Show endpoint readiness and ownership.
server stop --timeout 45 Gracefully stop the owned server. The shutdown deadline defaults to 30 seconds. Retry if the child is still shutting down.
attach 12345 Attach and select the process's session.
sessions List sessions and probes.
use s1 Switch to an existing session.
modules List eligible application ELF paths.
symbols --filter "add(" --limit 20 List DWARF callables. --filter TEXT and --module TEXT match case-sensitive substrings. --limit N sets the page size (zero is unbounded) and --page TOKEN resumes it.
detach s1 Restore and detach this session. Omit the session to detach the selected one.
probe resolve "add(int, int)" Resolve using DWARF. Accepts Python resolution options.
probe validate "add(int, int)" --callback hook.cpp --level compile Compile and check a local callback for the target. --level syntax selects syntax-only validation. Accepts Python resolution options.
probe inject "add(int, int)" --callback hook.cpp --stack full --print-result Resolve and install a callback. --stack N|full captures entry stacks. --internal-frames includes runtime and JIT frames. --print-arguments and --print-result include snapshots. --package SERVER_PATH selects a shared-context package lineage. Accepts Python resolution options.
probe add probe.textproto Install an explicit ProbeSpec from a local Protobuf text file.
probe remove 1 Restore the original target entry for this probe.
events --count 2 --timeout 30 Stream events until a count, deadline, or Ctrl+C. Accepts console stream options.
collect 2 --name "add(int, int)" Stream and display events. Optional positional count limits the capture. Accepts console stream options.
record capture.db 2 --sqlite Save a required positive count to a new framed Protobuf file or append to SQLite. Accepts console stream options. Default deadline 30 seconds.
drain capture.db --listen --count 10 Commit to SQLite then acknowledge shared history. --listen includes future events. Omit it to drain the initial snapshot. --count N limits writes and acknowledgements. Accepts console stream options.
help probe inject Show help for a topic. Omit topic for the index. help colors describes color options.
! pwd Run the rest of the line in a local /bin/sh. Working-directory changes stay in that shell.
exit or quit Exit and stop any server this console owns.

Python resolution options are repeatable --include HEADER and --compile-option ARG, plus --compdb PATH, --module TEXT, --debug-max-entries N, and --debug-max-depth N. The headers and database are on the server. Zero DWARF budgets mean unlimited traversal.

Console stream options are repeatable --session ID and --name NAME, plus --pid PID, --after SEQUENCE, and --timeout SECONDS. The default session filter is the selected session, or all sessions when none is selected. Names match an exact selector, linkage name or emitted context event name. Ctrl+C interrupts the stream and returns to the prompt. An expired cursor reports OUT_OF_RANGE.

Automate tracing with Python

Start the target from the first lab and a server listening on loopback. In the same directory as hook.cpp, run the Python client example with the real PID. Trigger one target call when prompted. The script prints two events, removes the probe and detaches. Repeat with watch_events for a cursor-based stream or use record_traces to write a framed recording that the native REPL can replay.

bash
clang-tracer-server --listen 127.0.0.1:50051

The Python client walkthrough includes launch, readiness and shutdown, console examples, and recording. Installed examples in share/clang-tracer/examples/python exercise the Python API end to end.

Trace from the Python console

Use the running target and server from the Python automation example. Run clang-tracer-console --endpoint 127.0.0.1:50051, then enter these commands. Trigger one call while collecting.

bash
attach 12345
symbols --filter "add("
probe validate "add(int, int)" --callback hook.cpp
probe inject "add(int, int)" --callback hook.cpp --print-result
collect 2 --timeout 30
detach
exit

Use the generated Python gRPC stub

Use the generated stub when you need request fields beyond the Python convenience methods. This example lists verified runtime addresses. The mapping token binds the result to the target's current image mapping.

python
from clang_tracer import Client, messages

with Client() as client:
    session = client.attach(12345)
    try:
        reply = client.stub.ListSymbols(
            messages.ListSymbolsRequest(
                session_id=session.id, query="add(", include_addresses=True,
            ),
            timeout=10,
        )
        print(reply)
    finally:
        client.detach(session.id)

Test the Python client

From the repository root, install the development extras and point the native integration tests at a built tracer.

bash
python -m pip install -e './python[dev]'
CLANG_TRACER_NATIVE_BUILD="$PWD/build-rhel" python -m pytest python/tests

For Python module indexing and preparation, see the Python client walkthrough.

C++17 branch Python extensions

Python method RPC Behavior
allocate_memory(session_id, size) AllocateMemory Return the allocation ID, address, and size.
free_memory(session_id, allocation_id) FreeMemory Free the session allocation and report its state.
load_target_library(session_id, path) LoadTargetLibrary Load a trusted library on the target host.
apply_memory_patch(request) ApplyMemoryPatch Submit an executable patch, import redirect, or writable patch with a mapping token and expected bytes.
restore_memory_patch(session_id, patch_id) RestoreMemoryPatch Restore and verify original bytes.
start_page_monitor(request), stop_page_monitor(session_id) StartPageMonitor, StopPageMonitor Arm dedicated pages, then restore them and return first touches.
start_instruction_trace(session_id, address, size, *, tid, mapping_token, **options) StartInstructionTrace Start bounded instruction capture. Options are max_records=256, timeout_seconds=5, registers=False, callback_library="", memory_address=0, memory_size=0, and discover_calls=False.
stop_instruction_trace(session_id) StopInstructionTrace Stop and return original PCs in execution order.

Python validate_probe and inject also accept allow_call_original and trace_exceptions. Both default to false. Other opt-ins can be set in the corresponding Protobuf requests on a compatible server.

python
allocation = client.allocate_memory(session.id, 4096)
try:
    mapping = client.list_memory_mappings(session.id)
    initial = client.read_memory(
        session.id, allocation.address, 1, mapping_token=mapping.mapping_token,
    )
    assert initial == b"\x00"
finally:
    client.free_memory(session.id, allocation.id)

Clang Tracer Python client

The console supports drain capture.db to save and consume retained history, or drain capture.db --listen to keep collecting generated events until Ctrl-C. Use --count N or --timeout SECONDS to bound it. Existing stream filters apply; the default is the selected session, or all sessions when none is selected. record capture.db 100 --sqlite saves without consuming server history.

For larger history, launch with server start --event-history-limit 16384 --context-history-limit 512 --context-history-bytes 67108864 on one line. Defaults remain 4096 events, 128 context events, and 16 MiB of serialized context data.

The API equivalents are Client.drain_traces(path, listen=True, timeout=60) and Client.record_sqlite(path, count=100). read_events() snapshots a bounded batch; acknowledge_events(server_instance_id, sequences) consumes exact stored IDs. SQLite appends and deduplicates full Protobuf payloads. Writes commit before drain acknowledgement; retry a failed drain into the same database. Consumption affects all readers, and overflow can still lose events before storage. See event storage for the schema and failure semantics.

The Python API covers every public Tracer gRPC operation. The interactive console uses that same API, a Lark LALR command grammar, and prompt-toolkit for live command highlighting, completion, history and input validation. All network traffic and recorded traces use binary Protobuf.

Python requires 3.12 or newer. Clients can run on macOS, Linux or Windows and connect to a reachable tracing server. Launching the native server and tracing processes require Linux x86_64 with the existing Clang Tracer installation and attachment permissions. The Python wheel does not bundle the native server or agent. See the native build instructions.

Install and open the console

From the repository root:

sh
python3.12 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/python -m pip install ./python
.venv/bin/clang-tracer-console --endpoint 127.0.0.1:50051
# Equivalent:
.venv/bin/python -m clang_tracer --endpoint 127.0.0.1:50051

CLANG_TRACER_ENDPOINT supplies the endpoint when no explicit endpoint is given. The default is 127.0.0.1:50051, matching the existing C++ client. A server launched by Python is always passed this endpoint explicitly. Native servers launched separately default to a private Unix socket; use the same explicit endpoint on both sides. unix:///absolute/path/control.sock is supported.

On linux-dev, the normal startup needs no server or agent paths:

sh
/home/husam/.local/bin/clang-tracer-console --color always

Then enter server start at the prompt. The installed server is found on PATH, and it automatically finds its installed agent library. --agent is an optional override for a custom installation.

For an isolated Unix endpoint, create its directory directly in the launch command, avoiding an unset shell variable:

sh
/home/husam/.local/bin/clang-tracer-console --color always --endpoint "unix://$(mktemp -d /tmp/clang-tracer-console.XXXXXX)/control.sock"

An empty variable in unix://$TRACER_RUN/control.sock produces unix:///control.sock, which attempts to create a socket under /.
